PREFACE. 

John  de  Grandisson  was  the  Seventeenth  Bishop  of  Exeter. 

He  was  born  at  Ashperton,1  in  Herefordshire,  in  the  year  1292, 
and  was  the  second  son  of  William  de  Grandisson,  who  was,  after- 
wards, summoned  to  Parliament,  as  a  Baron  of  the  Realm,  from 
the  6th  of  February,  1299,  to  the  10th  of  October,  1325.  His 
mother  was  Sibilla,  second  daughter  and  coheiress  of  John  de 
Tregoz,  Lord  of  Ewyas  in  the  same  County  (who  was,  also,  a 
Baron  by  Writ),  and  grand-daughter  of  Juliana  de  Cantilupe,  sister 
of  St.  Thomas  of  Hereford  and  wife  of  Robert  de  Tregoz,  who 
was  slain  in  the  battle  of  Evesham  in   1265. 

At  an  early  age  John  was  sent  to  the  University  of  Paris,  where 
he  had  the  great  advantage,  as  we  learn  from  himself,2  of  studying 
Theology  under  the  direction  of  a  most  eminent  teacher,  James 
Fournier,  who,  on  the  20th  of  December,  1334,  succeeded  John 
XXII  in  the  Papal  Chair.  And  he  must  have  begun  his  career  as 
an  Ecclesiastick  at  a  very  early  age  ;  for  in  the  year  1309,  when  he 
was  only  seventeen  years  old,  he  was  collated  to  the  Prebend  of 
Masham,  in  the  Cathedral  Church  of  York.  He  appears  to  have 
held  this  Benefice  till  the  year  1315,  when  it  was  conferred  on 
William  de  Ayremynne,  afterwards  Bishop  of  Norwich.  On  the 
12th  of  October,  1310,  he  was  collated  by  Archbishop  William 
de  Grenefelde  to  the  Archdeaconry  of  Nottingham,  and  he  held  this 
Office  till  his  Provision  to  the  Bishoprick  of  Exeter.  His  brother 
Thomas,  William  de  Grand isson's  third  son,  was  Prebendary  of 
Heydore,  in  the  Cathedral  Church  of  Lincoln,  and  on  his  death, 
which  occurred  on  the  14th  of  July,  1317,  John  succeeded  him 
by  Papal  Provision.  The  Pope,  also,  provided  him,  in  1322,  to 
the  Prebend  of  Stoke  in  the  same  Church,  in  succession  to  Roger 
de  Northburghe  (who  had  been  provided  to  the  See  of  Coventry 
and  Lichfield) ;  but  he  retained  this  preferment  only  for  a  year. 

As  Chaplain  to  Pope  John  XXII,  he  resided,  for  some  time,  with 
his  Patron  at  Avignon  :  to  wrhom,  as  numerous  references  in  his 
Register  shews,  he  was  greatly  attached.  The  attachment,  indeed, 
was  mutual ;  and,  although  I  have  not  been  able  to  discover  any 
distinct  record  to  that  effect,  I  think  it  can  scarcely  be  doubted 
that  when,  on  the  death  of  Bishop  Stapeldon,  the  Pope  claimed  the 
right  of  Provision  to  the  vacant  See,  it  was  his  intention  to  promote 
his  friend.  He  yielded  the  point,  reluctantly,  when  he  heard  of 
the    Capitular   Election  of   James  de  Berkeley ;   after  whose  brief 

1  pp.  1519,  1555.— See  Note  at  the  end  of  this  Preface.         2  p.  110. 


vi  PREFACE. 

Episcopate,  of  only  a  few  months,  he  provided  Grandisson,  without 
hesitation  or  delay.  He,  evidently,  regarded  him  as  a  rising  man, 
and  was  determined  that  he  should  rise  j  and,  in  the  event,  his 
high  estimate  of  the  young  Clerick's  powers  and  attainments  was, 
certainly,  fully  justified.  We  know,  too,  that  he  had,  already, 
shewn  his  entire  confidence  in  Grandisson's  zeal  and  prudence  by 
associating  him  with  the  Archbishop  of  Vienne  and  the  I'.ishop 
of  Orange  in  an  important  Embassy  for  negotiating  the  Peace 
of  Gascony  ;  a  full  account  of  which  will  be  found  at  the  beginning 
of  the  Register.1 

Bishop  Berkeley  died  on  the  24th  of  June,  1327  ;  and,  although 
the  Dean  and  Chapter  of  Exeter  immediately  obtained  the  Royal 
Licence,  and  elected  John  de  Godeleghe,  one  of  their  number  and 
Dean  of  Wells,  as  his  successor,  the  Pope  was  not  to  be  frustrated 
a  second  time.  He  wrote  to  Grandisson  on  the  10th  of  August, 
in  cordial  terms,  providing  him  to  the  See,  commanding  him  to 
accept  the  onerous  Charge,  and  expressing  a  confident  belief  that 
his  government  of  the  Diocese  would  be  abundantly  fruitful,  and 
that  he  would  merit  not  only  the  approval  and  favour  of  the 
Apostolick  See  but  the  blessing  of  an  eternal  reward.  He  wrote, 
also,  to  the  Ambassadors  on  the  28th,  expressing  his  sorrow  at 
hearing  that  the  negotiations  were  not  proceeding  as  prosperously 
as  he  desired,  and  exhorting  them  not  to  lose  heart,  but,  trusting 
in  the  succour  of  the  Prince  of  Peace,  to  persevere  in  their  good 
work  to  the  end.  They  were  at  St.  Macaire  when  these  letters 
reached  them. 

Grandisson  was  in  his  thirty-sixth  year  when  he  was  consecrated,2 
in  the  Church  of  the  Friars-Preachers  at  Avignon,  on  the  18th 
of  October,  1327,  by  Peter,  Cardinal  Bishop  of  Palestrina  (Prseneste), 
in  the  presence  of  many  Cardinals  and  other  Prelates  and  Nobles. 

He  was  immediately  confronted  with  a  grave  difficulty,  the 
circumstances  of  which  and  his  method  of  dealing  therewith  he 
relates  in  full.3  It  appears  that,  when  he  was  preparing,  with 
characteristick  alacrity,  to  start  for  his  distant  Diocese,  he  was 
informed  that  it  would  be  necessary  fcr  him  to  meet,  forthwith,  a 
heavy  pecuniary  Obligation,  which  he  then  heard  of  for  the  first  time, 
in  which,  it  was  alleged,  the  See  of  Exeter  had  been  involved  in 
the  year  1297  by  the  action  of  Bishop  Thomas  de  Byttone,  and 
subsequently  by  the  action  of  Grandisson's  immediate  Predecessor, 
Bishop  James  de  Berkeley,  who  was  said  to  have  renewed  the 
Obligation  in  his  own  person.  The  amount  was  very  large, — 
ten  thousand  florins  for  services  rendered  in  the  Papal  Camera, 
and  one  thousand  eight  hundred  florins  on  account  of  certain  other 
like  services ;  and   the   Bishop  was  informed   that  he   must   make 

1  pp.  315-321  ;  1212.  *  p  322.  s  p>  323. 


PREFACE.  Vil 

himself  personally  responsible  for  the  payment  of  the  money  !  He 
was  not,  at  that  time,  a  rich  man  by '  any  means  ;  and  he  knew 
that  he  would  have  to  meet,  and  at  once,  the  unavoidable  expenses 
connected  with  taking  possession  of  his  See.  He  was  aware,  too, 
that  the  Episcopal  Manors  were  dilapidated1  and  unproductive, 
having  fallen  a  prey  to  grasping  and  dishonest  men,  who  had 
availed  themselves  of  the  confusions  caused  by  the  murder  of 
Bishop  Stapeldon  and  the  very  brief  Episcopate  of  Bishop  Berkeley, 
to  enrich  themselves  at  the  expense  of  the  Church.  It  was 
impossible  for  him  to  comply  with  the  demand  made  upon  him, 
and  he  resolved  to  resist  it  to  the  uttermost.  He  went  at  once 
to  the  Pope,  his  Friend  and  Patron,  and  begged  him  to  intervene 
on  his  behalf.  But  he  had  to  deal  with  others,  who  were  not 
likely  to  be  lenient.  The  College  of  Cardinals  had  to  be  consulted  ; 
and  he  was  summoned  by  Cardinal  Peter,  the  Treasurer  of  the 
College,  to  appear  before  him  immediately,  and  make  provision 
for  the  payment  of  the  debt.  He  appeared  accordingly,  and  said, 
at  once,  that  he  had  not  got  the  money,  and  could  not  pay ;  but 
he  offered  to  pledge  the  third  part  of  the  taxed  value  of  his  See, 
for  the  gradual  extinction  of  the  debt ;  alleging  that,  by  antient 
custom,  such  an  arrangement  was  permitted  in  the  case  of  those 
who  were  promoted  to  Bishopricks  by  the  Apostolick  See.  But 
the  Cardinal,  Grandisson  says  plainly,  denied  him  justice  herein, 
and  required  him  to  submit  absolutely ;  and  some  of  the  other 
Cardinals,  astounded  at  his  resistance  and  despairing  of  his 
success,  advised  him  to  give  way.  Nothing  daunted,  however, 
the  Bishop  sought,  and  obtained,  a  second  and  private  inter- 
view with  the  Pope,  to  whom  he  related  all  the  details  of  his 
hard  case  ;  submitting  to  him,  also,  a  written  statement  of  the 
more  important  points.  He  boldly  accused  the  Cardinal  of  dealing 
with  him  harshly  and  in  violation  of  his  own  conscience,  and  declared 
that  he  could  prove  that  the  demand  rested  on  no  solid  foundation, 
as  his  Predecessors  had  not  been  promoted  by  the  Apostolick  See, 
but  had  been  elected  by  the  Dean  and  Chapter,  and  confirmed  and 
consecrated  by  the  Primate.  The  Pope  took  his  part,  commanding 
Cardinal  Peter  and  the  Archbishop  of  Aries  to  inspect  the  Registers 
of  the  "  Camera,"  and  to  settle  the  matter  amicably  and  in  accord- 
ance with  justice.  Armed  with  this  Mandate,  Grandisson  again 
appeared  before  the  Cardinals,  bringing  with  him  ten  trustworthy 
witnesses  to  prove  the  truth  of  his  allegations ;  but  he  failed  to 
secure  an  impartial  hearing.  The  Cardinals  quietly  ignored  the 
important  point  as  to  his  Predecessors  having  been  saddled  with 
these  charges  unlawfully,  seeing  that  they  had  been  elected  by  the 
Dean  and  Chapter,    and   not  promoted  by  Papal  Provision ;    they 

1  p.  172. 


Vlll  PREFACE. 


were  afraid,  the  Bishop  says  plainly,  that  the  result  of  an  honest 
examination  of  the  records  would  be  to  convict  them  of  falsehood  ; 
so  they  examined  the  witnesses  only  as  to  the  value  of  the  revenues 
of  the  See,   and   subsequently  Cardinal   Peter,    in   the   absence   of 
his   colleague,    stated,    in   the    Consistory,   "  with  but  little  regard 
to    truth,"    that    they    were    found    to    be    worth    three    thousand 
marks.       Whereupon    the    Pope    and    the    Cardinals,    agreeing    to 
adopt  ihe  unjust1  proposals  of  Cardinal  Peter,  taxed  the  Bishop  and 
the  See  of  Exeter  in  the  sum  of  five  thousand  florins,  computed  at 
the  rate  of  five  florins  per  mark  ;   and  on  the  same  day,  the  9th  of 
December,  they  required  him  to  bind  himself,  on  oath,2  to  pay  the 
money    (being    the    third    part    of    the    alleged    Taxation-value)    in 
moieties,   the  first  on  the   27th  of  March   next  following,   and  the 
second  on  that  day  year ;   failing  which  he  was  to  return,   within 
four  months,  to  the  Curia,  and  remain  there  till  the  money  should 
be  paid  in  full.      To  this  settlement  he  reluctantly  bound  himself 
and  his  Successors,   on  the  security  of   the  whole  of  the    revenues 
of    his    See,     under    pain    of    Excommunication,    Suspension,    and 
Interdict,  and  Suspension   from  his   Pontifical   Office,   if  he  should 
fail    therein.      He    had    done    his   best   for   his    Diocese,    and    not 
without  a  large  measure  of  success  ;  for  the  unjustifiable  demand  on 
account    of    the   alleged    liabilities   of   his    Predecessors    had    been 
quietly  dropped.    The  figures  of  the  Taxation  had  been  manipulated, 
and  an  unjustly  heavy  burden  had,  by  that  means,  been  laid  upon 
himself  personally  ;  but  he  had  delivered  his  Church  from  a  fictitious 
accumulated   debt,  and  this,  he  tells  us,  was  his  chief  care.     His 
personal  inconvenience  was,  in  comparison,  a  trifling  matter ;  and  he 
content  to  suffer.      But,  as  we  shall   see  later  on,   the  cruel 
exaction  to  which  he  was  forced  to  submit  was  the  cause  of  much 
trouble  and  anxiety,  and  must  have  hampered  him  seriously  in  his 
w<-rk.     For  the  moment,  however,  he  dismissed  the  whole  painful 
subject  from  his  mind  ;  and,  having  obtained  divers  Privileges  and 
Indnltfl  fr.u:  the  Pope,  copies  of  which  he  caused  to  be  entered  in 
m,    lie  set  out  for  England  on  the  23rd  of  December.4 
The    weather    was    most   unpropitious,    the   roads  being  blocked 
with  snow  ;  and  it  was  not  until  the  3rd  of  February,  1327-8,  that 
U  able  to  reach  the  sea-shore  and  cross  to  Dover.      On  the  5th 
he  entered  Canterbury/'  where  he  was  received  with  the  customary 
Bolemnitiei  by  the  Prior  and  Chapter;  to  whom  he  took  the  Oath  of 
Canonical  Obedience,  the  See  being  void  by  the  death  of  Archbishop 
Reynold!   on    the    16th   of    November,    1327.       On    the   following

King  and  the  Council  were  considering  their  purport.  When  he 
was  recalled,  the  Archbishop  of  York  explained  to  him,  on  the 
King's  behalf,  the  custom  of  the  Realm  in  all  such  cases ;  telling 
him  that  he  was  bound  to  renounce  all  words  that  might  be 
prejudicial  to  the  rights  of  the  King  and  of  the  Realm,  submitting 
himself  to  the  King's  grace  therein.  The  Bishop  replied  that, 
saving  his  Profession  made  in  the  Roman  Court,  the  rights  of 
the  Apostolick  See,  his  own  Episcopal  Order,  and  the  rights  and 
dignity  of  his  Church  of  Exeter,  he  was  prepared  to  renounce 
all  such  words,  in  such  manner  as  all  Prelates  promoted  by  the 
Pope  had  been  accustomed  to  do,  submitting  himself  absolutely 
to  the  King's  grace  as  to  the  Temporalities  of  his  See.  Whereupon, 
the  Temporalities  having  been,  by  word  of  mouth,  restored,  he 
did    fealty2   to  the   King,  according  to  the  custom  of  the  Realm ;

2  fecit  Fidelitatem  (fealty),  not  homagium.  In  Bishop  Stapeldon's  "  Itinerary  "

"Homage"  was  first  demanded  by  Henry  VIII,  after  he  had  assumed  the 
Supreme  Headship  of  the  Church  of  England.  It  is  true  that  Bishops  some- 
times did  homage  to  the  King  before  Henry's  time,  but  not  for  the  Temporalities 
of  their  Sees  ;  only  when  they  held  lands  of  the  King  in  capite,  in  their  own 
right,  as  if  they  were  laymen. 

It  may  be  well,  also,  to  explain  the  Act  of  Renunciation  mentioned  in  the 
Text,  which  presents  an  obvious  difficulty.  It  arose  in  this  manner.  "When 
Pope  Clement  V  appointed  Walter  de  Jorze  to  the  Archbishoprick  of  Armagh,

him  the  Cure  and  Administration  in  Spirituals  and  Temporals.  _  The  King's 
advisers,  who  were  all  Ecclesiasticks,  took  exception  to  the  Pope's  including  the 
Temporalities,  as  the  Publick  Document  drawn  up  on  the  occasion  sets  forth, — 
"  Perpendit  Dominus  Rex  memoratus  ipsas  Literas  Apostolicassibi  et  juri  suo

On  the  16th  of  May,  having  obtained  permission  from  the 
King,2  he  left  Northampton,  reaching  Oxford  on  the  17th  and 
[his  Manor  of  Faringdon,  Hants,  on  the  21st.  There  he  held  an 
Ordination,  on  the  28th,  by  Commission  from  the  Bishop  of  the 
Diocese;  and  on  the  30th  he  started  for  Exeter,  resting  at  Win- 
chester on  his  way.  We  find  him  at  Salisbury  on  the  2nd  of 
June  and  at  Shaftesbury  on  the  4th  ;  and  on  the  9th  he 
entered  his  Diocese,  putting  up  for  the  night  at  Honiton  Rectory.3 
Proceeding  to  his  Manor  of  Clyst,  near  Exeter,  on  the  following 
:day,  he  was  met  on  the  road  by  the  Dean,  the  Treasurer,  the 
Subdean,  and  many  of  the  Canons,  who  conducted  him,  with  all 
due  honour,  to  his  House,  where  all  partook  of  his  hospitality. 
He  remained  at  Clyst  till  the  end  of  September,  engaged  chiefly 
in  the  inspection  of  his  Manors  in  that  neighbourhood, — Chud- 
leigh,  Paignton,  and  Crediton,  and  spending  many  days  in  his 
Palace  at  Exeter.  On  the  22nd  of  August  (the  Octave  of  the

losses  by  his  self-sacrificing  labours  on  behalf  of  his  Church,  and 
the  consequent  delay  in  leaving  Avignon  which  had  proved  so 
costly  to  him,  and  they  were  well  disposed  to  help  him;  but  they 
wished  him  to  meet  them  in  Chapter  and  hear  what  each  of

they  hoped,  as  there  could  be  no  great  danger  in  delay,  that  he 
would  not  take  offence.  The  Religious  Houses  had,  as  yet,  taken 
no  notice  of  the  Mandate  of  the  15th  of  July ;  and  on  the  4th  of 
August  the  Bishop  wrote  to  them,  in  terms  of  reproach,  complaining 
that,  whereas  the  Dean  and  Chapter  and  the  Incumbents  of  the 
Diocese,  had  promptly  promised  assistance,  they  had  failed  to  justify 
his  confident  belief  that  they,  of  all  others,  would  be  the  most

all  the  Houses,  in  charge  of  John  de  Nassington,  the  Chancellor

of  the  acquittances  are  duly  recorded  in  his  Register.1  From  one 
of  his  relatives,  his  cousin,  Lord  Courtenay,  of  Okehampton,  he 
received,  instead  of  the  help  and  sympathy  which  he  expected, 
an  almost  savage  rebuff.  He  wrote  to  his  cousin  on  the  24th  of 
January,  1328-9,  telling  him  of  the  debt  to  the  Court  of  Rome, 
the  time  for  the  full  payment  of  which  was  close  at  hand,  and 
begging  him  to  lend  him  £200  for  a  year,  on  any  security  he 
might  be  pleased  to  name.2  The  bearer  was  to  wait  for  an  answer, 
and  a  very  unsatisfactory  answer  it  proved  to  be.3  The  writer 
informed  the  Bishop  that,  having  been  put  to  great  expense  lately 
on  the  marriage  of  his  daughter  Elizabeth,  and  in  connection  with 
the  settlement  of  the  affairs  of  his  mother,  recently  deceased,  he 
had  no  money  to  spare ;  and  as  to  lending  money  to  Bishops  of 
Exeter,  he  had  assisted  the  late  Bishop,  James  de  Berkeley,  and 
saw  very  little  prospect  of  the  repayment  of  the  loan.  It  would 
have  been  well  if  he  had  laid  aside  his  pen  at  this  point ;  but  he 
was  angry  with  Grandisson,  and  apparently  jealous  of  him  as  a 
formidable  rival  amongst  the  magnates  of  the  County.  Your 
Clergy,  he  wrote,  are  complaining  of  you,  all  through  your  Diocese, 
on  account  of  the  heavy  demand  which  you  have  made  on  their 
purses,  the  like  of  which  no  Bishop  has  ever  attempted  before. 
With  a  callous  indifference  to  the  hardness  of  the  Bishop's  position, 
he  advised  him  to  live  within  his  means,  and  to  render  to  all, 
both  rich  and  poor,  their  due ;  taking  care  not  to  make  himself 
too  conspicuous,  but  devoting  himself,  as  a  Bishop  ought,  to 
comforting  the  souls  of  his  people,  ready  to  listen  to  all  and  not 
ready  to  give  credence  to  every  idle  tale,  but  like  a  just  judge, 
slo  wto  pronounce  judgement  without  taking  counsel  with  others. 
It  was  not  likely  that  a  man  of  Grandisson's  temperament,  whose 
whole  soul  was  devoted  to  the  fulfilment  of  his  duty,  with  a 
fervent  desire  to  magnify  not  himself  but  his  Office,  would  submit 
quietly  to  such  a  gratuitous  onslaught  as  this;  and  he  answered 
Courtenay's  letter  on  the  27th,  telling  him  his  mind  without 
restraint.4  As  to  the  marriage  of  his  daughter,  and  the  business 
connected  with  his  mother's  Will,  he  sympathized  with  him  entirely, 
and  was  ready  to  accept  his  excuses  for  his  inability  to  help  his 
Spiritual  Father.  But  the  charges  brought  against  him  so  recklessly 
compelled  him  to  speak  plainly  in  self-defence.  It  was  true  that 
he  had  appealed  to  the  whole  Diocese  for  money,  and  that  the 
response  had  been  most  generous.  And  it  was  possible  that  he 
was  the  first  Bishop  to  do  such  a  thing.  But  his  cousin  ought 
to  be  aware,  for  the  facts  were  well  known  to  all  men,  that  never 
before  had  a  Bishop,  on  entering  his  Diocese,  found  it  so  utterly 
wrecked  and  so  heavily  burdened  with  debt  as  he  had  found   the

the  writer  was  wise  in  his  own  conceits,  and  justified  the  French

While  all  this  troublesome  and  disturbing  business  was  in  hand, 
the  Bishop  was  diligently  engaged  in  the  general  work  of  his 
Diocese.      We  must  retrace  our  steps,  that  we  may  follow  him. 

Remaining,  as  we  have  seen,  at  Clyst,  and  in  the  immediate 
neighbourhood,  till  the  30th  of  September,  1328,  he  proceeded, 
on  the  2nd  of  October,  to  visit  several  of  the  Religious  Houses  in 
Devonshire.  He  reached  Buck  fast  Abbey1  on  that  day,  and  on 
the  3rd  we  find  him  at  Modbury  Priory,2  on  the  4th  at  Plympton,2

where  he  spent  three  days  ;  crossing  the  Tamar  to  Stoke-Climsland 
in  Cornwall  on  the  10th.4  From  thence  he  went,  on  the  same  day, 
to  Lawhitton,  his  Manor  near  Launceston,  where  he  remained  for 
a  few  hours  only5;  for  on  the  11th  we  find  him  at  St.  Ive,  where 
he  had  to  deal  with  a  case  of  divorce,  and  with  the  recalcitrant 
parishioners  of  Liskeard  who  had  refused  to  pay  the  procurations 
due  on  the  Reconciliation  of  their  Churchyard  early  in  August.6 
On  the  13th  he  commenced,  in  earnest,  his  first  Visitation  of 
Cornwall,  mainly  with  a  view  to  inspecting  the  Episcopal  estates 
and  property,  beginning  at  Launceston  {see  p.  95)7;  from  whence  he 
passed,  by  way  of  Southill,8  to  his  Manor  of  Cotynbeke,  close  to 
St  German's  Priory.  He  spent  about  a  week  there,  engaged,  of 
course,  in  dealing  with  the  dilapidations  and  making  arrangements 
for  the  future  well-being  of  the  estate.  Peculation  had  been  going 
on  there  on  a  large  scale ;  and  Stephen  and  Baldwin  Crabbe,  John  de 
Dessere,  and  John  le  Hyne,  of  Devyoke,  who  refused  to  make 
restitution,  were  excommunicated.  Stephen  Crabbe  was  absolved,  on 
his  submission,  on  the  26th.9  On  the  22nd  we  find  him  at  Men-

the  Bishop  solemnly  excommunicated  the  offenders,  the  chief  of  whom

his  jurisdiction,  confessing  that  they  had  sinned  in  siding  with  the 
rebels,  and,  on  taking  an  oath  never  again  to  rebel  against  the

payment  of  a  hundred  marks,  he  was  absolved.3 

The  Bishop  remained  at  Exeter,  and  in  the  neighbourhood,  till  the 
beginning  of  March,  1329-30,  engaged  chiefly,  no  doubt,  in  the  great 
work  of  rebuilding  the  Nave  of  the  Cathedral,  which  now  demanded 
his  earnest  attention  and  care.  The  entries  in  his  Register  during 
this  period  are  concerned  with  the  ordinary  routine  of  Diocesan 
work,  with  a  few  noteworthy  exceptions. 

On  the  18th  of  December,  1328,  being  the  Sunday  next  after  the 
Feast  of  St.  Lucy  the  Virgin,  he  dedicated  the  High  Altar  in  the 
Choir  of  the  Cathedral  Church — Stapeldon's  magnificent  "Silver 
Altar" — in  honour  of  the  most  Blessed  and  ever  Virgin  Mother  of  God, 
and  of  the  Blessed  Apostles  Peter  and  Paul,  commending  it  to  their 
guardianship,  and  granting  an  Indulgence  of  forty  days  to  all  who, 
being  in  a  state  of  grace,  assisted  at  the  ceremony.4 

To  this  period  must  be  attributed  the  very  interesting  undated 
Letter  to  the  Pope,  his  patron,5  which  I  have  already  quoted  for 
the  account  of  his  Enthronization,  and  the  dispute  with  the  Arch- 
deacon of  Canterbury,  proceedings  which,  he  says,  interfered  with 
the  scheme  of  work  which  he  had  laid  down,  and  compelled  him 
to  postpone  for  a  time  his  General  Visitation  of  the  Diocese.  He 
found  it  necessary,  he  wrote,  to  go  into  Cornwall  as  soon  as 
possible,  in  order  to  visit  and  inspect  his  Manors  in  that  County, 
a  journey  the  details  of  which  I  have  set  forth  above.  And  he  gives 
the  Pope  a  curious  account  of  his  first  impressions  of  the  County 
and  its  inhabitants.  He  describes  it  as  a  foreign  land,  adjoining 
England  only  along  its  Eastern  boundary,  being  surrounded  on 
every  other  side  by  the  sea,  which  divides  it  from  Wales  and 
Ireland  on  the  North.  On  the  South,  he  adds,  it  looks  towards 
Gascony  and  Britanny  ;    and  the  Cornish  speak  the  language   of 

1  p.  426.  2  p.  1267.  3  p.  427.  4  p.  434.  5  p.  95. 


xx  PREFACE. 

those  Lands.  In  the  far  West,  beyond  St.  Michael's  Mount,  it 
overlooks  the  boundless  expanse  of  the  Ocean.  His  Diocese,  he 
found,  included  a  group  of  islands— the  Scilly  Isles— on  which 
his  Predecessors  had  never  set  foot,  contenting  themselves  with 
sending  certain  Brothers  thither,  to  look  after  the  islanders,1  but 
he  had  not  himself,  as  yet,  done  even  so  much  as  that.  As  for 
his  Manors*2  he  had  found  them  ruinated  and  stript  bare  ;  the 
land  was  sterile  and  uncultivated  ;  the  very  cattle  had  been 
taken  away,  and  nothing  remained  to  sow  the  fields  withal.  A 
few  paltry  rents  had  come  in  ;  but  he  was  obliged  to  buy  the 
very  necessaries  of  life,  and  there  was  an  enormous  expense 
before  him  for  repairs.  It  grieved  him  exceedingly  to  be  com- 
pelled to  write  in  such  a  strain  as  this,  and  as  if  he  had  no 
gratitude,  to  one  who  had  treated  him  generously,  far  beyond 
his  deserts. 

He  wrote,  at  the  same  time,  to  certain  Cardinals,3  his  friends, 
telling  them  that,  on  account  of  his  isolated  position,  they  would 
probably  hear  little  of  him,  or  he  of  them,  for  a  long  time  to 
come.  I  am  not  only  set  down,  he  tells  them,  in  the  ends  of 
the  earth,  but  in  the  very  end  of  the  ends  thereof.  My  Diocese, 
which  embraces  Devon  and  Cornwall,  is  separated  from  all  the 
rest  of  England,  and,  except  on  one  side  only,  surrounded  by 
seas  so  tempestuous  that  they  can  scarcely  be  called  navigable. 
The  people  of  Cornwall  speak  in  a  tongue  which  is  unknown  to 
the  English,  and  only  known  to  Bretons.  The  wines  of  Gascony, 
indeed,  find  their  way  thither,  and  flesh-meat  is  fairly  abundant ; 
but  there  is  scarcely  any  corn  in  the  County,  or  anything  else 
for  the  use  of  mortals.  To  his  friend,  Cardinal  Orsini,4  who 
had  written  to  ask  how  he  fared,  he  writes  in  a  more  hopeful 
strain.  He  was  grateful  to  find  that,  although  he  was  removed 
bo  far  out  of  sight,  he  had  not  been  altogether  forgotten.  He 
was  well  and  happy  ;  for  there  was  at  least  this  comfort  in  his 
isolation,  that  he  was  far  removed  from  the  pressure  of  the 
populace  ;  and,  if  he  was  unable  to  take  his  place  among  the 
Nobles  of  the  Land,  he  was,  at  any  rate,  free  from  their  incursions, 
and  could  not  be  shaken  by  the  storms  of  life  ;  he  was  spending 
his  days,  as  it  were,  in  the  bosom  of  Abraham. 

His  position,  however,  was  one  of  great  and  increasing  difficulty  ; 
and  we  find  him  writing  to  the  Pope5  on  the  22nd  of  February, 
1328-9,  to  tell  him  that,  if  he  could  have  foreseen  what  he  had 
:  lure  daily  at  the  hands  of  the  wonderful  people  who  inhabited 
this  remote  corner  of  the  world,  he  would  have  entreated  that 
someone  more  fitted  for  such  work  than  he  could  ever  be  might 
have  been  sent  to  them, — words  which    must   have  been   written 


1  p.  3.07.  ■  p.  862;  •  p.  97.         4  pp.  101,  310  (note).         5  p.  102. 


preface,  xxi 

in  a  moment  of  despair;  but  he  was  a  man  of  dauntless  spirit,  as, 
indeed,  his  next  words  shew, — "  nevertheless,  I  am  striving,  God 
approving  and  you  commanding,  to  do  my  duty,  according  to  my 
poor  powers  and  slender  attainments,  relying  on  your  prayers 
and  timely  succour."  And,  in  the  end,  he  was  not  without  his 
reward. 

He  refers,  also,  in  these  Letters,  to  other  matters  of  great 
importance,  which  demanded  his  immediate  attention.  In  the  first 
of  them1  he  tells  the  Pope  that  his  Cathedral  Church  was  in 
course  of  rebuilding,  and  had  been  about  half  finished  by  his 
Predecessors.  He  had  recently  dedicated  the  High  Altar,  and  he 
longed  to  provide  for  the  resumption  of  the  work  ;  for  it  was 
an  exceedingly  beautiful  Church,  and  destined  to  exceed  in  glory 
all  other  Churches  of  its  class  in  England  or  in  France,  if  only 
it  could  be  completed  and  brought  to  perfection.  Alas,  a  rich 
Bishop  had  been  succeeded  by  one  who  was  poverty-stricken  ; 
and  he  did  not  see  how  anything  could  be  done  for  a  long  time  to 
come,  unless  the  Pope  could  help  him.  He  wrote  to  the  same  effect 
to  the  Cardinals.2  Nevertheless,  with  his  usual  energy,  he  set  to 
work  almost  immediately  ;  and,  following  loyally  and  wisely  the 
lines  which  had  been  laid  down  by  Bishops  Byttone  and  Quivil, 
on  which  Bishop  Stapeldon,  also,  had  been  prepared  to  work  (thus 
securing  a  marvellous  unity  of  design  throughout  the  Church, 
scarcely  affected  at  all  by  the  changes  of  style  which  had  taken 
place  everywhere  in  the  interval),  he  was  able  to  complete  the 
magnificent  Nave,  as  we  see  it  to-day,  more  than  ten  years  before 
his  death.  Unfortunately,  we  know  very  little  as  to  the  details 
of  the  progress  of  the  work ;  for  the  records  are  all  but  silent, 
and  even  the  famous  Fabrick-Rolls  fail  us :  they  are  nearly  con- 
tinuous, indeed,  throughout  the  period ;  but  the  details,  which 
we  have  found  so  valuable  hitherto,  are  no  longer  given,  and  we 
find  little  more  than  a  record  of  the  weekly  payments  made  to 
the  workmen.  The  lack  of  funds  did  not  turn  out  to  be  so 
serious  a  matter  as  Grandisson  had  anticipated  ;  money  soon  came 
in  from  several  quarters,  and  especially  from  the  Executors  of 
Bishop  Stapeldon.  He  saw  his  way  to  begin  ;  but  he  was  disturbed 
by  the  fear  that  he  might  not  be  able,  miserably  poor  as  he  then 
was,  to  finish  so  vast  a  work.  There  still  remained  in  hand  the 
greater  part  of  Stapeldon's  final  gift  of  a  thousand  marks,  and  a  large 
quantity  of  marble  and  other  stone,  as  well  as  timber  in  abundance, 
which  that  Bishop  was  engaged  in  accumulating  when  he  was  so 
cruelly  murdered.  Much  of  it  had  not  been  paid  for,  but  remained 
as  a  charge  on  the  available  funds;  and  there  were  other  arrears, 
for  £92  3s.  had  to  be  paid,  in  1328,  to  William  Canon,  of  Corfe,  for

marble.  Grandissou,  himself,  gave,  or  collected  from  his  friends,

It  must  be  remembered  that  the  Norman  Nave,  begun  by  Bishop 
"William  de  Warelwast  and  completed  by  Bishop  Henry  Marshall 
before  1206,  was  still  standing,  with  the  exception  of  the  eastern 
bay,  which  had  been  rebuilt  by  Bishop  Quivil.  It  was  at  this  point 
that  Grandissou  took  up  the  work  ;  and  it  made  such  rapid  progress 
that  by  the  end  of  1334  the  great  piers  of  the  Nave  arcades  were 
in  their  places.  We  learn  this  fact  from  an  important  memorandum 
attached  to  the  Fabrick-Roll  of  1331-2,  the  date  (21  Jan.)  of  the 
first  reckoning  for  the  work  in  question  with  William  Canon,  but 
dated  9  September,  1334,  on  the  completion  of  the  transaction. 
The  contract  was  for  eleven  and  a  half  great  columns,  to  wit,  the 
ten  columns  west  of  Quivil's  work,  and  the  two  responds— equal 
to  one  column— at  the  West  End ;  the  half-column  being,  as  Arch- 
deacon Freeman  has  shown,  divisible  in  like  manner  for  two  quarter- 
columns  required  for  the  aisles,  where  we  see  them  to-day,  at  the 
north-east  and  south-east  angles.  The  cost  of  the  whole  was 
£124  is.  There  were,  also,  included  sixty  groups  of  small  columns 
for  the  triforia,  and  twenty-nine  columns  for  the  cloister,  bringing 
the  total  cost  of  this  work  up  to  £140  5s.  9d.,  or  nearly  £3,000 
of  our  money.  Canon  was  bound  to  repair  all  damaged  stones 
and  make  good  all  defects,  and  he  had  done  so.  The  arches,  of 
course,  had  not  then  been  built.  It  has  been  supposed  by  some 
antiquaries,  and  notably  by  Archdeacon  Freeman,  that  Grandissou 
reconstructed  the  Norman  Nave,  without  taking  it  down;  but  I  am 
bold  to  say  that  I  cannot  accept  this  theory.  The  Norman  work 
at  Winchester,  and  elsewhere,  lent  itself  easily  to  reconstruction 
in  the  "  Perpendicular  "  style ;  but  it  is  impossible  to  believe  that 
Grandisson's  "Decorated"  work  is  the  result  of  a  similar  trans- 
formation. He  retained  as  much  as  he  could  of  the  external  walls, 
the  walls,  I  mean,  of  the  aisles1  and  the  west  wall ;  but  by  the  time 
he  had  substituted  for  the  narrow  Norman  windows  the  large  windows 
which  we  see  to-day,  there  would  not  have  been  very  much  of  those 
walls  left.     Of  course,  the  arches  of  the  Nave  arcades  cannot  be

regarded  as  reconstructions  of  the  old  arches,  which  must  have 
been  on  entirely  different  lines,  being  semi-circular  and  narrower, 
and  springing  of  necessity  from  a  higher  level  than  the  present 
arches.  The  Norman  roof  may  have  been  of  wood ;  but  if  it  was 
vaulted  in  stone,  it  must  have  been  taken  down ;  for  the  present 
magnificent  vaulting,  obviously  a  new  and  complete  work  from 
end  to  end,  cannot  be  the  result  of  a  transformation  of  a  roof 
built  by  Marshall.  Nothing  would  remain  after  the  rebuilding 
of  the  arcades  and  the  removal  of  the  Norman  vaulting  except 
such  fragments  of  the  clerestory  walls  as  might  have  been 
spared  when  the  present  great  windows  were  inserted,  and  there 
could  have  been  no  such  "  fragments  "  even  ;  for  there  is  no 
triforium  in  the  ordinary  sense  of  the  word.  There  is  a  quasi- 
triforium,  indeed,  but  there  is  no  passage  behind  it.  The 
passage  is  above  it,  carried  through  the  said  "fragments,"  and 
protected  by  a  beautiful  pierced  parapet  where  it  crosses  the 
clerestory  windows.  This  fact  alone  suffices  to  demolish  the 
reconstruction  theory.  I  may  mention  here  that  the  great 
architect  sloped  the  roofs  of  his  aisles  inwards,  instead  of  outwards 
as  was  usual,  in  order  that  his  clerestory  windows  might  fall  in 
with  this  necessary  arrangement.  From  every  point  of  view, 
therefore,  I  cannot  but  regard  the  reconstruction  theory  as 
absolutely  incredible.  Grandisson  would  not  have  wasted  money 
and  risked  the  lives  of  the  workmen  on  a  scheme  which  would 
not  have  been  worth  the  cost  and  trouble  even  if  it  had  been 
practicable.  That  he  never  even  made  the  attempt  is  proved 
by  the  fact  that  his  bays  do  not  correspond  with  the  bays  of 
the  structure   which  he    superseded. 

It  was  supposed,  for  a  long  time,  that  Grandisson  lengthened 
the  Church  considerably  at  the  west  end,  a  theory  which  may, 
probably,  be  traced  to  a  statement  by  Leland,  who  wrote,1  about 
two  centuries  after  these  great  works  were  carried  out,  to  the 
effect  that  the  Bishop  "enlargid  the  west  part  of  the  Chirche, 
making  vij  archis,  wher  afore  the  plot  was  made  out  of  v." 
Evidently,  as  Archdeacon  Freeman  points  out,  the  historian  had 
seen  the  contract  with  William  Canon,  and  had  misunderstood  it : 
he  did  not  know  that  Quivil  rebuilt  the  eastern  bay,  which  included 
four  piers.  Dr.  Oliver,  in  his  History  of  the  Cathedral,2  falls  into 
the  same  error.  But  the  Fabrick-Roll  of  1329-30  shews  that  one 
of  the  first  things  that  Grandisson  did  was  to  rebuild  the  Chapel 
of  St.  Radegunde  "juxta  fontem,"  which  he  designed  for  his  own 
last  resting-place ;  and  it  is  actually  in  part  contained  within  the 
west  wall.  This  was  evidence  enough  for  Archdeacon  Freeman ; 
and  that  he  was  fully  justified  in  his  contention  has,  quite  recently,

work ;  but  above  it,  and  below  it,  and  on  both  sides  of  it,  the 
substance  of  the  wall  is  of  Salcombe  stone.  The  Bishop's  work

it  once  projected  into  the  Cathedral-Yard.  On  the  left  hand  of

it  a  mass  of  masonry  was  built  by  way  of  an  effectual  buttress,

it  is  worthy  of  the  building  which  it  supports  and  adorns."

repeated  with  advantage  in  more  recent  years ;  and  the  windows, 
which  had  been  glazed  with  plain  glass  were  painted  with  a  prepara-

the  Nave  was  completed  and  ready  to  be  restored  to  its  sacred  use.

and  other  muniments  of  the  Church.  He  was  doing  all  he  could  to 
meet  the  mischief,  and  did  not  despair  of  success  if  the  Pope  wTould 
help  him.    He  was  anxious,  also,  about  his  rights  in  connection  with

the  Collegiate  Church  of  Bosham — one  of  the  King's  Free  Chapels, — 
of  which  the  Bishops  of  Exeter  were  Ordinaries  ex  officio.  There 
had  been  much  trouble,  in  times  past,  between  his  Predecessors 
and  the  Bishops  of  Chichester,  who  were  unwilling  to  recognize 
this  imperium  in  imperio  ;  and,  as  the  controversy  remained 
unsettled,  he  earnestly  intreated  the  Pope  to  intervene.1  Again, 
while  he  was  "  labouring,  with  all  zeal,  in  the  Vineyard  of  the  Lord 
of  Hosts,  in  his  remote  corner  of  England,"  the  Court  of  Can- 
terbury was  still  pursuing  him  with  its  Inhibitions,  Citations,  and 
Plaints,  based  on  certain  "  musty,  uncertain,  and  doubtful  cus- 
toms," contrary  to  all  law,  so  that  it  was  out  of  his  power  to 
devote  himself  as  he  desired  to  the  care  of  the  churches  and  the 
salvation  of  souls  ;  and  he  begged  the  Pope  to  protect  him. 
And  there  was  another  matter2  as  to  which  he  hesitated  to  trouble 
the  Pope,  though  he  felt  strongly  that  he  was  bound  to  reveal 
the  diseases  which  affected  his  flock  to  their  chief  Pastor  and 
Physician.  "  I  speak  the  truth  in  God,  I  lie  not,"  he  wrote, 
referring  to  Robert  Bonus,  Abbat  of  Tavistock  ;  "  but  this  man, 
a  native  of  Aquitaine,  promoted  by  your  Holiness3  through  the 
deceit  of  others,  has  shewn  himself  to  be  utterly  irreligious  and 
a  despiser  of  the  worship  of  God  from  the  first  day  of  his  arrival 
amongst  us ;  worrying  his  Monks  with  base  charges  and  insults, 
and  provoking  the  Nobles  and  all  others  in  his  neighbourhood, 
so  that  he  is  hated  of  all  men,  and  will  bring  destruction  to  his 
House,  and  to  himself  also,  through  his  furious  madness,  if  he 
cannot  be  effectually  checked."  The  Bishop,  out  of  consideration 
for  the  Pope  (as  Patron  of  Bonus),  and  "  de  Peragrua,  de  Garvo, 
and  de  Mota,"  who  had  recommended  him,4  had  dealt  very  gently 
with  the  offender,  resorting  at  first  even  to  blandishments,  and 
then  visiting  him  in  an  informal  way,  and  trying  to  mediate 
between  him  and  his  Convent ;  finally  threatening  him  with  the 
vengeance  of  God  and  of  the  Pope  ;  but  all,  so  far,  without  any 
result.  "  Nevertheless,"  the  Bishop  adds,  "  I  will  do  what  in 
me  lies  to  bring  him  to  a  better  mind,  as  long  as  it  may  be 
found  possible  to  tolerate  such  a  man."  He  refers  also  in  the 
same  letter  to  the  heavy  burden  of  debt  which  had  been  laid 
upon  him  by  the  Curia,4  expressing  a  hope  that,  with  the  help 
of  his  Flock,  he  might  be  able  to  pay  it  off  by  the  appointed 
time.  And  he  wrote  to  William  de  Laudun,  now  Archbishop  of 
Toulouse,  asking  him  to  bear  with  him  if  he  postponed,  till  the 
Feast  of  the  Assumption,  repayment  of  the  500  florins  kindly 
lent  to  him,  in  his  distress,  at  Avignon.5

destined  to  be  his  head-quarters  throughout  his  Episcopate),  from 
November,  1328,  till  the  beginning  of  March,  1329-30.  He  visited 
the  Cathedral,  as  we  have  seen,  after  his  Enthronization ;  and 
that  it  was  far  from  being  a  merely  formal  Visitation  is  shewn 
by  the  "  Decrees "  which  he  sent  to  the  Dean  and  Chapter  on 
the  19th  of  December.  He  had  discovered  that  the  confusion 
consequent  on  the  death  of  Bishop  Stapeldon,  which  had  greviously 
affected  the  Diocese  at  large,  had  found  its  way  into  the  Mother- 
Church  itself.1  There  had  been  a  serious  relaxation  of  discipline. 
Some  of  the  Canons,  greedy  of  filthy  lucre,  could  only  be  regarded  as 
mercenaries, — he  was  tempted  to  call  them  robbers.  Their  so-called 
lence  was  a  mere  farce  ;  for  they  spent  their  time  on  their 
private  business,  or  in  amusing  themselves  in  the  chace;  and 
whrii,  at  rare  intervals  and  reluctantly,  they  took  their  places  in  the 
Choir,  they  could  not  behave  themselves  even  there  with  decency, 
but  indulged  in  idle  chattering,  the  Canons  and  the  inferior 
Ministers  alike,  not  shewing  the  least  reverence  and  devotion 
even  during  the  celebration  of  the  Holy  Mysteries,  and  rattling 
through  the  Canonical  Hours,  talking  to  one  another  the  while, 
and  frequently  going  out  of  the  Church  before  the  Office  was 
finished.  Moreover,  they  wholly  neglected  the  hospitality  to  which 
they  were  bound,  seeking  their  own,  not  the  things  which  are 
Jesus  Christ's  ;  claiming  their  share,  as  if  they  had  earned  it, 
in  the  daily  distribution  and  the  quarterly  division,  thus  defrauding 
their  Brethren,  and  even  the  very  boys  of  the  Choir,  of  their 
due.  And  so,  as  the  Bishop  adds,  the  worship  of  God,  the 
devotion  of  the  people,  and  the  honour  of  the  Church  were  being 
destroyed,  and  a  grievous  scandal  occasioned.  He  told  them  that 
it  was  impossible  for  him  to  pass  over  in  silence  such  flagrant 
transgressions  as  these,  and  he  called  on  the  Dean  to  provide  a 
remedy  immediately.  The  Canons  and  their  Vicars  were  to  be 
compelled  to  do  their  duty,  no  longer  preying  upon  the  goods 
of  the  Church  while  their  services  were  either  withheld,  or  per- 
formed with  shameless  irreverence.  Hurrying  through  the  Sacred 
Offices  could  no  longer  be  tolerated.  In  chanting  the  Psalms 
they  were  to  observe  the  necessary  pauses  in  the  middle  and 
at  the  end  of  every  verse  ;  and  in  singing  the  Antiphons,  Hymns, 
and  Responses  they  were  to  keep  together,  instead  of  jumbling 
the  sentences  one  upon  the  other  ;  for  which  end  the  Dean  was 
required  to  see  that  all  the  books  in  use  corresponded  exactly 
both  as  to  the  notation  and  the  text.  Unless  this  Mandate  were

While  this  important  business  was  in  hand,  the  Bishop  was 
summoned  to  London,  to  take  part  in  a  Provincial  Council  about 
to  be  opened  in  St.  Paul's  Cathedral  on  the  27th  of  January.2 
The  Mandate  reached  him,  at  Chudleigh,  on  the  22nd  of  December ; 
and  on  the  18th  of  January  he  wrote  to  the  Archbishop,  informing 
him  that  he  had  cited  all  who  were  expected  to  attend  from  his 
Diocese.  He  sent  a  list  of  their  names,  and  enclosed  a  copy  of 
the  Gravamina  which  his  Clergy  desired  to  submit  to  the  Council. 
These  were  three  in  number,  and  referred  to  the  tyranny  of  certain 
Lords  in  the  Diocese  who  had  deprived  their  nativl  of  their  antient 
right  to  dispose  of  their  property  by  Will,  the  encroachments  of 
the  Secular  Judges  on  the  Privileges  of  the  Clergy,  and  the  abuse 
of  the  right  of  Appeal  to  the  Court  of  Canterbury  on  the  part 
of  many  who,  in  that  way,  sought  to  escape  from  the  Ecclesiastical 
censures  and  punishments  which  they  had  incurred  by  their  mis- 
deeds. He  wrote,  also,  privately  to  the  Archbishop,  telling  him 
that  he  could  not  appear  in  person,  and  chiefly  because  the  Council 
was  to  meet  in  London.  The  blood  of  the  murdered  Stapeldon  still 
cried  to  Heaven  for  vengeance ;  and  the  lay-folk,  their  degenerate 
sons,  had  compelled  their  Bishops  (so  he  had  been  told)  to  swear 
that  they  would  take  no  steps  in  the  matter,  and  would  allow  the 
murderers  to  escape  with  impunity.  The  mob  was  on  their  side, 
and  universal  chaos  prevailed.  The  magnates  of  the  City  had  made 
a  show  of  endeavouring  to  restrain  the  madness  of  the  people,  but  it 
was  notorious  that  they  were  as  guilty  as  the  rest.  He  knew  that, 
in  due  time,  the  Angel  of  the  Lord  would  put  a  bit  into  their 
mouths ;  but,  meanwhile,  he  did  not  see  his  way  to  mount  either 
horse  or  mule  that  hath  no  understanding.  The  citizens3  had 
already    torn    his   London   House  in   pieces,  and  carried  off  all  its

where  he  remained  till  about  the  16th  of  October.  While  he  was 
there  he  discovered  that  disturbances  had  broken  out  again  in  the 
Cathedral,  in  consequence,  no  doubt,  of  his  absence ;  and,  this  time, 
the  Vicars  were  chiefly  to  blame.  He  had  been  informed,  on 
trustworthy  authority,  that  their  conduct  was  disgraceful ;  they 
were  not  ashamed  to  indulge  in  loud  and  indecent  laughter  during 
Divine  Service,  and  some  of  those  who  occupied  the  upper  forms  in 
the  Choir  at  Matins,  holding  lighted  candles  in  their  hands,  had  even 
dared  to  drop  the  melted  grease,  deliberately  and  wilfully,  on  the 
heads  of  those  who  sat  beneath  them.  They  also  disturbed  the 
service  by  jeering  at  mistakes  made  in  singing  and  reading  by  the 
less  educated  members  of  the  choir,  for  whose  deficiencies  they 
ought  rather  to  have  shewn  sympathy ;  correcting  their  blunders 
aloud,  and  in  English,  in  a  tone  of  derision.  Also,  they  deliberately 
jumbled  together  the  separate  parts  of  the  service,  causing  the 
greatest  confusion  ;  and  it  was  clear  that,  though  they  might  be  in 
the  Choir  in  the  body,  their  heart  was  anywhere  else— in  the 
market,  in  the  streets,  or  in  their  beds.  The  Bishop  wTrote,  on  the

From  Poutone  the  Bishop  went  to  Penryn,1  where  he  remained

remained  there,  or  in  the  neighbourhood,  till  the  end  of  the  year. 
The  Register,  now,  for  a  time,  records  only  the  ordinary  routine 
work  of  the  Diocese,  with  a  single  exception :  grievous  sacrilege 
had  been  committed  at  Whitchurch,  near  Tavistock,  where  an 
armed  band  of  lay  folk  had  seized  the  Parish-Church  by  force, 
and  refused  to  give  up  possession  or  allow  any  services  to  be  held 
in  it ;  and,  as  nothing  else  could  be  done,  the  Bishop  wrote  to 
the  King,  on  the  21st  of  March,  1330-1,  entreating  him  to  deal 
with  the  rebels  by  his  Royal  authority.4  Early  in  1331  (on  the 
25th  of  April)  we  find  him  at  Lambeth,5  from  whence  he  returned 
by  way  of  Bosham,6  where  there  had  been  trouble  for  a  long  time 
past,  his  Jurisdiction  being  constantly  disputed  by  the  Bishop  of 
Chichester  and  his  officials;  but  the  Register  is  silent  as  to  what 
he  did  there.  He  visited  his  Manors  of  Farringdon7  and  Chidham, 
and  returned  by  a  circuitous  route — by  Lambourue,8  Ashperton  in 
Herefordshire,9  his  birthplace,  Donyatt  in  Somerset,9  and  Petris- 
heghes9  to   Clyst,   where  he  arrived   on  the  9th  of  July. 

The  time  was,  now,  approaching  when  it  would  be  necessary  for 
him  to  visit  the  Papal  Court.  He  set  out  on  the  18th  of  September, 
resting  at  Forde  Abbey10  on  that  day,  and  at  Salisbury  on  the  21st. 
He  reached  London  on  the  3rd  of  October  and  remained  there 
till  the  22nd,  when  we  find  him  at  Canterbury.11  On  the  23rd 
he  sailed  from  Dover,11  and,  after  spending  a  few  days  in  Paris,11 
reached  Avignon12  on  the  29th  of  November,  where  he  remained 
till  the  19th  of  December.  It  is  recorded  that,  while  he  was 
there,  he  obtained  a  special  "  Privilege "  from  the  Pope,  and  we 
are  referred  for  a  copy  of  it  to  a  separate  quaternus  (p.  138).  It 
was  granted  on  the  20th  of  December.  It  will  be  remembered 
that  the  Bishop  visited  Lambeth  on  the  25th  of  April,  and 
there  can  be  little  doubt  that,  while  he  was  there,  he  dis- 
cussed with  Archbishop  Mepeham  the  question  of  his  general 
Visitation  of  the  Province  which  was  then  impending.     The  consul-

if  we  are  to  judge  his    action  at  all,  wTe    are  bound   to    consider

putting  ourselves,   as   far   as   may  be,  into  his  place.       Mepeham,

the    affairs   of   his    Diocese    on    several   occasions  ;    and   he   could 
scarcely    be    expected    to    regard    with    complacency   the    formal 
Visitation  of  a   Primate  who  had  not  hesitated  to  visit  his  Flock 
by  Letters,  informally,  and  behind  the  Diocesan's  back.     He  had 
found  the  whole  Diocese,  including  even  the  Cathedral  itself,   in- 
dire    disorder,    as    we    know  ;    his    very  means   of  sustenance    had 
been   cut  off  by  the  almost  universal   peculation  which  had  been 
going   on    for  years ;  and  every  corner  of  his  vast  and  most  diffi- 
cult   Charge    demanded    the    vigorous    rule    of    a    firm    hand,    if 
reformation  was  ever  to  be  accomplished.       He   could    not   brook 
interference    with    his    plans,    which   had    been,    already,    crowned 
with  a  large  measure  of  success,  especially  on  the  part  of  one  who 
had  shewn  that  he  was  of   a  meddlesome  disposition,   and  would 
probably    do    great    mischief    by    superseding    his    authority   and 
unsettling  the  minds  of  his  people,  just  as  many  of  them,  recog- 
nising and  appreciating  the  faithfulness  and  unselfishness  of  their

Aimed  with  his  Indult,  he  returned  to  England,  after  a  short

As  soon  as  our  Bishop  found  that  Mepeham  was  actually  coming,

Bishop  was  down,  at  once,  on  what  he  called  their  "  damnable

was  the  punishment  due  to  such  an  offence,  and  sending  them

Early  in  1333  the  Scots  invaded  England,  and  the  King  forth- 
with marched  against  them.  He  wrote  to  the  Bishops  from 
Newcastle-on-Tyne  on  the  23rd  of  April,  requesting  the  prayers 
of  all  Christian  people  for  the  success  of  his  arms.  Grandisson 
was  prompt  to  take  action,  and  on  the  31st  of  May,  feeling, 
probably,  that,  in  his  remote  Diocese,  the  people  would  scarcely 
understand  the  matter,  and  would  take  little  or  no  interest  in  a 
danger  so  distant,  he  appealed  to  them  in  moving  terms, — "Who 
is  there  that  dwells  in  any  part  of  this  Realm  of  England,  who 
that  has  any  ardent  desire  for  the  peace  and  honour  of  the  King, 
and  can  fail  to  be  roused  by  hearing  of  the  savage  fury  and  insolent 
pride  of  our  enemies,  or  remain  unmoved  when  so  noble  a  Prince 
asks  us  for  our  prayers  ? "  He  had  undertaken  the  war  for  the  sake 
of  his  people,  and  to  ward  off  the  dangers  which  threatened  them 
all ;  not  regarding  himself,  nor  shrinking  from  the  risk  or  turmoil 
of  the  conflict,  but  caring  only  that  his  subjects  might  dwell  at 
ease  and  be  refreshed  in  the  multitude  of  peace.  And  he 
ordered  the  Celebration  of  Masses  with  Litanies,  Processions,  and 
devout  prayers  in  every  parish.2  On  the  17th  of  June  he  appro- 
priated the  Rectory  of  Rockbeare  to  the  Abbess  and  Convent  of 
Canonsleigh,  the  patrons  of  the  Benefice,  reserving  to  himself  and 
his  Successors  the  right  of  Collation  to  the  Vicarage.3  In  July 
he  spent  a  few  days  with  his  father  at  Oxenhall ;  but  he  was  soon 
recalled  to  Exeter  to  deal  with  fresh  troubles  in  the  Cathedral.4 
He  had  recently  collated  his  nephew,  his  sister's  son,  John  de 
Northwode,  to  a  Canonry,  with  expectation  of  the  first  Prebend 
that  might  fall  vacant.  But  the  preferment  was  claimed  by  one 
William  le  Gyldene,  who  behaved  so  violently  that  the  Bishop 
excommunicated  him.  The  Dean,  though  but  lately  absolved  on 
his  submission,  was,  evidently,  a  turbulent  man,  for  we  find  him 
again  in  trouble,  suspended  and  excommunicated.5  And  on  the 
23rd  of  August  the  Bishop  commissioned  the  Subdean  and  William 
de  Nassington  to  take  the  Dean's  place  in  correcting  the  misconduct 
of  the  Vicars,  who  were  not  likely  to  mend  their  ways,  with  such 
an  evil  example  before  them.  On  the  11th  of  September  he 
commissioned  another  of  the  Canons,  John  de  Xassington,  to 
exercise  the  Dean's  right  of  patronage.5  There  was  trouble,  also, 
with  the  Deans-Rural,  many  of  whom,  instead  of  doing  their 
work  themselves,  had  presumed  to  appoint  as  substitutes  men 
of   no    character  and  wholly  unfit   for   such   an  office,    creating  a

and,  the  Primatial  See  being  vacant  by  reason  of  Mepeham's 
death,  he  had  induced  the  Official  of  the  Court  of  Canterbury 
to  intervene  in  the  matter  and  impugn  the  Bishop's  right  and 
jurisdiction.  Accordingly  the  Bishop  issued  an  Inhibition  to  his 
four  Aichdeacons,  from  Hartland,  on  the  21st  of  November,6 
forbidding  them  to  obey  the  said  Official  or  pay  any  attention  to 
the  Mandate  which  he  had  directed  to  them  on  the  9th  of  that 
month.7  On  the  12th,  moreover,  he  had  ordered  the  Subdean 
to  sequestrate  the  Dean's  revenues.6  Leaving  Hartland  he  reached 
Torrington  on  the  16th,  and  Winkleigh,  where  he  dedicated  the 
High  Altar,  on  the  17th;  after  which  he  remained  in  his  Manor- 
House  of  Crediton  till  the  14th  of  January,  1333-4.  But  he  was 
not  suffered  to  rest  long  ;  the  Vicars  in  the  Cathedral  were  again 
causing  grievous  scandal  by  shameless  misconduct  in  the  Choir, 
encouraged,  we  can  scarcely  doubt,  by  the  evil  example,  in  another

way,  of  the  Dean,  their  immediate  head ;  and  the  Bishop,  re- 
membering their  abominable  conduct  on  the  Feast  of  the  Holy 
Innocents'  in  the  previous  year,  when  they  not  only  disturbed 
the  Services  by  loud  laughter  and  other  gross  improprieties,  but 
even  disgraced  themselves  by  indulging  in  vulgar  revellings  and 
obscene  gestures  before  the  people,  wrote  to  them,  on  the  16th 
of  December,  through  the  Subdean  and  William  de  Nassington, 
to  tell  them  that,  if  they  dared  to  repeat  such  conduct  on  the 
same  holy  Feast,  now  near  at  hand,  he  would  deal  with  them 
with  the  utmost  rigour.1  To  Grandisson,  who  was  a  man  of  the 
most  reverent  and  devout  mind,  and  who  was  engaged  at  the 
time,  at  great  self-sacrifice  and  with  abounding  zeal,  in  the 
arduous  work  of  completing  the  Cathedral  Church,  which,  he 
tells  us,  over  and  over  again,  he  regarded  as  his  beloved  Spouse, 
the  very  thought  of  such  sacrilege  as  this  must  have  caused 
nothing  short  of  agony.  But  he  was  dauntless,  and  the  work 
went  on  unceasingly  in  the  face  of  all  rebuffs  and  discouragement. 
We  soon  find  him  in  Exeter  again;2  where,  on  the  16th  of 
January  he  appropriated  the  Rectory  of  Bere- Ferrers  for  the 
endowment  of  an  Archpresbitery  in  that  Church.3  On  the  20th 
of  January  he  was  at  Ottery,4  a  place  which  was  very  near  his 
heart,  and  for  the  benefit  of  which  he  was,  already,  contemplating 
great  things. 

On  the  defeat  of  Douglas,  the  Regent  of  Scotland,  Baliol  was 
received  as  King  in  a  Parliament  held  in  October  at  Perth ; 
but,  on  his  ceding  to  the  English  the  South  of  Scotland,  he  was 
driven  out,  and  fled  to  Berwick  early  in  February  :  it  was, 
doubtless,  in  consequence  of  these  stirring  events  that  our 
Bishop  journeyed  to  the  North,  to  attend  the  Parliament  which 
was  summoned  to  meet  at  York5  on  the  21st  of  February, 
1333-4.  We  find  him,  on  his  way,  at  Lutterworth6  on  the  12th 
of  February,  and  he  remained  in  York  till,  apparently,  the 
middle  of  March.  The  Register  only  records  his  movements,  and 
gives  no  account  of  his  doings  in  Parliament.  He  appears  to 
have  been  in  London7  on  the  16th  of  March  on  his  way  to 
Faringdon,  Hants,  where  he  remained  till  the  middle  of  April, 
1334.  On  the  20th  of  April  he  passed  through  Wid worthy  and 
Gittisham8  on  his  way  to  Clyst,  where  he  arrived  on  the  same 
day  ;  remaining  there,  or  at  one  of  his  Manors  in  the  neighbour- 
hood and  at  Exeter,  till  the  13th  of  May,  1336.  Evidently,  the 
great  work  in  the  Cathedral,  which  must  have  been  then  advancing 
rapidly,  demanded  his  almost  continuous  presence.

mitted in  Plymouth  at  this  time  :  the  bailiff  of  Plympton  Priory, 
John  Haywarde  by  name,  while  engaged  in  his  ordinary  duties 
on  the  Priory  estates,  had  been  set  upon  by  a  band  of  men,  to 
escape  from  whom  he  took  refuge  in  the  Church  of  Suttone. 
The  ruffians  broke  down  the  door,  dragged  their  victim  out,  and 
not  only  slashed  him  with  their  swords  and  beat  him  with  clubs, 
but  even  went  so  far  as  to  break  his  legs.  They  escaped,  and 
it  appeared  that  no  one  could,  or  would,  identify  them ;  so  the 
Bishop  issued  a  general  Sentence  of  Excommunication  against 
them  on  the  8th  of   July.3 

The  King  was  still  in  the  North,  ravaging  Scotland,  in  concert 
with  Baliol.  And  the  Bishop,  to  whom  Edward  had  appealed  from 
Newcastle-on-Tyne  on  the  28th  of  June,  issued  his  Mandate,  on  the 
3rd  of  August,  for  the  renewal  throughout  his  Diocese  of  prayers 
for  the  success  of  the  English  arms.4 

It  will  be  remembered5  that  Dean  Coletone  had  written  to  the 
Bishop  from  Avignon,  expressing  his  desire  to  be  reconciled,  once 
more,  to  his  offended  Father  in  God,  and  asking  for  a  partial  relax- 
ation of  the  sequestration  of  his  revenues,  as  he  could  not  return 
to  England  for  lack  of  money ;  and  that  his  request  was  granted 
on  the  28th  of  June,  1334.  About  a  year  elapsed  before  he  set 
out :  the  negotiations  and  necessary  arrangements,  of  course,  took 
time  ;  and  probably  he  was  detained  by  illness,  broken  down,  we 
can  well  believe,  by  his  utter  failure  to  influence  the  Pope  against 
the  Bishop.  He  died  on  his  way  home,6  on  the  4th  of  August7, 
1335.     On  the  14th,  two  Licences  were  granted — to  the  Treasurer,

of  the  Precious  Blood  of  Jesus  Christ,"  not  to  hesitate  to  enforce 
the  penal  statutes  against  all  offenders,  remembering  that  he  had 
assumed  a  share  in  the  Bishop's  responsibilities.4 

Grandisson,  as  we  have  seen,  was  a  strenuous  reformer  of  abuses ; 
and  we,  now,  find  him  directing  his  attention  to  the  state  of  his 
Consistory  Court.  There,  as  elsewhere,  grievous  abuses  were  preva- 
lent. Men  who  had  no  standing  as  judges  were  presuming  to 
exercise  judgement ;  and  even  the  lawful  Judges,  Officials,  and 
Notaries  were  taking  part  in  oppressing  all  who  came  within  their 
clutches,  blinded  by  a  love  of  private  gain  which  "ought  rather  to 
be  called  rapacity."  Cases  were  heard  not  in  open  Court  but  in 
secret  chambers ;  and  many  innocent  persons  were  condemned, 
without  resistance  on  their  part,  being  simply  worn  out  by  the 
treatment  which  they  received,  and  driven  into  submission  as  the 
least  of  the  evils  which  threatened  them.  The  fame,  or  rather,  as 
the  Bishop  says,  the  infamy,  of  these  misdeeds  at  last  reached 
Grandisson's  ears,  and  he  promptly  took  measures  to  secure  a 
remedy,  issuing  on  the  3rd  of  February,  1335-6,  a  series  of  Rules, 
fourteen  in  number,  for  the  better  governance  of  the  Court,  and, 
at  the  same  time,  appointing  a  Commission  to  inquire  into  the 
excesses  of  which  he  was  informed  the  Advocates,  Proctors,  and 
others  serving  in  the  said  Court  were  guilty.  He  insisted  on 
immediate  obedience,  and  reminded  the  offenders  that  he  was 
making  no  new  demands  upon  them,  but  only,  as  they  were  well 
aware,  insisting  on  their  submitting  themselves  to  the  antient  and 
time-honoured  regulations  of  the  Court,  which  pertained  to  his 
Spiritual  Jurisdiction.5 

On  the  14th  of  May,  1336,  he  dedicated  the  High  Altar  at 
Stoke-in-Teignhead6 ;  after  which  he  resided  for  about  a  month  at 
Paignton,  and  then  set  out   to  conclude   his  General  Visitation  of

lay  their  hands  on — a  large  number  of  silver  cups  and  spoons,  all 
the  Vicar's  provisions  and  his  bedding,   and  £20  in  money. 

It  must  have  been  with  a  feeling  of  great  relief  that  the  Bishop 
set  out,  on  the  1st  of  July,  to  traverse  the  quiet  highways  and

Lostwithiel  and  Fowey,  had  been  recently  rebuilt ;  and  he  dedi-

also  the  Church,  originally  dedicated  to  St.  Finbar,  had  been 
rebuilt,5  he  dedicated  it,  with  its  three  Altars,  in  honour  of  St. 
Nicholas,  Bishop  and  Confessor,  on  the  3rd.  On  the  10th  he

just  beyond  that  town  on  the  west.  His  headquarters  -were  at 
Alvertone,  in  the  suburbs  of  Penzance,  a  Manor  of  the  Baronial 
Family  of  Tyes.6     On  the    12th   he   proceeded,  with  great  state,

where,  for  so  many  years,  both  he  and  his  Predecessors  had  been

as  prejudicial  to  the  rights  of  the  King,  claiming  only  spiritual 
authority  over  them  as  their  Bishop.  All  submitted,  and  quite 
unanimously;  the  principal  inhabitants  speaking  in  English  or 
in  French,  and  the  others  in  their  own  language.  This  was  done 
with  great  solemnity,  all  kneeling  at  the  Bishop's  feet,  with  up- 
lifted hands,  confessing  that  they  had  been  rebels  against  the 
unity  of  the  Church.  The  Hymn  Veni,  Creator,  was  then  sung 
and  prayers  were  said,  after  which  the  Bishop  absolved  them  all. 
And  then  he  preached  to  them  from  the  text— "  Ye  were  as  sheep 
going  astray,  but  are  now  returned  unto  the  Shepherd  and  Bishop 
of  your  souls."  The  sermon  was  in  Latin,  the  interpreter  after- 
wards reciting  the  substance  of  it  to  the  congregation  in  their 
Cornish  tongue.  Many  of  the  younger  parishioners  then  came  forward 
and  received  the  First  Tonsure  at  the  Bishop's  hands ;  and  children, 
"almost  more  than  could  be  numbered,"  gathered  from  all  parts 
of  the  large  Parish  and  its  dependent  Chapel ries,  were  confirmed. 
The  priests  who  served  the  Church  took  the  oath  of  Canonical 
Obedience ;  but  the  Dean,  still  rebellious,  was  conspicuous  by 
his  absence  j  and,  two  days  later,  at  Alvertone,  the  Bishop  com- 
mitted the  administration  of  the  Deanery  to  Henry  Marseley,  the 
interpreter  mentioned  above.  The  names  of  the  five  Chaplains 
are  given,  and  also  those  of  the  principal  inhabitants,  thirteen  in 
number  j  some  of  which,  such  as  Vyvyan,  Boscawen,  and  Penrose, 
are  still  names  of  honour  in  this  far-western  land. 

On  the  13th  the  Bishop  visited2  St.  Just  and  St.  Madron, 
dedicating  the  High  Altars  of  both  Churches;  and  on  the  14th 
he  celebrated  the  same  solemn  rite  in  the  Churches  of  St.  Ludgvan, 
and  St.  Colan  (near  St.  Columb),  not  far  from  his  Manor  of 
Poutone,  where  he  remained  till  about  the  23rd  j  visiting  Lezant, 
where,  also,  he  dedicated  the  High  Altar,3  on  the  27th,  and 
Lawhitton  on  the  31st,  on  his  homeward  way.  He  had  made  a 
complete  circuit  of  the  County  ;  and  there  can  be  no  doubt  that 
he  had  confirmed  or  admitted  to  the  first  Tonsure  in  many  places.

But  there  is  no  record  of  such  work  except  in  the  case  of  St. 
Buryan ;  and  the  Register  of  his  Ordinations  (referred  to  on  p.  820) 
has,  unhappily,  been  lost.  The  works  in  the  Cathedral,  of  course, 
required  his  constant  supervision,  and  he  resided  in  Exeter,  or 
at  Clyst  hard  by,  till  the  12th  of  February,  1336-7,  and,  probably, 
later ;  and  the  Register  contains  a  full  record  of  his  ordinary 
routine  work  during  the  interval.  Roger  de  Trevyliaus,  "  the 
ringleader  and  charioteer  of  the  rebels "  at  Plymouth,  submitted 
and  was  absolved ;  and  the  Church  of  Suttone  was  released  from 
Interdict  on  the  9th  of  August.1  Even  Dean  Maunte,  finding,  of 
course,  that  he  was  no  longer  supported  at  St.  Buryan,  obeyed 
the  Bishop's  summons  to  Clyst,  and  made  his  submission  there, 
taking  the  oath  of  Canonical  Obedience  on  the  16th.2  John  of 
Eltham,  Earl  of  Cornwall,  died  in  September;  and  on  the  30th 
the  Bishop  sequestrated  his  goods.3  He  had,  probably,  good 
reason  for  doing  so,  for  the  officials  of  the  Earls,  as  the  Registers 
abundantly  testify,  had  long  been  accustomed  to  oppress,  and 
sometimes  even  grievously  outrage  the  Clergy,  presuming,  no 
doubt,  on  their  position  as  the  agents,  indirectly,  of  the  Crown.4 
But  on  this  occasion  he  found  that  might  was  stronger  than  right ; 
and  on  the  8th  of  October  he  wrote  to  his  Commissaries,  informing 
them  that  it  had  never  been  his  intention  to  derogate  the  rights 
of  the  King,  and  that  they  would  have  to  accept  John  de 
Mountvyroun  as  their  colleague,  on  the  King's  behalf.5  On  the 
30th  of  October  the  Rectory  of  St.  Madron  was  appropriated  to 
the  Hospital  of  St.  John  of  Jerusalem  in  England.6  On  the  12th 
of  November  the  Bishop  dedicated  the  High  Altar  of  the  Chapel 
of  St.  John's  Hospital,  Exeter;  and  on  the  14th  he  reconciled  the 
churchyard  at  Exminster,  which  had  been  polluted  by  the  shedding 
of  blood.7  On  the  19th  he  settled  finally  with  the  Executors  of 
Bishop  Stapeldon,  receiving  from  them  the  sum  of  two  hundred 
marks.8  There  had  been  troubles  for  some  time  past  in  connec- 
tion with  the  Collegiate  Church  of  St.  Crantock,  in  Cornwall, 
which  had  been  seriously  hampered  by  the  negligence  and  mal- 
practices of  the  late  Dean.  The  Vicars  appointed  by  the  Canons 
were  ignorant  men,  who  could  neither  sing  nor  read  properly,  and 
some  of  them  were  not  in  priests'  Orders.  On  the  8th  of  October 
he  had  issued  his  Mandate  to  the  Dean,  William  de  Lunday, 
requiring  him  to  provide  a  remedy  against  all  such  abuses 
for  the  time  to  come.9  And,  now,  he  found  that  the  Canons  were 
non-resident,   and   that,   in    consequence,   the    worship  of   God   was

Priory,  Adam  de  Knoll e,  the  Prior,  being  a  man  of  evil  repute, 
unworthy  of  his  Profession,  and  given  to  spending  much  of  his  time 
outside  his  House,  consorting  not  only  with  men  of  the  world  but 
even  with  dissolute  women.  And  on  the  10th  of  February,  1336-7, 
the  Bishop  ordered  Richard  de  Gomersale  and  Bartholomew  de 
Castro  to  hold  an  Inquisition  in  the  Priory  and  report.3 

Early  in  March  (being  summoned  to  Parliament),  he  went  to 
London, — one  of  his  rare  and  brief  absences  from  his  Diocese.4  He 
had  long  been  troubled  about  the  affairs  of  the  Earldom  of  Cornwall, 
which  was  erected  into  a  Duchy  on  the  17th  of  March,  when  Prince 
Edward  was  invested  as  the  first  Duke.  Two  Documents  were 
inserted  in  the  Register,  both  without  context,  the  first  relating  to 
the  Charter  of  King  Edward  II,  confirming  to  the  Bishops  of  Exeter 
the  Grant  of  the  Tithe  of  Royal  Fish,  in  Devon  and  Cornwall,  made 
by  King  Henry  II  to  Bishop  Robert  de  Chichester5;  the  second 
containing  a  series  of  Petitions  to  the  King  touching  the  manage- 
ment of  the  Royal  Duchy,  and  complaining  of  the  many  oppressions 
and  exactions  committed  in  the  name  of  the  Earls  of  Cornwall 
against  the  Church,  in  past  times.6  By  the  end  of  the  month  he 
was  at  home  again;  at  Honiton  on  the  31st,  and  soon  after  at 
Chudleigh,7  and  at  Exeter,  where  he  appropriated  the  Rectory  of 
Northmolton  to  Lilleshull  Abbey.8  There  were  fresh  troubles  at 
Bosham ;   the  See  of  Chichester  was  void  by  the  death  of  Bishop

John  de  Langetone  in  June,  1337,  and  the  Archbishop  seized  the 
opportunity  to  visit  the  College  which  had  always  been  exempt  from 
his  Jurisdiction ;  but  Grandisson,  as  the  Ordinary  of  the  place, 
appealed,  on  the  22nd  of  September,  to  the  Pope.1  There  were 
troubles,  also,  again,  in  the  Cathedral,  arising  from  the  persistent 
non-residence  of  Walter  Meriet,  the  Chancellor.  This  had  been 
going  on  for  ten  years,  and  had  caused  great  anxiety  to  the  Bishop, 
who  complains  that  the  man  was  incorrigible,  and  that  reproof, 
rebuke,  and  exhortation  were  simply  thrown  away  upon  him ;  the 
offender  was  careful  to  secure  every  penny  of  his  revenues,  but  he 
did  nothing  to  earn  them ;  he  had  even  allowed  the  buildings  at 
Stoke-Gabriel  and  St.  Newlyn, — Churches  appropriated  for  the  en- 
dowment of  his  Office, — to  fall  in  ruins  to  the  ground,  while  the 
parishioners  were  wholly  neglected.  This  was  more  than  the  Bishop 
could  stand,  and  on  the  31st  of  October  he  took  vigorous  measures 
to  compel  the  Chancellor  to  reside  and  fulfil  his  duties.2  On  the 
14th  of  November  an  Archpresbytery,  for  an  Archpriest  and  five 
associate-priests,  was  established  in  the  Church  of  Haccombe3  by 
Sir  John  Lercedekne,  fulfilling  the  intention,  frustrated  by  his  death, 
of  Sir  Stephen  de  Haccombe,  from  whom  Sir  John  had  inherited  the 
Manor  through  his  wife  Cecilia  de  Haccombe.  The  Church  of  St. 
Hugh,  of  Quethiock,  in  Cornwall,  was  appropriated  to  the  new 
Foundation.4  On  the  26th  of  November  the  Bishop  visited  the 
Cathedral  in  person,  and  he  caused  a  full  account  of  the  proceedings 
to  be  entered  in  his  Register.5  The  names  of  all  the  Cathedral 
Body,  the  officials  and  ministers,  are  recorded,  from  the  Dean  to  the 
junior  custos,  and  the  Articles  of  Visitation,  fifty-one  in  number  and 
of  a  most  searching  character,  are  set  forth  at  large.  The  result  of 
the  Bishop's  investigations  was  far  from  satisfactory,  and  in  his 
consequent  Decree,  issued  on  the  4th  of  January,  1337-8,  he  de- 
nounced the  offenders,  in  withering  terms,  as  guilty  of  avarice  and 
fraud  ;  nay,  in  God's  sight,  of  theft  and  sacrilege ;  commanding 
them  to  obey  the  Statutes.  The  Dean  was  to  send  to  the  Bishop 
full  particulars,  with  the  names,  in  all  cases  of  colourable  and 
fictitious  Residence,  within  fifteen  days. 

We  have,  now,  reached  the  date  of  the  Foundation  of  the  College 
of  St.  Mary  of  Ottery,  which  takes  rank  amongst  the  chief  achieve- 
ments of  Grandisson's  Episcopate.  The  Church  is  a  truly  magnificent 
building,  recalling,  with  its  transept-towers,  the  good  Bishop's  own 
well-loved  "  Spouse  "  of  Exeter.  It  must  have  been  a  fabrick  of 
some  pretensions  originally ;  but  as  remodelled,  enlarged,  and  in 
great  measure  rebuilt  by  Grandisson,  it  is  justly  regarded  as  one  of 
the  glories  of  Devon,  and  a  marvellous  monument  of  the  great 
Bishop's  architectural  knowledge,  munificence,  and  devotion.     From 

1  pp.  846-850.      2  pp.  283,  851.      3  pp.  852,  1333.      4  p.  1346.      5  pp.  855-863.

end  to  end  it  breathes  his  spirit ;  and  in  every  detail  we  see  and  feel 
the  evidence  of  the  continuous  influence  of  his  master-mind  and 
matchless  skill.  It  is  impossible,  within  the  narrow  limits  of  a 
Preface,  to  do  justice  to  such  a  subject  as  this  ;  and,  happily,  I  have 
no  need  even  to  attempt  the  task.  The  Church  has  been  described 
at  length,  with  many  excellent  illustrations,  in  the  Transactions  of 
the  Exeter  Architectural  Society1 ;  Dr.  Oliver  has  dealt  exhaustively 
with  the  history  and  Statutes  of  the  Foundation  in  his  Monasticon  of 
the  Diocese ;  and,  while  I  am  writing,  the  Rev.  J.  R.  Dalton,  Canon 
of  Windsor,  is  engaged  on  yet  another  such  history,  which  will  be 
far  more  full  and  accurate  than  its  predecessors.  I  have  had  the 
advantage,  through  his  courtesy,  of  reading  many  of  his  proofs  ;  and 
I  may  be  permitted  to  say,  here,  that  he  has  extended  his  researches 
beyond  the  fabrick  of  the  Church,  tracing  and  identifying,  with 
marked  success,  all  that  can  now  be  traced — a  fragment  here  and 
there,  and  long-buried  foundations — of  the  Collegiate  Buildings, 
which  were  swept  away  after  the  Dissolution.  I  must  be  content, 
simply,  to  refer  the  reader  to  the  numerous  documents  relating  to 
the  College  which  are  included  in  these  Volumes,2  beginning  with 
the  purchase  by  the  Bishop  of  the  Manor  and  Advowson  of  Ottery, 
in  1335,  from  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of  Rouen,  who,  he  tells  us, 
drove  a  hard  bargain,  compelling  him  to  pay  an  exorbitant  price 
for  property  which  they  were  forced  to  acknowledge  was  of  small 
value  to  themselves.  The  date  of  the  actual  Foundation  was 
Christmas  Eve,  1337;  the  sanction  of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of 
Exeter  for  his  Ordinances  was  obtained  on  the  22nd  of  January, 
1337-8,  and  they  were  sent  to  Avignon  for  Confirmation  soon  after- 
wards; the  Pope  objected  to  them  as  too  prolix,  and  advised  the 
Bishop  to  cut  them  down ;  which  he  did,  issuing  the  Statutes  on  the 
29th  of  September,  1339,  and  sending  the  revised  Document  to 
Avignon  at  the  same  time,  or,  perhaps,  early  in  1340.  Benedict  XII 
died  on  the  25th  of  April,  1342,  before  a  Bull  of  Confirmation  had 
been  issued.  It  was  issued  by  Clement  VI  on  the  27th  of  June 
following,  and  was  one  of  the  first  of  his  Pontifical  Acts. 

On  the  25th  of  May,  1338,  the  Church  of  Newton-St.  Cyres 
was  appropriated  to  Plympton  Priory,3  and  that  of  St.  Merry n  to 
the  Dean  and  Chapter.4  Roger  de  Charleton,  Archdeacon  of  Totnes, 
died  in  April,  and  his  successor,  John  de  Northwode,  was  collated 
on  the  13th  of  June.5  He  was  the  Bishop's  nephew;  and,  pro- 
bably, there  was  a  suspicion  of  nepotism,  for  the  appointment  was 
resented  by  certain  persons  "blinded  by  avarice  and  overcome  by 
ambition,"  against  whom  the  Bishop  issued  a  strongly  worded  de- 
nunciation on  the   24th.6     There   was  trouble  again,   at  this   time,
