£1,300,  a  very  large  sum  in  those  days.4     It  will  be  remembered 
that  as  long  ago  as  July,   1333,  an  outrage  had  been  committed  in 
the  Cathedral  by  one  William  de  Gyldene  (or  Guldene),  for  which  he 
was  excommunicated.5    He  had  then  resisted  the  Collation  of  John  de 
Northwode  to  a  Canonry,  and  he  appears  to  have  been  the  ringleader 
in  the  opposition  to  his  promotion  to  the  Archdeaconry  of  Totnes, 
referred  to  above.     This  man  was  suspected  of   heresy,  and  it  is 
certain   that   he   was   a   turbulent   fellow,   ambitious,  envious,  and 
utterly  unscrupulous.6     On  this  second  occasion  he  again  resorted 
to   open   and   sacrilegious   violence,    in   order   to   secure   his   ends. 
The  Bishop  requested  the  Dean  to  send  him  a  full  report  of  what 
had    taken   place,   and    Dean   Brayleghe  complied  on   the    13th   of 
November.7     It  appears  that   Gyldene   invaded    the    Choir,  on  All 
Saints'   Day,  during   Divine  Service,  followed  by  a  large  band  of 
armed  ruffians.     The  Psalms  of  the  Daily  Office  were  being  chanted 
at   the   moment ;  but    Gyldene  did  not   hesitate    to   interrupt  the 
Clergy  violently,  and   some  of  his  followers,  approaching  the  Dean, 
demanded   of    him   that   he   should,    there  and    then,   admit  their 
leader  to  the  Stall  which  had  formerly  belonged  to   Reginald  de 
Campo  Arnulphi.     Efforts  were  made  to  pacify  the  intruders,  but 
with  little  effect;  for  afterwards,  while  Mass  was  being  celebrated, 
the   tumult   was  renewed,    each   of  the    Canons   being   assailed  in 
turn,  with  the    same    purpose   in    view.      All,   whether   known  or 
unknown,  who  took  part  in  this  scandalous  scene  were,  of  course, 
excommunicated,  and  we  hear  no  more  of  Gyldene.8

the  President  of  his  Consistory  Court  in  1336,1  working,  as  we

At  length,  feeling  that  his  work,  in  such  a  Avidely  extended  and 
scattered  Diocese,  was  overwhelming,  and  fearing  that  any  part 
of  it  might  be  neglected,  he  commissioned  Richard  Fraunceys, 
Bishop  of  Waterford,  to  serve  as  his  Coadjutor,  on  the  18th  of 
February,  1338-9 ;  the  immediate  result  being  that  Churches  and 
Altars  were  dedicated  in  twelve  places,  and  Confirmations  were 
held.2  The  Chancellor  of  the  Cathedral,  Walter  Meriet,  was  still 
guilty  of  persistent  non-residence  ;  and  the  Bishop,  declaring  that 
he  "  could  no  longer  endure  to  sew  pillows  for  his  arm-holes,  or 
supply  a  bolster  for  a  mad  man's  head,"  cited  him,  on  the  1st  of 
July,  1339,  to  appear  before  him  at  Clyst  on  the  10th.3  We  hear 
no  more  of  him  after  this.  He  was  a  wealthy  man  and  had  large 
estates,  in  the  enjoyment  and  management  of  which  he  was, 
apparently,  wholly  absorbed.  But  he  seems  to  have  retained  his 
Dignity  in  our  Cathedral  till  his  death  on  the  17th  of  May, 
13454;  his  successor  (as  far  as  we  know,  for  the  Register  is  silent 
on  that  point)  was  Thomas  de  Bokynham,  who  was  collated  on 
the  25th  of  March,  1346.5  The  Bishop  had  great  trouble,  from 
time  to  time,  throughout  his  Episcopate,  with  the  scions  of  great 
Families,  who,  often,  seem  to  have  thought  that  they  were  entitled 
to  take  liberties  with  him;  but  he  was  no  respecter  of  persons, 
and  did  not  spare  them.  Walter  de  Botriaux,  a  member  of  a  power- 
ful Baronial  Family,  was  Rector,  at  this  time,  of  St.  Ruan-Lanyhorne, 
in  Cornwall.  He  could  not  be  induced  to  reside  on  his  Benefice,  but 
wandered  about  in  all  directions,  absorbed  in  secular  pursuits  and 
committing  other  offences,  "as  to  which,"  the  Bishop  says,  "we 
remain  silent  for  the  present."  On  the  2nd  of  July  he  was  cited  to 
appear  at  Clyst,  having  been  previously  admonished,  but  without 
effect.6  He  must  have  satisfied  the  Bishop,  in  the  end,  by  full 
submission ;  but  it  was  considered  advisable  that  he  should  resign 
Lanyhorne,  and  the  Bishop  sent  him  away,  almost  to  the  Land's  End, 
to  St.  Just-in-Penwith,  to  which  he  was  collated  (by  lapse)  on  the 
12th  of  November,  1340.7  On  the  8th  of  August  in  that  year,  the 
Bishop,  having  discovered  that  there  were  great  irregularities  in 
Frithelstock  Priory,  commissioned  the  Abbat  of  Hartland  to  deal 
with  the  matter,  and  specially  with  the  misconduct  of  the  Sub-prior, 
who  had  been  guilty  of  incontinency.  The  Abbat  was  to  take  with 
him  the  Bishop's  Ordinance  for  the  correction  and  reform  of  all 
abuses.8 

On  the  23rd  of  December  Hugh  de  Courtenay,  Earl  of  Devon,  died.

On  Sexagesima  Sunday,  the  11th  of  February,  1340-1,  there  was 
great  excitement  in  Exeter.  The  Cathedral  bells  were  set  ringing 
early  in  the  morning,  and  a  message  was  sent  to  the  Bishop,  who 
was  at  Chudleigh,  to  the  effect  that  a  notable  miracle  had  been 
wrought  on  a  blind  man,  one  John  le  Skynnere,  whose  sight  had 
been  restored.2  Grandisson  was  suspicious  from  the  first,  fearing 
that  the  people  might  be  deceived  and  that  grave  evils  might  ensue  ; 
and  he  wrote  immediately  to  the  Dean,  his  Official-Principal,  and  the 
Subdean,  forbidding  them,  under  pain  of  Suspension,  Interdict,  and 
Excommunication,  to  allow  the  bells  to  be  rung  again,  or  to  take  any 
other  steps  to  celebrate  the  alleged  miracle  till  the  case  had  been 
fully  investigated  :  such  portents,  he  told  them,  were  often  the  work 
of  the  devil,  and  of  men  who  were  greedy  of  filthy  lucre  and  vain- 
glory. No  time  was  lost ;  and  on  the  13th  the  Bishop  wrote  to  the 
Dean  and  Subdean,  informing  them  that,  as  he  had  feared,  Satan 
had  been  transforming  himself  into  an  Angel  of  Light.  Skynnere 
had  appeared  before  him,  and  had  been  closely  examined.  At  first 
the  man  had  stoutly  protested  that  the  miracle  had  indeed  been 
wrought,  declaring  that  he  was  ready  to  confirm  his  statement  by  an 
oath  ;  but  he  wavered  and  contradicted  himself,  and  at  last  broke 
down,  confessing  that,  being  a  poor  man,  he  had  concocted  this  story 
in  the  hope  of  being  able  to  make  money  :  for  seven  years  past 
he  had  been  quite  blind  of  one  eye,  and  so  remained  ;  he  was  always 
able  to  see  a  little  with  the  other,  and  he  could  see  no  better  now  ; 
he  must  have  been  tempted  by  the  devil  both  to  lie  and  to  perjure 
himself.  The  Cathedral  authorities  were  severely  rebuked  for  their 
credulity,  and  advised  to  follow,  in  future,  the  example  of  the  Jews, 
who  called  the  parents  and  friends  of  the  blind  man  whom  our  Lord 
had  healed,  and  strictly  examined  them.  On  Quinquagesima  Sunday 
the  imposture  was  publicly  exposed  in  the  Cathedral,  by  the  Bishop's 
mandate.3

A  Provincial  Council  was  held  in  London  in  1342,  to  deal  with 
general  questions  of  Ecclesiastical  Jurisdiction.1  The  Bishop  wrote 
to  excuse  himself  from  attending,  being  ill  and  afraid  to  undertake 
so  long  a  journey  in  the  winter ;  but,  in  the  end  he  was  forced  to  go, 
in  obedience  to  a  Royal  Writ,  requiring  him  to  appear,  at  West- 
minster, on  the  29th  of  September,  to  shew  cause  why  he  had 
resisted  John  de  Sodbury,  H anion  de  Direworthi,  and  others,  whom 
the  King  had  commissioned  to  deal  with  certain  alleged  outrages, 
committed,  in  Devon  and  Cornwall,  by  Ecclesiastical  persons  under 
cover  of  the  Privileges  of  the  Clergy  and  the  Liberties  of  the  Church.2 
It  is  evident  that  these  men  acted  in  a  high-handed  manner.  They 
commenced  their  operations  by  arresting  Paul  Brey,  Professor  of  Civil 
Law,  Richard  Giffard,  and  John  de  Piltone,  priests,  and  Rectors 
of  Churches  having  cure  of  souls,  whom  they  condemned  to  banish- 
ment and  outlawry,  even  going  so  far  as  to  pronounce  them  worthy 
of  death.  It  was  not  likely  that  the  Bishop  would  sit  still  while  this 
was  going  on.  He  forthwith  cited  them  all,  as  having  incurred  the 
Sentence  of  Excommunication,  to  appear  before  him,  at  Clyst,  on  the 
first  Juridical  day  after  the  8th  of  September,  the  Feast  of  the 
Nativity  of  the  Blessed  Virgin  ;  and  it  is  evident  from  the  con- 
sternation which  ensued  that  they  had,  at  any  rate,  exceeded  their 
instructions.  Hamund  de  Direworthi  could  not  wait  till  the  appointed 
day,  but  presented  himself  at  Clyst  on  the  4th.  The  Bishop  was,  of 
course,  surprised  to  see  him  so  soon,  and  asked  him  what  he  wanted. 
He  replied  that  he  had  ventured  to  anticipate  the  date  of  the 
appointment,  because  he  was  anxious  to  tell  the  Bishop  that  he  had 
been  an  unwilling  agent  from  the  first,  having  been  forced  to  serve 
under  the  Royal  Commission  by  threats  of  forfeiture  of  all  his  goods; 
and  he  confessed  that  he  could  offer  no  excuse  for  his  conduct,  as  he 
had  acted  with  his  eyes  open,  and  in  violation  of  his  conscience. 
After  a  searching  examination  on  all  crucial  points,  the  Bishop 
received  his  confession  and  absolved  him,  requiring  him,  by  way  of 
penance,  to  make  publick  confession  of  his  errors,  before  the  King's 
Council  and  elsewhere,  and  to  take  every  step  in  his  power  to  undo 
the  mischief  which  he  had  done.  Another  of  the  Commissioners, 
John  Berde,  Under-sheriff  of  Devon,  also  anticipated  the  appointed 
day ;  he  appeared  at  Clyst  on  the  6th,  and  confessed  that  he  was 
guilty  of  the  charges  brought  against  him,  except  that  he  had  not, 
personally,  taken  part  in  pronouncing  the  sentences  of  outlawry. 
The  Bishop  pronounced  him  excommunicate;    but,   on  his  humble

Malet,  was  the  most  hardened  and  violent  of  all.  The  Bishop 
describes  him  as  "  a  priest,  delicately  nurtured  by  the  Church,«his 
holy  Mother,  from  the  patrimony  of  the  Crucified,  who  had 
sharpened  his  tongue  like  a  sword,  uttering  mad  and  blasphemous 
words  against  his  Mother,  her  Ministers  and  Liberties  " ;  he  had 
even  ventured  to  arrest  certain  clerks  in  the  Cathedral,  before 
the  High  Altar.  This  man  was  determined  to  resist  the  Bishop's 
authority  to  the  last ;  and,  instead  of  appearing  in  person,  he  sent 
his  proctor  to  Clyst,  who,  imposing  on  the  Bishop's  patience,  con- 
trived to  waste  eight  days  in  making  frivolous  excuses  for  the 
absence  of  his  principal.  Sodbury  wras,  then,  excommunicated ;  but 
he  had  already  complained  of  Grandisson's  strenuous  resistance  to 
the  King,  who  issued  a  Writ  on  the  3rd  of  September,  commanding 
the  Bishop  to  appear,  and  shew  cause,  at  Westminster  immediately 
after  Michaelmas.  By  a  happy  coincidence,  as  the  Bishop  tells  us, 
the  Provincial  Council  was  in  full  session  at  the  time,  and  he  resolved 
to  make  the  most  of  the  opportunity.  Accompanied  by  all  the 
Prelates  and  other  Magnates  of  the  Realm,  he  appeared  before  the 
Council,  which  was  presided  over  by  the  Duke  of  Cornwall,  in  the 
King's  absence;  and  the  case  was  heard  and  determined  in  the 
Bishop's  favour  by  an  unanimous  vote,  the  sentences  of  outlawry 
being  declared  null  and  void,  and  all  other  proceedings  of  the  Com- 
missioners within  the  two  Counties  suspended  till  the  next  Session 
of  Parliament.  By  this  time  Sodbury  was  penitent  enough,  and  the 
Duke  interceded  with  the  Bishop  on  his  behalf,  promising  for  him 
that  he  would  be  faithful  to  the  Church  for  the  time  to  come,  and 
make  amends  for  the  evil  that  he  had  wrought.  He  made  his 
submission  before  the  Provincial  Council;  and  on  the  21st of  October, 
in  the  presence  of  the  Archbishop  and  his  Suffragans,  Bishop  Gran- 
disson  absolved  him,  in  the  Lady-Chapel  of  St.  Paul's,  after  he  had 
taken  oath,  on  the  Archbishop's  Cross,  to  stand  by  the  Mandates  of 
the  Church. 

The  Bishop  left  London  shortly  after  these  events,  and  we  find  him 
at  Ottery  on  the  31st  of  October,  1342.1  He  remained  at  Exeter,  or 
in   its  neighbourhood,   till   the  beginning  of   May,    1343,   when  he

started  for  London,  on  his1  way  to  the  Roman  Court  at  Avignon. 
He  reached  Dover2  on  the  25th,  where  he  appointed  William  de

Though  it  was  dated  on  the  31st  of  October,  it  had  not  been

And,  certainly,  no  time  was  lost,  for  the  Acquittance  is  dated  only 
ten  days  later.4 

At  this  point,  the  character  of  the  Register  becomes  wholly  changed: 
with  few  exceptions,  only  the  more  important  Acts  of  the  Bishop 
are  recorded ;  and,  as  these  were,  in  nearly  every  case,  performed 
at  Exeter,  Clyst,  or  Chudleigh,  we  are  no  longer  able  to  follow 
his  movements  about  the  Diocese.  Dispensations,  Licences,  Letters- 
Dimissory,  and  the  like,  which  he  was  accustomed  to  issue  from 
all  sorts  of  places,  have  nearly  altogether  disappeared,  and  there 
can  be  no  doubt  that  they  were  recorded  in  separate  quaterni 
(which  have  been  lost),  as  they  were  at  the  beginning  of  his 
Episcopate.5  I  must  be  content,  therefore,  to  give  brief  notices 
of  the  more  important  of  the  existing  entries.6

On  the  18th  of  October,  1343,  the  Bishop  was  at  Bishop's  Tawton, 
keeping  the  Anniversary  of  his  Consecration  by  the  celebration 
of  Mass  in  the  Parish-Church  ;  and,  after  the  Gospel,  while  he  was 
preaching,  a  body  of  armed  men  suddenly  rushed  in,  intending,  it 
was  believed,  to  murder  him.  He  was  rescued  from  their  violence, 
for  the  Church  was  full  of  Clergy  and  Lay-folk  ;  and  he  immediately 
excommunicated  all  the  offenders — "sons  of  perdition,"  as  he  calls 
them,  "  blasphemous  and  barbarous  men,  behaving  like  infidels." 
This  outrage  was  due  to  the  old  enmity  against  Archdeacon  John 
de  Northwode,  the  Bishop's  nephew,  and  had  been  organized  by 
John  Peris,  an  intruder  who  claimed  the  Archdeaconry  of  Totnes 
for  himself  and  had  been  excommunicated.  Amongst  the  rioters 
were  John  atte  Watere,  of  Combe  Martyn,  the  pretender's  nephew, 
and  John  de  Bodevile,  his  cousin.1 

On  the  30th  of  November,  the  Bishop,  finding  it  necessary  to 
intervene  again  in  the  case  of  Bodmin  Priory  (which,  through  gross 
mismanagement,  was  being  brought  to  desolation),  wrote  to  the 
Prior  and  Convent  in  severe  terms,  telling  them  that  his  patience 
was  quite  exhausted,  and  that,  unless  they  immediately  obeyed  his 
Mandate,  the  Prior  would  be  deprived,  as  utterly  unworthy.2  On 
the  1st  of  December,  1346,  the  Bishop  issued  his  Mandate  for 
the  Visitation  of  the  Priory,  which  was  followed  on  the  20th  of  April, 
1347,  by  the  issue  of  an  Ordinance  for  its  reform  and  better  govern- 
ance, during  the  Suspension  of  the  Prior.3 

On  the  21st  of  December,  1345,  Juliana  Lampre,  who  had 
succeeded  Margaret  Aunger  as  Abbess  of  Canonsleigh,  received  her 
Benediction  at  Chudleigh.  An  interesting  account  is  given  of  all 
the  proceedings  in  her  election.4  Brother  John  Gras  (or  Cras),  Abbat 
of  Torre,  received  his  Benediction  at  the  same  time.  Polsloe  Priory 
became  vacant  on  the  15th  of  April,  1347,  by  the  death  of 
Margery  (or  Margaret)  de  Wydepole  ;  whose  successor,  Juliana 
de  Brutone,  was  elected  on  the  22ud  of  the  same  month  :  in  this 
case,  also,  a  full  account  of  the  proceedings  is  recorded.5 

The  Cathedral  was  the  scene  of  a  memorable  event  in  1347.

of  July  with  great  solemnity;  the  Bishops  of  Bath  and  Wells,

Newenhatn,  and  Buckfast  were  present  on  the  occasion  with  many 
Clerks,  and  Knights  and  other  laymen.      And  we  are  told  that,  after 
the  conclusion  of  the  ceremony,  the  Archbishop  rode  through  the 
streets  of  Exeter,    in    his   Pontificals,    on   a   palfrey   covered    with 
a  white  cloth,  after  the  custom  of  the  Roman  Court.1     Five  days 
later  he  was  commissioned  by  Bishop  Grandisson2  to  act  for  a  time, 
as   his   coadjutor;   and  it  is  recorded  that    "he   made  the  circuit 
of   nearly  the   whole    Diocese,   confirming  children   and   dedicating 
Churches,  etc."     It  is  probable  that  the  Bishop  availed  himself  of 
the  opportunity  to  make  this  arrangement,  that  he  might  be  free  to 
deal  with  certain  serious  disorders  in  the  north  of  his  Diocese,  which 
demanded  his  immediate  intervention.       The  peace  of  the  Church 
had,  for  a  long  time  past,  been  disturbed  and  the  Liberties  of  the 
Clergy  infringed,  by  influential  but  turbulent  laymen,  who  did  not 
hesitate  to  resort  to  acts  of  gross  violence,  in  order  to  secure  their 
ends.     They  had  been  denounced,  as  we  have  seen,  by  the  Council 
recently  held  in  London,  and  had  been  condemned  by  the  King  to 
whom  some  of  them  appealed;  and  these  excesses  were  not  confined  to 
the  Duchy  of  Cornwall,  but  were  rampant  in  all  parts  of  the  Province 
of  Canterbury.     The  King  was  greatly  moved  by  the  reports  which 
reached  him,  and  he  requested  the  Archbishop  and  Bishops  to  issue  a 
general  sentence  of  Excommunication  against  the  offenders,  and  that 
without  delay.3     The  chief  offender  in  the  Diocese  of  Exeter,  at  this 
time,  was  Sir  Theobald  de  Grenevile,  head  of  a  most  antient  and 
influential  Family  in   North  Cornwall,  who  had  been  lords  of  the 
great  Manors  of  Kilkhampton  and  Bideford  from  time  immemorial. 
He    wras    only    four     years     old     when     his     father,     Henry     de 
Grenevile,    died   in  1328;    so    he    must   have    been  in  his  twenty? 
third  year  at  this  time.     The  Bishop,   with  habitual  plainness  of 
speech,   describes  him  as  "  a  youthful   Knight,   or  rather  a   mere 
tyro,  prodigal  of  his  knightly  honour,  having  no  fear  of  God  before 
his  eyes,  no  reverence  for  the  Church  ;  regardless  of  the  opinion  of 
his  fellow  men  and  of  his  own  reputation.     When  he  ought  to  have 
stood  by  the  side  of  his  King  in  the  battlefield,  he  skulked  at  home ; 
and  when  he  brandished  his  sword,  it  was  not,  as  he  was  in  duty 
bound,  against  the  enemies  of  the  Church  and  Realm,  but  against 
God  himself,  His  Church  and  her  Ministers,  and  against  simple,  poor, 
and  unoffending  country-folk,  all  alike  the  objects  of  his  ungovern- 
able  rage."       He  had    many  adherents,  including  such  "  notorious 
malefactors  "  as  Thomas  de  Mertone,  Richard  Tyrel,  John  de  Lunes- 
cote,  and  John  Trenger;  a  significant  list,   shewing  how  widespread 
and  serious  were  the  dangers  which  Grandisson  had  to  face.     These 
men  and  their  retainers,   to  the    number   of   about  five   hundred, 
invaded  the  Manor  of  Bishop's  Tawton  on  the  24th  of  March,  1347,

at  dawn  of  day.  They  were  all  armed,  "  after  the  manner  of  men 
arrayed  for  mortal  combat "  ;  and,  having  disposed  their  forces  on 
every  side,  so  that  no  one  could  escape,  they  attacked  the  Manor-

by  surprise,  and  resistance  was  almost  impossible  ;  but  the  victims 
did  their  best  to  defend  themselves  and  were  mercilessly  maltreated, 
some  of  them  being  killed.1  All  the  offenders  were  excommunicated; 
but  the  rebellion,  for  it  was  nothing  else,  was  by  no  means  quelled. 
The  next  outrage  was  committed  in  Grenevile's  own  parish  of  Kilk- 
hampton.'  Thomas  de  Stapeldon,  who  had  been  Rector  since  1324,3 
died  in  1342  ;4  and  the  Bishop,  soon  afterwards,  sequestrated  all  the 
revenues  of  the  Benefice,  the  buildings  having  been  allowed  to  fall 
into  a  scandalous  state  of  dilapidation.5  The  Greneviles  were  the 
Patrons ;  but  Theobald  wras  a  minor  at  the  time,  and  the  right  of 
patronage  was  claimed  and  exercised  by  Sir  John  de  Raleghe,  of 
Charles,  who  presented  Thomas  de  Cruce,  Hector  of  Whitstone,  and 
the  Bishop  admitted  him.  But  Theobald  was  determined  that  his

the  new  Rector  ;  and  the  latter,  being  quite  unscrupulous,  forthwith 
intruded  himself  and  took  possession,  in  defiance  of  the  Bishop.  This

and,  of  course,  the  Bishop  could  not.  Monitions,  requisitions,  and

fused by  the  action  of  the  rival  Patrons,  who  had  carried  their  case

favour,  mistaking  the  case  (per  errorem),  and  the  Court  of  Canterbury, 
misled  by  their  error,  ordered  Walter  to  be  instituted  forthwith. 
The  Iiishop,  however,  immediately  declared  that  the  Admission  of

And  he  was  not  mistaken  ;  for  the  Roman  Court,  by  Decree,  restored 
the  expelled  Rector  to  his  Benefice,  and  condemned  the  intruder  in 
the  costs  of  the  suits,  requiring  him  to  refund  the  large  sum  of 
money  of  which  he  had  plundered  the  Benefice  during  his  usurpation. 
The  case  was  re-heard  in  the  King's  Court,  with  the  result  that  the 
former  Judgement  was  annulled,  and  Sir  Theobald  was  ordered  to 
refund  the  costs  which  he  had,  in  error,  recovered  from  Sir  John  de 
Raleghe.  The  proceedings  were,  officially,  reported  to  the  Bishop, 
who  was  directed  to  regard  the  Benefice  as  void,  and  admit  thereto 
any  fit  clerk  who  might  be  presented  to  him  by  Sir  John  de  Raleghe. 
But  Walter,  and  his  wrong-headed  Patron,  Sir  Theobald,  were  not 
disposed  of  so  easily,  and  they  did  not  hesitate  to  defy  both  the  Courts 
and  the  Bishop.  On  the  5th  of  July,  1348,  Grandisson  issued  a 
Commission  to  the  Abbat  of  Hartland  and  the  Prior  of  Launceston, 
who  were  directed  to  proceed  to  Kilkhampton  and  deal  with  the 
offenders  on  the  spot.1  They  were  warned  that  they  would  not  find 
the  task  an  easy  one,  as  it  was  known  that  Theobald  and  his  minions 
had  taken  possession  of  the  Church,  and  were  prepared  to  hold  it,  by 
force  of  arms,  against  all  comers.  This  was  not  encouraging ;  but  the 
two  Commissaries  set  out  on  their  dangerous  enterprise  on  the  22nd, 
and  on  the  30th  they  reported  the  results  to  the  Bishop.2  They  told 
him  that,  as  they  were  entering  a  narrow  lane  close  to  the  Rectory- 
house,  they  were  stopped  by  a  crowd  of  armed  men,  who  had  painted 
their  faces  or  wore  masks  lest  they  should  be  recognised,  and  dared 
them,  at  peril  of  their  lives,  to  approach  the  Church.  The  bows  of 
these  ruffians  were  bent ;  and,  as  the  Commissaries  and  their  atten- 
dants seemed  inclined,  for  the  moment,  to  hold  their  ground,  they 
were  immediately  attacked  with  the  utmost  violence ;  arrows  flew 
amongst  them  in  all  directions,  and  their  very  horses  were  belaboured 
with  clubs.  Resistance  was  out  of  the  question  ;  and,  to  save  their 
lives,  they  fled  from  the  place,  their  enemies  pursuing  them  along  the 
road  for  a  mile,  pelting  them  with  stones,  and  beating  brutally  some 
of  the  Abbat's  servants  whom  they  overtook.  The  ringleaders3  were 
Sir  Theobald,  Walter  de  Mertone,  his  intruded  nominee,  and  Thomas, 
Walter's  brother ;  who,  as  soon  as  the  defeated  Commissaries  were 
out  of  sight,  returned  to  the  Church,  with  their  followers,  and 
proceeded  to  fortify  it  effectually,  building  stone  walls  against  some 
of  the  windows.  They  all  remained  in  the  sacred  building  for 
several  days  and  nights,  defiling  it  abominably,  as  the  outraged 
Bishop  tells  us,  and  turning  it  into  a  den  of  thieves.  As  for  the 
Commissaries,  they  had  been  driven  out  of  Kilkhampton,  but  they 
were  not  utterly  defeated.  It  was  the  Feast  of  St.  Mary  Magdalene, 
and,  anticipating  their  failure  at  the  head-quarters  of  the  rebellion, 
they  had  requested  the  Vicars  of  three  adjacent  parishes,  Launcells,

Stratton,  and  Poughill,  to  keep  their  congregations  in  Church  as  long

the  14th  of  January,  1349-50,  Sir  Theobald,  accompanied  by  Sir 
John  de  Raleghe,  of  Beaudeport,  appeared  before  him  at  Chudleigh, 
and,  on  bended  knee,  confessed  his  sin  and  prayed  the  Bishop  to

in  full  in  the  Register),  was  read  by  Sir  John,  on  Grenevile's  behalf  ; 
and,  the  Bishop  having  addressed  him,  with  all  solemnity,  as  to  the 
heinousness  of  his  offences  against  God  and  the  Church,  he  was 
sworn  on  the  Holy  Gospels  to  be  obedient  and  faithful  for  the  time 
to  come;  his  sureties  being  Sir  John  de  Dynham,  Sir  John  de 
Raleghe,  and  Almaric  Fitz-Waryn,  Sheriff  of  Devon.  Thereupon 
the  Bishop  absolved  him,  enjoining  on  him,  as  part  of  his  penance, 
that  he  should  immediately  proceed  to  Ottery,  and  offer  a  wax  taper 
in  the  Collegiate  Church.  The  Precentor  of  Exeter,  the  Provost  of 
Glasney,  the  Precentor  of  Crediton,  and  nineteen  other  clericks  and 
laymen,  summoned  as  witnesses,  were  present  on  this  important

was,  soon  afterwards,  settled  by  compromise  :  Thomas  de  Cruce 
disappears  from  the  scene  ;  and  John  de  Raleghe,  priest,  was  insti-

of  Charles,  and  the  Bishop  now  admitted  him  on  the  presentation  of 
the  repentant  Sir  Theobald,  who  was  declared  to  be  the  true  Patron.3 
John  de  Engleborne,  Prior  of  Plympton,  died  on  the  14th  of 
September,  1347,  and  was  succeeded  by  Brother  Robert  de  Forde  on

who  was  instituted  to  the  Vicarage0  on  the  21st  of  September,  1347,

within  little  more  than  a  month,  on  the  28th  of  October,  the  Bishop 
issued  his  Ordinance,  securing  to  the  Vicar  and  his  successors  a  very

The  times  were  lawless,  especially  in  this  remote  far-western  land  ; 
and  before  the  troubles  in  North  Devon  were  settled  the  Bishop  was 
compelled  to  cope  with  a  serious  outbreak  in  the  extreme  south  of 
the  County.  There  had  been  dissensions  for  some  time,  in  several 
parishes;  and,  at  last,  the  Archdeacon  of  Totnes,  John  de  North- 
wode,  sent  William  de  Tounstalle,  to  make  inquiry  on  the  spot,  and 
try  to  restore  peace  between  the  disputants.  The  Commissary  sum- 
moned the  parties  to  appear  before  him  in  the  Parish- Church  of 
Yealmpton ;  but  no  sooner  had  he  taken  his  seat  at  the  High  Altar, 
and  attempted  to  open  the  proceedings,  than  he  was  set  upon  by  a 
howling  mob — "  sons  of  perdition,"  as  Grandisson  called  them, — 
about  two  hundred  of  whom,  armed  to  the  teeth,  made  their  way 
through  the  Church,  assailed  Tounstalle  and  the  Advocates  and 
Proctors  who  were  with  him  with  drawn  swords,  and,  snatching  out 
of  their  hands  the  Rolls  and  Registers  and  other  Muniments  of  the 
Archdeaconry,  drove  them  all  out  of  the  Church,  assaulting  them 
violently  as  they  fled.  Murder  would,  doubtless,  have  been  com- 
mitted, the  Bishop  tells  us,  had  not  a  brave  Lady,  Dame  Margaret 
de  Monthermer,  whose  house  was  close  to  the  Church,  opened  her 
doors  to  the  fugitives  and  sheltered  them  from  "  the  satellites  of 
Satan."  "  0  how  wretched  and  miserable  is  our  fate,"  he  exclaimed, 
as  he  wrote  his  Mandate,  and,  after  his  manner,  committed  the 
utterance  which  was  forced  from  him  to  his  pen,  for  us, — "  what 
place  can  ever  be  safe,  who  among  us  can  ever  feel  secure,  if  even 
the  Church  is  exposed  to  such  calamities,  and  the  Clergy,  her 
favoured  sons,  to  such  dreadful  peril?"  He  wrote  on  the  21st  of 
March,  1347-8,  to  the  Abbat  of  Tavistock,  the  Prior  of  Plympton, 
the  Kectors  of  North  Bovey  and  Petertavy,  and  the  Vicar  of  Suttone, 
commanding  them  to  meet  in  the  parish-church  of  Suttone  on  the 
13th  of  April,  Palm-Sunday,  there  to  pronounce  Sentence  of  Ex- 
communication against  all  the  offenders,  whose  absolution,  on  their 
submission,  he  reserved  specially  to  himself.2

Pestilence,  which,  originating  in  the  Far  East  and  following  the 
trade-routes,  had  already  overspread  great  part  of  Europe,  reached 
our  shores  at  the  port  of  Melcombe-Regis  (Weymouth),  in  Dorset- 
shire.1 It  spread  with  great  rapidity  through  the  Southern  and 
Western  Counties,  carrying  death  and  desolation  in  every  direction, 
and  especially  in  Devonshire  ;  in  Cornwall,  apparently,  except  in  a 
few  localities,  and  notably  at  Bodmin,  the  visitation  was  less  severely 
felt.  We  do  not  know  exactly  when  it  entered  the  Diocese;  pro- 
bably, as  early  as  July.  The  average  number  of  Institutions  in 
ordinary  years,  on  avoidance  by  death,  resignation,  or  exchange, 
was  thirty-six,  and  in  June  1348,  there  were  only  three  Institutions ; 
but  in  July  there  were  eight,  which  would  give  a  yearly  average 
of  ninety -six  ;  in  August  there  were  only  three  (the  normal  number) ; 
but  it  must  be  remembered  that  Institution  did  not,  as  a  rule, 
follow  immediately  on  a  vacancy,  and  this  would  be  true,  especially, 
of  the  period  in  question,  when  the  sudden  outbreak  of  the  plague 
had  thrown  everything  into  confusion.  In  September  there  were 
seven,  bringing  the  annual  average  up  to  eighty-four.  In  October2 
there  were  only  two ;  which  does  not  prove  that  there  were  fewer 
deaths  amongst  the  Beneficed  Clergy,  but  rather  that,  in  the  general

Monasteries  suffered  most  severely,  and  in  many  instances  were 
almost  depopulated.  At  Newenhain,  for  instance,  Abbat  Walter  de  la 
Houe,  and  two  of  his  Monks,  alone  survived  j  no  fewer  than  twenty 
Monks  and  three  lay-brothers  having  been  cut  off.1  At  Bodmin  the

Bishop's  intervention  having  been  found  necessary,  a  full  account  of 
the  visitation  and  its  results  is  given  in  the  Register.2  John  de

Honytone  and  William  de  Tregawythan.  These  terrified  survivors

him  that  they  wrere  left  like  orphans,  and  entreating  him  to  provide 
a  Superior  for  their  House  as  quickly  as  possible.  On  the  19th  the 
Bishop  wrote  to  the  Prior  of  Launceston,  telling  him  of  this  Letter, 
and  adding  that,  as  he  could  not  see  his  wTay  to  appoint  either  of  the

of  his  House,  Brother  Oger  Bante,  in  whose  general  fitness  and 
prudence  he  had  all  confidence.  The  Prior  of  Launceston  replied 
on  the  2 1st,  consenting  to  the  Bishop's  proposal,  but  saying  that  he 
did  so  writh  great  reluctance,  as  he  could  ill  spare  a  Brother  so

was  past :  there  were,  indeed,  eight  Institutions  in  June  ;  fifteen  in

become  vacant  when  the  plague  was  at  its  height,  and  to  many 
Benefices  the  Bishop,  as  before,  was  left  to  collate  by  lapse.2

at  Chudleigh,  on  the  16th  of  August,  1336,1  was  reopened  by  the 
King  on  the  18th  of  February.  1351-2.  The  King's  Writ  and  the 
Bishop's  Return  are  given  in  the  Register,  together  with  a  Letter 
addressed  to  the  Bishop  on  the  23rd  of  February  and  his  reply

It  appears  that,  in  the  interval,  the  Dean  and  the  Prebendaries 
had  rebelled  again,  repudiating  the  Bishop's  Jurisdiction,  but  expect- 
ing him,  as  they  could  not  dispense  with  his  services  altogether,  to 
ordain  and  confirm  at  their  bidding,  and  to  send  them  the  Holy  Oil 
whenever  they  required  a  supply.  Of  course,.  Grandisson  refused  to 
be  made  a  mere  episcopal  hack  after  this  fashion,  and  the  King 
commanded  him  to  shew  cause  for  his  refusal  before  the  18th  of 
March.  His  claim  to  exercise  Jurisdiction  was  indisputable,  as  he 
had  no  difficulty  in  shewing;  but  the  King  and  the  Duke  had  made 
up  their  minds,  and  he  was  forced  to  submit.  From  that  time  till 
the  preferment  of  Dean  Stanhope,2  in  1817,  the  Deans  received  Insti- 
tution from  the  King,  or  from  the  Duke  of  Cornwall,  as  Ordinary. 
Grandisson,  was,  of  course,  greatly  moved  ;  and,  when  his  clerk 
brought  to  him,  for  his  signature,  the  fair  copy  of  his  Return,  he 
could  not  resist  the  temptation  to  speak  his  mind, — 

"  J.  Exon.,  by  my  own  hand.  And  I  would  that  my  Lords  the 
King  and  the  Prince,  and  his  lieges,  could  only  know  all  the  circum- 
stances of  this  business ;  for  then  they  would  clearly  see  and  would 
determine  that,  for  the  avoiding  of  all  manner  of  perils,  it  is  far  better 
that  these  men  should  submit  themselves  to  their  Bishops  than  that 
they  should  thus,  with  no  one  to  rule  over  them,  be  left  to  perish 
utterly.  For  who  can  absolve  them  from  such  outrageous  sins  and 
excesses  as  they  have  been  guilty  of,  apart  from  the  authority  of 
the  Apostolick  See  ?  For  very  shame  I  hold  my  peace  as  to  the 
reports  which  have  reached  me.  But  I  may  be  permitted  to  speak 
as  to  things  which  are  manifest  to  all  men.  Forasmuch  as  they  are 
herded  together,  like  brute  beasts,  in  the  very  tail  of  the  world,  they 
contract  marriages  within  all  prohibited  degrees,  and  get  themselves 
divorced  when  they  have  been  married  lawfully.  And  so  they  fall 
under  the  Sentences  imposed  by  Canon-Law,  and  never  rise  up  again."3

blood,  commanding  ns,  by  the  mouth  of  His  Apostle,  to  live,  as  far 
as  lieth  in  us,  at  peace  with  all  men.1  In  the  following  year  the 
French  were  totally  defeated,  on  the  19th  of  September,  at  Poitiers, 
and  the  French  King  was  amongst  the  prisoners.  On  the  10th 
of  October  the  King  ordered  his  subjects  to  join  him  in  giving  God 
thanks  for  this  signal  success  ;2  and  on  the  28th  our  Bishop 
complied  with  the  terms  of  the  Mandate, — "  pro  capcione  Regis 
Francie  "  :  it  was  a  glorious  victory ;  but  let  us,  he  wrote,  implore 
our  Saviour,  Who  hath  shewed  so  great  a  token  upon  us  for  good,  to 
over-rule  it  all  to  the  increase  of  His  own  praise  and  the  comfort  and 
peace  of  His  people.3  No  reference  is  made  to  the  landing  of  the 
Royal  prisoner  at  Sandwich  in  1357,  or  to  his  being  set  at  liberty  in 
1360,  only  to  find  that  he  could  not  govern  his  subjects  under  the 
terms  of  release  imposed  on  him  by  the  victors ;  but  we  ha^e  a  copy 
of  a  Letter  addressed  by  the  Bishop  to  his  Diocese  on  the  25th  of 
September,  1359,  shortly  before  the  renewal  of  hostilities,  in  which 
he  exhorts  the  Faithful  to  pray  earnestly  for  the  success  and  safety 
of  the  King  and  the  Prince  and  their  army,  trusting  in  the  King  of 
Kings  and  the  grace  of  His  Heavenly  succour.4 

On  the  25th  of  July,  1331,  Ralph  de  Tremur  was  instituted5  to 
Warleggan,  in  Cornwall,  on  the  resignation  of  his  uncle,  John6 :  they 
were  of  an  antient  family  long  seated  at  Tremur,  a  manor  in  the 
adjacent  parish  of  Lanivet.  The  parish  is  remote  and  small,  con- 
sisting of  a  narrow  strip  of  land  between  the  parishes  of  Blisland  and 
St.  Neot,  and  bounded  on  the  north  by  Temple  and  the  Bodmin 
Moors ;  an  insignificant  Benefice  in  itself,  but  it  was  destined,  as  we 
shall  see,  to  become  famous  throughout  the  land.  At  the  time  of  his 
Institution  he  appears  to  have  been  studying  in  Oxford,  and  he  at 
once  obtained  Licence  of  non-residence  for  a  year  from  the  ensuing 
Michaelmas,  the  Bishop  requiring  him  to  take  accolite's  and  sub- 
deacon's  Orders  forthwith,  and  granting  him  Letters-Dimissory.7  On 
the  17th  of  October,  1332,  this  Licence  was  renewed  for  another 
year,8  and  again,  for  yet  another  year,  on  the  10th  of  October,  1333.9 
It  is  evident  that  he  preferred  residence  in  the  University  to  the 
quiet  routine  of  a  country  clergyman's  life  in  the  wilds  of  Cornwall ; 
and  in  September,  1334,  he  resigned  Warleggan.10  After  this  he  is 
not  mentioned  in  the  Register  for  the  space  of  twenty  years.  In  the 
interval  he  had  taken  deacon's  Orders ;  and  he  must  have  devoted 
himself  assiduously  to  his  studies  at  Oxford,  for  the  Bishop  tells  us 
that  he  was  a  renowned  Master  of  Arts,  and  a  learned  grammarian, 
able  to  speak  fluently  in  four  languages,   in   Latin,    French,  and 

1  p.  1173.     3  p.  1191.     5  p.  1285.     7  p.  627.     9  p.  715. 

2  p.  1190.     4  p.  1200.     6  p.  621.      8  p.  660.     10  p.  1303.

English,  and  in  the  Cornish  and  Breton  tongue."1  But  he  adds  that 
he  was  ashamed  to  remember  that  Tremur  was  a  native  of  the  Diocese 
of  Exeter,  for  he  was  a  most  determined  heretick,  and  spent  his  time 
in  wandering  about  Devon  and  Cornwall,  and  in  many  other  parts  of 
England,  spreading  his  pernicious  errors,  which  were  all  the  more 
dangerous  because  he  was  such  a  learned  man.  The  case  is  of  con- 
siderable interest ;  for  Tremur  must  be  regarded  as,  in  some  sort, 
the  pioneer  of  the  "New  Learning," — "un  savant  diacre,"  to  quote 
the  words  of  a  Reviewer  of  my  Books,  "  qui  trente  ans  avant  Wy  cliff e, 
allait  prechant  un  peu  partout  contre  le  dogme  de  la  transsubstantia- 
tion."2  This  man,  says  the  Bishop  (in  a  letter  addressed  through  his 
Official  Principal,  the  Dean,  and  the  four  Archdeacons,  to  the  whole 
Diocese,3  on  the  7th  of  March,  1354-5),  has  lapsed  into  deadly  heresy 
touching  the  Sacrament  of  our  Lord's  Body  and  Blood — "  the  Sacra- 
ment in  which  all  other  Sacraments  are  completed,  perfected,  and 
established ;  by  which  the  people  of  Christ  are  daily  refreshed 
spiritually,  that  they  may  not  faint  by  the  way ;  than  which  it  is 
impossible  to  imagine  anything  more  worthy,  or  more  conducive  to 
the  salvation  of  men,  seeing  that  thereby  the  Faithful  grow  in  grace, 
through  the  corporal,  though  invisible,  Presence  of  their  Saviour. 
Our  Lord,  Who  is  the  Truth,  said — My  Flesh  is  meat  indeed,  a?ul  My 
Blood  is  drink  indeed ;  and,  again,  Except  ye  eat  the  Flesh  of  the  Son 
of  Man,  and  drink  his  Blood,  ye  have  no  life  in  you  :  he  that  eateth 
My  Flesh  and  drinketh  My  Blood  hath  eternal  life,  and  I  will  raise 
him  up  at  the  last  day ;  and,  after  His  Resurrection,  before  he 
ascended,  in  the  body,  into  Heaven,  He  made  promise  to  His  disciples, 
referring  to  this  Sacrament,  and  saying — Lo,  I  am  with  you  all  the 
days,  even  unto  the  end  of  the  world.  But  this  man  proclaims  openly 
and  teaches  in  secret  otherwise  than  the  Holy  Catholick  and 
Apostolick  Church  believes,  preaches,  and  affirms ;  erroneously  and 
heretically  asserting  and  maintaining  that  the  bread  and  wine  are 
not  changed  substantially,  by  the  words  of  Consecration,  into  the 
Flesh  and  Blood  of  our  Lord  Jesus  Christ ;  which  manifestly,  and 
beyond  all  doubt,  is  to  subvert  entirely  the  Catholick  Faith,  to  make 
void  every  one  of  the  Sacraments,  and  utterly  to  destroy  the  Truth 
of  the  Gospel.  Worse  than  all,  he  does  his  best,  through  the  malice 
of  the  devil,  not  only  to  lead  others  along  with  himself  to  destruction, 
but  to  secure  the  secret  support,  for  the  purpose  of  spreading  his 
execrable  errors,  of  simple  and  unlearned  folk,  ignorant  of  Theological 
Verities,  and  already  prone  to  heresy."  In  recording  facts  of  history 
we  are,  of  course,  bound  to  put  ourselves,  as  far  as  possible,  in  the 
place  of  the  parties  concerned,  abstaining  from  all  comment  and 
controversy,  and  allowing  the  actors  to  speak  for  themselves ;  and, 
knowing,  as  we  do,  how  greatly  the  Bishop  must  have  been  moved

by  the  promulgation  in  his  Diocese  of  a  doctrine  which  he  could  not 
but  regard  as  being  destructive  of  the  faith  and  teaching  of  the 
Church,  we  shall  not  be  surprised  by  the  strength  of  the  language  with

detestable  tongue,  more  poisonous  than  the  tongue  of  any  mad  dog, 
which  ought  to  be  cut  out  by  the  chirurgeons  of  the  Church  and  of 
the  Crown,  to  be  torn  into  little  bits,  and  cast  to  pigs  and  swine  !  " 
He  cited  Tremur  to  appear  before  him,  if  he  could  be  found,  and 
ordered  the  Mandate  to  be  read,  during  Mass,  in  the  Cathedral,  and 
in  every  Church  in  the  Diocese,  forbidding  the  Faithful,  under  pain 
of  Excommunication,  to  hold  any  sort  of  intercourse  with  the 
offender  ;  "  they  were  not  to  speak  to  him,  or  sit  near  him,  or  eat  or 
drink  with  him,  or  pray  with  him,  or  encourage  him  in  any  way, 
by  receiving  him  into  their  houses,  shewing  him  hospitality,  taking  his 
part,  or  supplying  him  with  anything  that  might  help  him  to  do  his 
deadly  work  ;  but  they  were  to  shun  him  utterly  till  the  time  should 
come  when  he  would  no  longer  walk  in  darkness  but  in  the  light." 
So  the  Bishop  was  then,  at  any  rate,  hopeful.  But  Ave  gather  from 
a  Letter  which  he  wrote,  about  a  year  later,  to  the  Bishop  of  London, 
that  he  had  found  the  case  a  hopeless  one.1  In  the  interval  he  had 
been  collecting  evidence,  and  he  brings  a  series  of  charges  against 
Tremur  which  certainly  prove  that  he  was  a  violent  and  lawless  man, 
"  This  iniquitous  and  blasphemous  fellow,"  he  WTOte,  "  vilifying  the 
Catholick  Faith  (and  that  not  only  in  the  Diocese  of  Exeter,  but  in 
that  of  London  also)  has  had  the  audacity  to  say,  in  the  presence  of 
many  persons  of  repute, — c  Ye  adore,  idiotically,  the  work  of  your 
own  hands  :  for  what  doth  a  priest  do  but  gape  over  a  small  bit  of 
bread  and  breathe  upon  it  1 '  Moreover,  deriding  Blessed  Peter,  he 
declared  him  to  have  been  a  mere  empty-pated  rustick  ;  and  he  called 
John,  the  Blessed  Evangelist,  a  false  and  lying  witness,  because  he  said 
of  himself  that  he  was  the  Disciple  whom  Jesus  loved  ;  and,  again, 
This  is  the  Disciple  which  beareth  ivitness  of  these  things,  and  we  know

than  these  and  more  horrible  to  pious  ears  ;  for,  secretly  stealing  from 
a  Church  the  Pyx  which  contained  Christ's  Body,  he  conveyed  it  into  a 
house,  took  out  the  Sacrament  and  threw  it  into  the  fire,  and  carried 
the  Pyx  away  with  him."  Moreover,  some  years  after  he  had  resigned 
Warleggan,  he  returned  to  the  place,  intruding  himself  with  much 
violence  on  the  Rector,  his  lawful  successor,  robbing  him  of  his  goods, 
and  then  setting  fire  to  his  house  !  Tremur  had  been  excommuni- 
cated by  the  Court  of  Canterbury,  when  Simon  de  Islepe  was  Dean  of 
the  Arches,  and  therefore  before  October,  1349,  when  he  became 
Archbishop.  But  Grandisson  was  not  satisfied,  and  he  pleaded  for  the 
degradation  of  the  offender.     "  I  have  done  everything  in  my  power,"

he  tells  the  Bishop  of  London,  "  and  I  have  been  careful  to  lay  before 
my  Lord  of  Canterbury  all  the  facts  of  the  case  :  unless  justice  be  done, 
I  will  deliver  my  own  soul  by  appealing  to  the  Apostolick  See."  There 
is  no  record  as  to  the  result ;  neither  is  Tremur  mentioned  again  in 
the  Register.  That,  in  spite  of  his  learning,  he  was  an  unscrupulous 
and  dangerous  fanatick  no  one  can  doubt ;  by  some  he  was  thought 
to  be  a  lunatick  ;  but  Grandisson  did  not  think  so,  maintaining 
throughout  that  there  was  too  much  method  in  his  madness. 

William,  Lord  Grandisson,  the  Bishop's  father,  died  on  the  27th 
of  June,  1335,  his  wife,  Sybilla,  having  predeceased  him  on  the  21st 
of  September,  1334.  Peter,  his  son  and  heir,  succeeded  him,  and 
died  without  issue,  on  the  10th  of  August,  1358,  the  Bishop  suc- 
ceeding to  his  honours,  but  not  to  his  estates.  He  was,  perhaps, 
as  his  biographer  says,  "  the  wealthiest  Lord  Bishop  that  Exeter 
had  hitherto  possessed,"1  but,  mainly,  as  the  result  of  his  frugality 
and  self-denial.  His  munificence  was  boundless;  and  his  gifts 
to  the  Cathedral  are  described  as  countless  by  the  compiler  of  a 
catalogue2  of  such  gifts,  beginning  with  those  of  the  first  Bishop, 
Leofric.  He  gave,  we  are  told,  "all  the  Books  of  the  Choir; 
Vestments  of  every  colour ;  Ornaments  and  jewels  of  gold  and  silver 
and  of  other  material,  the  number  of  which  is  not  fully  recorded, 
here  or  elsewhere,  because  in  his  lifetime  and  after  his  death  they 
were  multiplied  beyond  number;  as  God  knoweth  Who  knoweth  all 
things."3

The  Bishop's  Will  was  dated  at  Chudleigh,  on  the  8th  of  September,1 
1368.  It  is  an  elaborate  and  most  interesting  Document,  and  I  have 
printed  it  at  length,  with  a  translation2,  in  the  Appendix.  He  died, 
at  Chudleigh,  on  the  16th  of  July,  1369,  the  morrow  of  St.  Swithun's 
Day,  in  the  77th  year  of  his  age  and  the  42nd  of  his  Episcopate ;  and 
he  was  buried  in  St.  Radegunde's  Chapel,  just  outside  the  great  west 
door  of  the  Cathedral,  without  ostentation  or  display,  as  he  had 
been  most  careful  to  direct.  Would  that  it  were  possible  for  me  to 
end  my  narrative  here  !  But,  alas,  it  is  my  melancholy  duty  to 
record  that,  about  two  hundred  years  later,  his  modest  but  most 
venerable  tomb  was  brutally  desecrated,  and  his  bones  torn  from 
what  should  have  been  their  last  and  honoured  resting  place,3 — an 
indelible  blot  on  the  fair  fame  of  Exeter,  and  on  the  memory, 
especially,  of  those  who,  as  Guardians  of  the  Church  which  owed  so 
much  to  the  great  Bishop's  munificence  and  zeal,  were,  surely,  bound 
to  secure  his  grave  against  outrage  and  pollution.  I  find  it  impossible 
to  believe  that  such  a  deed  could  have  been  perpetrated,  whether  by 
ignorant  fanaticks  or  by  mere  robbers  of  churches  in  quest  of  trea- 
sure, without  the  knowledge,  I  refrain  from  saying  the  connivance,

of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of  the  day.1  But  the  times  were  dark  and

evil  day  which  saw  both  Church  and  King  go  down,  for  a  season,

The  precise  date  of  the  sacrilege  is  not  known.  Hoker,  writing  in 
1599,  tells  us  that  "his  tombe  was  of  late  pulled  up,  the  ashes 
scattered  abroad,  and  the  bones  bestowed  no  man  knoweth  where." 
Westcote,  whose  "Survey  of  Devon"  was  completed  in  1630,  tells 
us,  in  language  which,  certainly,  seems  to  reflect  on  the  Cathedral 
authorities  (for  he  gives  particulars  as  from  the  testimony  of  an 
eye-witness),  that  "he  was  taken  up,  shrouded  in  lead,  not  long  since, 
the  lead  melted,  and  the  Chapel  defaced — an  unworthy  deed  ;  and 
it  is  to  me  a  marvel  that  they  escaped  unpunished,  in  regard  the  very 
heathen  had  laws  against  violating  or  defacing  of  monuments  or 
sepulchres."  And  Izacke  refers  in  his  "Memorials"  to  this  monstrous 
wickedness  in  terms  which  I  endorse  with  all  my  heart, — "  Surely, 
the  reliques  of  this  worthy  Prelate  deserved  a  more  reverend  respect, 
even  amongst  savage  beasts."  I  shudder  whenever  I  pass,  by  the 
desecrated  spot,  into  the  glorious  Nave,  the  abiding  memorial  of  his 
surpassing  genius,  princely  munificence,  and  life-long  piety.  Lux 
perpetua  luceat  ei,  cum  Sanctis  Tuis  in  eternum,  quia  pius  es. 

F.  C.  H.  R. 

Ringmore  Rectory,  1  Sept.,  1899.

Chapter  ;  not,  I  need  scarcely  say,  from  any  motive  of  curiosity,  but  with 
all  becoming  sympathy  and  reverence.  It  was  found  that  the  grave  had  been 
ransacked  utterly  ;  nothing  was  discovered  but  a  fragment  or  two  of  lead  !  I  may 
add,  and  I  do  so  with  full  appreciation  and  gratitude,  that  the  present  Dean,  Dr. 
Cowie,  has  filled  the  west  window  of  the  south  aisle  of  the  Nave  with  stained

be  painted  on  the  ashlar  of  the  wall,  under  the  window,  which  is  close  to  the

was  the  poet  and  warrior  Chaucer  referred  to  at  the  end  of  his  Comphynt 
of  Venus  (Skeat's  Chaucer,  vol.  i,  p.  404). — J.  N.  D. 
Page  " Probably  consecrated  on  21  Nov.,  1367." — This  date  (21  Nov.)  was,  appar- 
xxv.  ently,  taken  from  the  Exeter  Kalendar  (prefixed  to  the  Chronicon 
Exoniense),  where  against  it  (11  Kal.  Dec.)  is  written — "  Dedicacio  Exonie, 
majus  duplex."  The  21st  of  November  is  the  Feast  of  the  Presentation  of 
the  B.  V.  M.,  and  it  may  have  been  supposed  that  Bishop  Grandisson  selected 
the  day  for  that  reason.  But  Pope  Paul  II  first  commanded  this  Festival  to 
be  observed  in  1464,  a  century  after  Grandisson's  time.  Of  course,  the  entry 
in  the  Kalendar  refers  to  the  original  Dedication  of  the  Cathedral  by  Bishop 
Marshall.  As  for  the  year — 1367 — it  is  a  mere  conjecture,  without  even  a 
shadow  of  proof. — F.  J.  B. 
Page  The  Patrons  of  Abbat  Bonus  referred  to,  here,  as  "  de  Peragrua,  de  Garvo, 
xxvii.  and  de  Mota,"  were  Arnaldus  de  Pelagrua,  created  Cardinal  Deacon  of 
St.  Mary  in  Porticu  by  Clement  V,  at  Lyons,  18  Dec,  1305,  who  died  at 
Avignon  in  1335  ;  Bernardus  de  Garvo,  created  Cardinal  Deacon  of 
St.  Eustachius'  by  the  same  Pope,  19  Dec,  1310  (he  was  afterwards 
Cardinal  Priest  of  St.  Clement's  and  died  at  Avignon  in  the  Pontificate  of 
John  XXII) ;  and  Gailardus  de  Mota  who  was  created  Cardinal  Deacon  of 
St.  Lucy's  in  Silice,  at  Avignon,  by  John  XXII,  17  Dec,  1316.  He  was 
Archdeacon  of  Oxford  1312 — 1345,  and  died  at  Avignon  in  1357. — F.  J.  B. 
Page  See  the  Kalendar  of  Papal  Registers,  vol.  ii,  page  290  (ed.  Bliss),  for  an 
xxxiii.  Indult  dated  14  July,  1329, — "To  Simon,  Archbishop  of  Canterbury. — 
The  ill-health  of  his  predecessors,  Robert  and  Walter,  has  hindered 
Visitations  being  made  for  so  many  years  that  a  doubt  has  arisen  as  to  the 
order  in  which  they  are  to  be  taken.  Indult  to  visit  his  Province  in  the 
following  order, — first,  his  own  Chapter  and  Diocese  ;  and  then  whatever 
Diocese  seems  most  to  need  it."  Probably,  it  was  under  this  Indult  that 
Mepeham  wished  to  visit  the  Diocese  of  Exeter  ;  and  it  would  seem  that 
no  Visitation  had  been  held  within  the  Province  since  Archbishop  Peckham's 
time,  in  1282,  except  in  the  case  of  vacant  Dioceses. — F.  J.  B. 


I  have  already  (vol.  i,  page  vii)  expressed  my  thanks  to  the  kind  Friends  who, 
for  many  years,  have  assisted  me  in  my  work.  Mr.  Baigent,  I  need  scarcely 
repeat,  has  helped  me  with  all  his  heart,  and  in  every  possible  way ;  and  I  am 
specially  indebted  to  him  for  his  great  kindness  in  compiling  the  admirably 
arranged  Pedigree  of  the  Grandisson  Family  which  enriches  the  present  Volume. 
I  have,  also,  received  great  assistance  from  Canon  Dalton,  of  Windsor,  Canon 
Edmonds,  of  Exeter,  Mr.  Macray,  of  the  Bodleian,  and  Professor  Meyer,  of  Paris. 
Alas,  I  have  to  mourn  the  loss  of  my  other  helpers,  who  have  been  called  away 
since  the  publication  of  the  First  Volume  of  this  Register, — Winslow  Jones, 
John  Maclean,  Charles  William  Boase,  Benjamin  Wyatt  Greenfield,  John  Ingle 
Dredge.  I  cannot  say  how  much  I  miss  their  most  useful  and  almost  continuous 
letters,  and  their  never-failing  encouragement  and  support.  May  they  rest  in 
peace  ! — If  I  am  spared  to  complete  the  two  Volumes  of  Bishop  Brantingham's 
fine  Register,  which  covers  the  interval  between  Bishop  Grandisson's  Register  and 
Bishop  Stafford's  (published  in  1886),  my  Series  will  be  complete  for  the  space  of 
nearly  200  years.  I  dare  not  venture  to  look  beyond  ;  neither,  on  the  other  hand, 
do  I  venture  to  assign  any  limitation  to  a  work  which  ought  to  be  continued,  by 
myself  or  by  another,  to  the  end  of  the  Medieval  period,  when  our  Registers 
become  little  more  than  Registers  of  Institutions  to  Benefices.  My  mind  is  to 
work  on  till,  my  eyes  becoming  dim  and  my  natural  force  abated,  I  am  compelled 
to  leave  to  others  the  completion  of  a  work,  which,  our  Lord  blessing  my 
endeavours,  I  have  carried  so  far  towards  completion.— Nunc  mea  ;  mox  hujus  ; 
set  crastina  nescio  cujus.

occurs  as  Treasurer  "  20th  Sept., 
1367  {Reg.  Ebor.)."  Oliver  omits  his 
name  ;  but  I  find  that  he  did  enjoy 
this  Dignity,  for  he  is  mentioned  as 

B2 


Treasurer  in  Bishop  Brantingham's 
Register  (vol.  i,  fol.  43),  19  Nov., 
1373.  He  had  been  appointed  War- 
den of  the  Collegiate  Chapel  of  St. 
George,  in  Windsor  Castle,  as  early 
as  18  June,  1349,  when  he  succeeded 
the  first  Warden,  John  de  la  Chambre, 
who  held  the  Office  only  for  a  few 
months,  and  was,  probably,  one  of 
the  victims  of  the  "  Black  Death." 
Mugge  retained  the  Office  till  his 
death  in  1380.

1  Nicholas  Makerel  (called  "  de  Carle- 
tone  ")  and  John  Tregoit  are  the  first 
Rector  and  Vicar  of  this  Parish  whose 
names  are  on  record.  After  them 
there  was  a  continuous  series  of 
Rectors  and  Vicars  down  to  the  year 
1844.  William  Greswell,  the  28th 
Rector  after  Carletone,  was  instituted 
in  1830  and  resigned  in  1840.  The 
32nd  Vicar  after  Tregoit  was  Robert 


Scott,  afterwards  Master  of  Balliol, 
and  Dean  of  Rochester.  When  Gres- 
well resigned  Scott  was  instituted  to 
the  Rectory,  retaining  the  Vicarage, 
the  two  Benefices  being  united  in  his 
person.  His  successor,  Paul  Bush, 
now  Honorary  Canon  of  Truro,  is 
Rector  of  "the  United  Rectory  and 
Vicarage  of  Duloe,"  to  which  he  was 
instituted  27  July,  1850.

Exeter  Cathedral  ;  Prebends1, — 

Master  William  de  Crauthorne  and 

Master  John  de  Northwode  exchanged  their  Prebends,  3  Oct. 
Item,  tercio  die  Octobris,  in  deambulatorio  juxta  Capellam  de  Cliste,  coram 
Domino,   Magistri  Willelmus  de  Crauthorne,   Canonicus  Exonie,  et  Pre- 


1  That  there  should  be  any  such  Ex- 
change as  this  seems,  at  first  sight, 
unaccountable  ;  for  the  Prebends  in 
the  Cathedral  were  all  of  equal 
value,  a  fact  which  is  frequently 
mentioned  in  the  Registers ;  no 
estates  or  property  of  any  kind 
were  appropriated  to  any  of  them  ; 
and,  consequently,  they  had  no 
names.  The  stalls  were  not  occupied 
in  consecutive  order,  according  to 
seniority,  as  Dr.  Oliver  supposed 
(History  of  the  Bishops  of  Exeter, 
pp.  220*,  221).  All  the  Prebendaries, 
as  Prebendaries,  were  of  equal  rank, 
and  a  junior  Prebendary,  just  col- 


lated, would  be  installed  not  (as  it 
were)  "  in  the  lowest  room,"  but  in 
the  Stall  which  had  been  occupied  by 
his  predecessor,  wherever  it  might 
be.  Exchanges  were  occasionally  de- 
sired for  reasons  which  had  nothing 
to  do  with  the  value  or  dignity  of 
the  Benefice,  but  on  personal  grounds; 
for  instance,  a  Prebendary  who  had 
weak  sight  might  desire  to  secure 
better  light  by  changing  from  one 
side  of  the  Choir  to  the  other  ;  or  a 
man  whose  hearing  was  defective 
might  desire  to  be  nearer  the  High 
Altar  or  the  singers.  In  every  case 
a  formal  process  was  necessary.

de  Louepitte,  nostre  Diocesis,  quam  dilecti  filii,  Abbas  et  Conventus  Monas- 
terii  de  Nyweham  .  .  .  tenent  et  possident  eis  et  eorum  Monasterio  appro- 
priatam  Canonice  et  unitam,  ordinare,  ponere,  et  taxare,  vocatis  eisdem 
Abbate  et  Conventu  et  aliis  in  hac  parte  vocandis,  de  facultatibus  et  oneri- 
busdicte  Ecclesie  informacionem  solertem  recepimus  et  fidelem.  Et  demum, 
de  eorundem  Abbatis  et  Conventus  consensu,  valore  annuo  dicte  Ecclesie 
et  ejus  facultatibus  ac  oneribus  matura  deliberacione  pensatis,  Vicariam  in 
ipsa  Ecclesia  ordinamus,  ponimus,  et  taxamus,  et  imperpetuum  consistere 
volumus  in  porcionibus  infrascriptis  ;  videlicet,  in  toto  altilagio  ejusdem 
Ecclesie,  scilicet  in  oblacionibus,  obvencionibus,  funeralibus,  anniversariis, 
purificacionibus,  decimis  de  proventibus  molendinorum,  de  pomis,  feno, 
agnis,  vitulis,  et  edis  [i.e.,  hsedis],  aucis,  porcis,  columbis,  caseo,  butiro,  et 
lacte,  lino,  canabo,  porro,  et  lana  provenientibus,  et  generaliter  in  omnibus 
decimis  minoribus  et  minutis  ad  eandem  Ecclesiam  pertinentibus,  exceptis 
tantummodo  mortuariis  et  decima  de  feno  dominici  de  Otery  et  terrarum 
de  Greneweye,  de  la  Putte,  et  de  la  Stone  provenientibus,  que  ad  Abbatem 
et  Conventum  pertineant  autedictos.  Item,  volumus  et  ordinamus  quod 
Vicarius  qui  ibidem  pro  tempore  fuerit  habeat  pro  manso  suo  aulam  quon- 
dam Rectoris  ejusdem  Ecclesie,  cum  cameris  et  ceteris  domibus  eidem  aule 
contiguis  et  grangia  juxta  Cimiterium  predicte  Ecclesie  situata  ;  necnon, 
unum  ortum  eisdem  domibus  contiguum  cum  columbario  in  eodem  exis- 
tente.  Habeat,  eciam,  tres  acras  terre  arabilis  juxta  Ryngburghe,  et  unum 
clausum  pasture,  cum  alnetis  ibidem  crescentibus,  quod  Meisbeare  vulgariter 
nuncupatur,  pro  focalibus  et  pastura.  Decimas,  vero,  majores  omuimodas  de 
garbis  et  bladis,  necnon  de  fabis  et  pisis  quibuslibet  et  ubilibet  infra  Paro- 
chiam  dicte  Ecclesie  excultis,  necnon  fructus,  redditus,  proven tus,  et  jura 
quecumque  ejusdem  Ecclesie  porcioni  Vicarie  per  nos  superius  non  ascripta, 
fQl-  ad  dictos  Abbatem  et  Conventum  volumus  insolidum  pertinere.  Ipsos, 
eciam,  Abbatem  et  Conventum  a  prestacione  decimarum  de  nutrimentis 
animalium  suorum,  et  pratis  ac  terris  quondam  Rectorie  dicte  Ecclesie, 
quas  jam  tenent,  omuibusque  fructibus  crescentibus  in  eisdem,  ceterisque 
bonis  aliis  decimalibus  in  eisdem  existentibus,  quomodocumque  provenien- 
tibus seu  eciam  proventuris,  dicto  Vicario  qui  pro  tempore  fuerit  facienda, 
liberos  esse  volumus  et  inmunes.  Item,  volumus  et  ordinamus  quod  Vi- 
carius .  .  .  onera  solucionis  Procuracionis  debite  Archidiacono  Exonie  cum

On  the  Cession  ["per  liberam  et  spontaneam  Cessionem  sive  Renunciacio- 
nem  "]  of 

Brother  Adam  de  Knolle, 

Brother  Thomas  de  Bourdon  e  (or  Burdone),  one  of  the  Canons,  was  elected. 
The  Bishop  wrote  to  him,  from  Clyst,  13  July,  informing  him  that  he  had 
refused  to  confirm  the  Election,  "  non  tue  persone  vicio  vel  defectu,  set  per- 
sonarum  eligencium,  utpote  in  substancialibus  omissa  forma  que  requiritur." 
It  was,  consequently,  null  and  void,  and  the  Patronage  had  lapsed  to  himself, 
the  Electors  having  been  deprived  of  the  power  to  proceed  to  another 
fol.  Election.  But,  having  regard  to  Bourdone's  merits  and  the  needs  of  the 
Priory,  the  Bishop  provided  him  thereto,  and  duly  invested  him  "  per  Libri 
nostri  tradicionem "  ;  issuing  his  Mandate  for  Induction  and  Installation 
on  the  same  day,  directed  to  Master  Bartholomew  de  Castro,  R.  of  St.  Ive, 
Sir  John  de  Aldestowe,  R.  of  St.  Mabyn,  and  Sir  William  Jaune,  R.  of 
Withiel.     See  pp.  1002—1008.

Ecclesie  predicte,  tarn  in  terra  quam  in  bosco  de  la  Slo,  ac  toto  altilagio, 
utpote  in  oblacionibus,  obvencionibus,  et  minutis  decimis  qualitercumque 
ad  predictam  Vicariam  spectantibus  ;  necnon,  legatis  pro  decimis  oblitis 
Vicario  qui  pro  tempore  fuerit  relictis,  et  in  decima  molendinorum  tocius 
Parochie  ;  decima  proveniente  de  quodam  molendino  quod  vocatur  Brod- 
wodemulle  dumtaxat  excepta.  Item,  volumus  et  ordinamus  quod  dicta 
Vicaria  consistat  in  decimis  pomorum  et  jampnorum  silve  cedue,  et  decima 
feni  tocius  Parochie,  excepta  decima  feni  Prioris  et  Conventus  de  Frithele- 
stoke,  proveniente  de  dominico  Manerii  de  Brodewodewyger ;  quod,  quidem, 
dominicum  Domini  quondam  dicti  Manerii  ante  Appropriacionem  Ecclesie 
predicte  in  suis  manibus  tenuerunt ;  et  quod  consistat  Vicaria  predicta  in 
annuo  redditu  duodecim  denariorum  proveniencium  de  terra  de  la  More  ; 
que,  quidem,  terra  collata  fuit  Deo  et  Capelle  Beati  Nicholai  de  la  More  ;

C2t>-  sueverunt.  Item,  volumus  et  ordinamus  quod  Prior  et  Conventus  de

ordinaria,  subeant  in  solidum  et  subportent ;  quodque  iidem  Prior  et 
Conventus  Vicarium  Ecclesie  predicte  qui  pro  tempore  fuerit  permittant

Richard  deEccleshale,  clerk,  having  been  presented  by  the  King,  the  Bishop 
commissioned  Master  Symon  de  Islepe,  Canon  of  Lincoln,  to  make  Inqui- 
sition as  to  his  merits,  etc.,  inasmuch  as  Eccleshale  was  in  continuous 
attendance  on  the  King,  and  could  not  appear  in  person  before  the  Bishop. 
He  was  to  institute  and  induct  him  if  he  proved  to  be  fit  in  all  respects, — 
"recepta  ab  eodem  sufficienti  caucione  quod  nos,  et  Ecclesiam  nostram 
Exoniensem,  erga  predictum  Dominum  nostrum  Regem,  super  quibuscum- 
que  litibus,  placitis,  seu  querelis,  occasione  non  Admissionis  ad  dictam  Eccle- 
siam, contra  nos  in  Curia  dicti  Domini  nostri  Regis  qualitercumque  penden- 
tibus  indecisis,  indempnes  in  omnibu3  pres^rvabit  "  (21  March).     Islepe,  in

Exeter  ;  St.  Nicholas  Priory  ;  Commissio  ad  recipiendum 
Besignacionem  Prioraius  Sancti  Nicholai  Exonie, — 

Directed  26  Feb.  1352-3  to  Master  John  de  Lecche,  Professor  of  Canon-Law, 
Canon  of  Exeter,  and  Master  Eenedict  de  Pastoue,  "clerico  nostro  familiari." 
The  Prior,  Brother  Thomas  Ovynge,  had  betaken  himself,  by  special  licence, 
to- Battle  Abbey,  but  had  failed  to  return  to  his  Priory  within  the  time 
assigned  ;  and  great  loss  and  injury  had  thereby  accrued  thereto.  The 
Bishop  declares  that  he  might  have  deprived  him,  if  he  had  so  pleased;  but, 
preferring  to  take  a  gentler  course,  he  directed  an  Inquisition  to  be  held  as 
to  the  cause  of  the  Prior's  prolonged  absence  and  any  excuses  he  might  be 
able  to  offer.  His  Resignation  was  to  be  accepted  if  he  wished  to  resign, 
foj-  and  could  give  good  reasons  for  doing  so.  On  the  14th  of  March  (ij  Idus 
March),  Lecche  and  Pastone  certified  the  Bishop  that  Ovynge  had  appeared 
before  them  on  the  12th,  in  the  Bishop  of  Hereford's  London  House^— "  qui 
quidem,  Prior,  licet  suam  diutinam  absenciam  a  dicto  Prioratu  ex  causis 
justis,  prout  decuit,  nulJatenus  excusaverit,  dicto  tamen  Prioratui  ad  hoc,  vi, 
metu,  dolo,  aut  fraude,  nullatenus  ductus,  ut  asseruit,  se  sponte  velle  re- 
uunciare  pluries  fatebatur,ex  bac causa  ;  quod  in  ipsius  regimiue  Deo  placere, 
anime  sue  et  eidem  Prioratui  proficere  non  potuit,  ut  in  vinculo  sue  Pro- 
fessions. Super  hoc  per  nos  firmiter  adjuratus  constauter  asseruit  vicibus 
iteratis,  petens  humiliter  et  instanter  suam  Resignacionem  per  nos,  vice 
vestra,  admitti."  Being  satisfied  with  Ovynge's  statements,  they  accepted, 
there  and  then,  his  formal  Resignation.  On  the  18th  of  March  (xv  Kalendas 
Aprilis),  Robert,  Abbat  of  Battle,  presented  Brother  Matthew  de  Exonia  ; 
and  on  the  14th  of  April  the  Bishop  issued  a  Commission,  directed  to  Master 
John  de  Shareshulle  and  Master  Stephen  Penpel,  Canons  of  Exeter,  for  his 
Admission  and  Institution,  which  took  place  on  the  17th,  and  they  certified 
the  Bishop  accordingly.  The  new  Prior  took  the  Oath  of  Canonical  Obedi- 
ence, at  Chudleigh,  on  the  same  day, — in  the  presence  of  Masters  B.  de 
Pastone,  Stephen  Penpel,  R.  Inkepenne,  and  T.  Tuggel,  Notary-Publick.

goes}  and  except  those  arising  from 
the  glebe-lands  of  the  said  Parish  ; 
and  that  the  Vicar  for  the  time  being 
is  entitled  to  all  other  tithes  of  the 
said  Parish,  and  also  to  the  corn  and 
grain  tithes  arising  from  lands  called 
part  of  the  Cr  eg  goes.  And,  whereas 
I  find  that  the  tithes,  both  great  and 
small,  arising  from  the  glebe- lands  of 


the  said  Parish  have  been  duly  merged 
in  the  said  lands,  and  such  a  merger 
has  been  duly  confirmed  by  the  Tithe- 
Commissioners  ;  upon  these  grounds 
the  award  is  that  £350  be  paid  an- 
nually, by  way  of  rent-charge,  to 
Stephen  Doble,  instead  of  all  the  corn 
and  grain  tithes  claimed  by  him  ; 
and  that  £215  annually,  by  way  of 
rent-charge,  be  paid  to  the  Vicar 
instead  of  all  other  tithes,  and,  also, 
instead  of  the  corn  and  grain  tithes 
of  the  lands  called  a  part  of  the 
Creggoes."

qui  de  cura  respondeant  animarum  ;  nos,  ad  id  debitam  consideracionem 
habentes,  Vicariam  Perpetuam  in  Ecclesia  Parochiali  et  Prebendali  de 
Holecombe,  Ecclesie  Wellensis,  in  nostra  situata  Diocesi,de  consensu  Vene- 
rabilis  in  Christo  Patris,  Domini  Radulphi  [de  Salopia],  Dei  gracia  Bath- 
oniensis  et  Wellensis  Episcopi,  necnon  Domini  Walteri  de  Aldebury, 
Canonici  Wellensis,  dictam  Prebendalem  Ecclesiam.  ex  nostra  Institucione, 
ad  Presentacionem  dicti  Venerabilis  Patris,  obtinentis,  ordinamus  et  taxa- 
mus  in  hunc  modum  ;  videlicet,  quod  ejusdem  Ecclesie  Vicarii  qui  pro 
tempore  erunt,  et  ad  Presentacionem  prefati  Domini  Walteri,  et  suorum  in 
ipsa  Ecclesia  successorum,  per  nos  et  Successores  nostros  instituentur, 
habeant,  nomine  Vicarie  sue  hujusmodi,  domos  et  terras  quascumque,  nec- 
non decimas  majores  et  minores,  et  obvenciones  omnes  et  singulas  ad 
eandem  Prebendalem  Ecclesiam  pertinentes  ;  exceptis  medietate  silve  per- 
tinentis  ad  ipsam  Ecclesiam  ex  parte  Boriali,  quam  prefato  Domino  Waltero, 
et  suis  ibidem  successoribus  volumus  remanere  ;  et  viginti  solidis  stei  lingo- 
rum  annuis,  quos  iidem  Vicarii  predicto  Waltero,  et  successoribus  suis, 
nomine  Prebende  sue,  in  Festis  Pasche  et  Sancti  Michaelis,  vel  infra 
Octabas  dictorum  Festorum  ad  ultimum,  annis  singulis  solvere  teneantur, 
sub  pena  quadraginta  soiidorum  Fabrice  Ecclesie  nostre  Exoniensis  tociens 
ab  ipsis  Vicariis  solvendorum  quociens  de  dictis  viginti  solidis  satisfacere 
distulerint  in  terminis  supradictis.  Ordinamus,  insuper,  quod  dicti  Vicarii 
omnia  onera  ordinaria  et  extraordinaria  debita  subeant  et  agnoscant,  ac 
eciam  sustentacionem  et  reparacionem  Cancelli,  Librorum,  et  Vestimen- 
torum,  et  aliorum  quorumcumque  que  dicte  Ecclesie,  nomine  Pectoris 
sive  Rectorie  predicte,  de  jure  seu  de  consuetudine  pertinere  dinoscuntur. 
Hanc,  vero,  Ordinacionem  nostram  augmentandi  vel  diminuendi,  cum  ex- 
pediens  visum  fuerit  nobis  aut  Successoribus  nostris.  potestatem  specialiter 
reservamus  (Chudleigh,  3  July).

Dr.  Oliver  states  (Eccles.  Antiq.,  ii, 
81)  that  "  this  most  ancient  Parish 
Church  .  .  .  has  had  a  regular  suc- 
cession of  Vicars  from  time  im- 
memorial." This  was  the  case  for  a 
short  time  ;  and  I  find  in  the  Taxa- 
tion of  Pope  Nicholas  IV — "Ecclesia 
Sancti  Pancracii,  xls.,  Decima  iiij».  ; 
Vicaria  de  eadem,  xxvjs.  viijd."  But 
it  is  nearer  the  truth  to  say  that 
this  Benefice  has  been  a  Rvctory  from 
time  immemorial.  In  the  earlier  En- 
tries of  Institution  it  is,  sometimes 
called  "  Capella,"  but  the  Incumbent 


is  referred  to  as  "  Rector."  In 
1473  I  find  "  Ecclesia  sive  Libera 
Capella  "  ;  in  1581,  "  Rectoria  sive 
Capella  "  ;  in  the  Valor  Ecclesiasticus 
(1536—^/?.  Veseys  Return),  "Rec- 
toria Sancti  Pancrasii."  The  Prior  of 
Lodres  (as  Proctor  of  the  Abbat  and 
Convent  of  Montburg)  was  Patron  of 
the  Rectory  till  1473  when  the  Pa- 
tronage passed  to  the  Crown.  Evi- 
dently, at  first,  the  Bishop  found  it 
necessary  to  insist  on  a  Vicar  being 
instituted  to  serve  the  Church  :  this 
was  often  done  in  similar  cases.

Exeter  Cathedral  ;  Archdeaconry  of  Cornwall, — 

As  we  have  seen  (page  1487,  note  3), 

William  de  Cnsancia  resigned  this  Archdeaconry,  and 

Nicholas  de  Newetone  succeeded  (by  way  of  exchange),  and  was  inst.  thereto  by 
the  Bp.  of  St.  David's,  26  Nov.,  1357.  There  appears  to  have  been  some 
difficulty  ;  for  he  was  presented  thereto  by  the  King  in  1362.  In,  or 
before,  Jan.  1367-8. 

Alexander  de  Nevyle  held  the  Archdeaconry,  as  the  following  Papal  Bull 
(preserved  iu  the  P.R.  0.)  conclusively  shews, — 

"  Urbanus  Episcopus,  Servus  servorum  Dei,  dilecto  filio,  Willelmo  de 
Wykham,  Archidiacono  Lincolnie,  carissimi  in  Christo  filii  nostri,  Edwardi, 
Regis  Anglie  illustris,  Secretario,  salutem  et  Apostolicam  benediccionem. — 
Ex  literarum  sciencia  et  nobilitate  generis,  super  quibus  dilectus  films, 
Alexander  de  Nevyle,  Archidiaconus  Cornubie  in  Ecclesia  Exoniensi,  apud 
nos  fidedignorum  commendatur  testimouio,  ac  venustate  et  mansuetudine 
morum  quos  in  eo  conspeximus  ad  dileccionem  ejus  allecti,  eumque 
habentes  singnlariter  acceptum  et  gratum  ;  ipsum  carissimis  in  Christo 
filiis  nostris,  Edwardo  Regi  et  Philippe  Regine  Anglie  illustribus,  affectuo- 
sius  commendamus.  Ideoque  discrecionem  tuam  rogamus  attente  quatinus, 
penes  dictos  Regem  et  Reginam,  eidem  in'  omni  honore  et  commodo  suis 
assistas  favoribus  et  auxiliis  oportunis. — Data  apud  Montem  Pessulanam, 
Magolonensis  Diocesis,  xij  Kalendas  Februarii,  Pontificatus  nostri  Anno 
quinto  (21  Jan.,  1366-7).     [F.  J.  B.]. 

Our  Register  contains  no  record  of  Nevyle's  appointment,  which  was, 
probably,  by  Provision,  and  at  about  the  above-mentioned  date ;  and 
Le  Neve  and  Oliver  do  not  mention  him  as  Archdeacon.  Neither  is  there 
any  record  of  his  Induction  or  of  Newetone's  resignation.  The  mystery, 
however,  is  cleared  up  in  the  Register  of  Bp.  Grandisson's  successor, 
Thomas  de  Brantingham,  who  found  both  Newetone  and  Nevyle  in  office, 
as  rival  Archdeacons  !     The  King  had  intervened,  Sede  vacante  ;  and  he

As   TO   THE   EAELY    EECTOES   OF   COMBE-RaLEIGH   AND    COMBEPYNE. 

Dr.  Oliver,  in  his  Ecclesiastical  Antiquities,  vol.  ii,  page  SS,  gives  the  followiug 
List  of  the  Rectors  of  Combepyne,  down  to  the  end  of  Bishop  Grandissou's 
Episcopate, — 

"Robert  de  Cestre,  admitted  by  Bishop  Bronescombe,  21  December,  1278,  'ad 
Ecclesiam  de  Cumbe,'  on  the  Presentation  of  Sir  Thomas  de  Pyn,  Knt. 

"  Martin  de  Sutton,  whose  Institution  is  not  entered  in  the  Episcopal  Registers; 
but  on  whose  resignation 

"  Henry  de  Mcdecroft.  de  Wyke  Risingdon,  was  admitted  20  April,  1334,  to 
this  Rectory  of  '  Comb  Coffyn,'  Pat.  Walter  de  Sutton,  See  fol.  28, 
Vol.  Ill  of  Grandissou's  Register.     Ou  whose  death — 

"N.B.  Occasionally  Comb  Kaleigh  is  called  Comb  Coffyn.  See  fol.  3,  Tur- 
berville's  Register. 

"  William  Toustreyn  succeeded  28  September.  1348. 

"  George  de  Umfravill  followed  13  March,  1348-9.      Pat.  Gilbert  de  Umfravil. 

"  John  Thresh,  whose  Institution  I  cannot  discover. 

"  He  was  Rector  of  Sutton  Montague,  in  the  Diocese  of  Bath  and  Wells,  at  the 
same  time.  From  folio  126,  Vol.  Ill  of  Grandissou's  Register,  I  collect 
that  he  must  have  thought  it  convenient  to  resign  Combpyne,  when 

"  William  Hullefelde  succeeded  him  21  July,  1361,  on  the  presentation  of  Sir 
William  de  Umfraville,  Knt.

William  de  Umfraville,  Knt."     And  then  he  passes  to 

"  William  Langerygg,  on  whose  death 

"  John  Knowst<>n,  admitted  9  January,  1411-12.     Pat.  Edmund  Pyn." 

This  List  is  most  unsatisfactory.  The  names  of  several  Rectors,  whose  Insti- 
tutions are  duly  registered,  are  omitted  ;  and  some  Rectors  of  Combe- 
Raleigh  have  been  entered  as  Rectors  of  Combepyne.  There  are  difficulties, 
no  doubt,  arising  from  the  various  names  attributed  to  Combe- Raleigh. 
"  This  place,"  says  Pole  {Collections,  page  131),  "  hath  often  altered  his  name, 
first  named  Cumb  singlely,  after  Cumb  Baunton,  and  Comb  Mathew,  of  the 
Dwellers";  to  which  I  may  add  '' Combe-St.  Nicholas,"  "  Comb  Coffyn," 
"  Combe  juxta  Honitone,"  and  "  Bisshopyscombe."1     It  will  be  observed, 


1  This  name  occurs  once  only,  as  far  as 
I  know,  in  our  Episcopal  Registers. 
Sir  Martin  de  Sottone,  Rector  of 
"  Bisshopyscombe,"  obtained  Licence 
of  non-residence  for  a  year,  11  June, 
1329  {see  page  507).  He  was  then 
Rector,  not  (as  Oliver  supposed)  of 
Combepyne,  but  of  Combe- Raleigh. 
Being  puzzled  by  the  name,  I  con- 
sulted the  Rev.  Oswald  Reichel  of 
Lympstone,  who  has  been  working  for 
some  time  on  the  Domesday  Hundreds, 
not  by  way  of  mere  conjecture  but 
scientifically,  and  who  is  a  reliable 
authority  on  the  subject.  He  writes. 
"  I  have  before  me  two  names,  which 
may  throw  light  on  your  question. 
The  first  is  a  '  Combe  '  of  some  500  to 
600  acres,  to  which  Gerwille  was  an- 
nexed. Gerwille.  held  by  Oliver  under 
Tetbald  Fitz  Berner,  is,  clearly,  Gor- 
well,  in  Hemyock,  because  the  amount 


of  Oliver's  exempt  land  in  that  Hun- 
dred exactly  tallies.  '  Cumbe  '  I,  at 
first,  put  down  as  the  adjacent  Med- 
combe  :  and  I  am  not  sure,  now,  that 
it  is  not.  Still,  two  difficulties  pre- 
sent themselves  in  that  case.  (1) 
Medcombe,  on  the  map,  appears  too 
small.  (2)  Why  was  not  Oliver's  ex- 
empt land  put  down  larger  ?  It, 
then,  occurred  to  me  that  it  might  be 
Combe- Raleigh.  But  against  this  (if 
I  have  got  the  other  places  in  Hemy- 
ock Hundred  correctly)  must  be  set 
the  fact  that  Hemyock  Hundred  will 
be  too  small  by  just  the  amount  of 
the  assessement  of  this  Combe.  Then, 
there  is  '  Scobecome,'  called  in  one 
place  '  Cobecume.'  This  is  stated  to 
have  been  appurtenant  to  Hembury, 
but  to  have  been  held  by  Ludo,  to- 
gether with  Luppitt  and  Gieenway 
(in  the  Palish  of  Luppitt),  the  lands
