THE    AVILL   OF   BISHOP   GRANDISSON.1 


[Translation  ] 

13*6?'  ^N  THE  Name  °f  our  Lord  Jesus  Christ,  Son  of  the  Virgin  Mary, 
with    the    Holy   Ghost   in    the    glory    of    God    the    Father 

103'b.       Almighty.     Amen. 

I,  John  de  Grandisson,  of  the  Church  of  Exeter  an  unprofitable 
and  unworthy  Minister,  being,  by  the  grace  of  God,  sound 
in  mind  and  body  do  make  my  Will  after  this  manner.  I 
commend  my  spirit  to  my  Creator,  the  Creator  of  all ;  but 
as  to  my  body,  which  is  corruptible  and  hath  weighed  down2 
my  soul,  I  will  that  it  be  buried  without  the  West  Door  of  the 
Church  of  Exeter,  as  quickly  as  can  possibly  be  arranged  in 
seemly  fashion  ;  without  inviting  my  near  kinsfolk  or  great 
Nobles,  but  only  any  neighbouring  Bishop  or  Bishoj)s.  And 
I  will  that  four  wax  tapers  be  set  about  my  body,  each 
of  twenty  pounds  in  weight,  one  at  the  head,  one  at  the 
feet,  and  one  on  the  right  hand  and  on  the  left  hand  one. 
As  for  the  other  tapers,  each  of  which  is  to  be  a  pound  in 
weight,  let  a  pair  be  set  on  each  Altar  throughout  the 
Church  •  and  let  one  of  them  there  remain,  and  the  others 
be  distributed  amongst  the  Parish-Churches  in  the  Citv. 
I  also  forbid,  under  pain  of  the  Divine  displeasure,  all  drinking 
of  spiced  wine  in  the  Choir,  by  night,  around  my  body;  but,  if 
such  things  must  needs  be  done,  let  it  be  in  the  Chapter- 
House,  or  in  some  other  place  suitable  for  such  a  purpose ;  or, 
instead  thereof,  let  a  hundred  shillings  be  distributed  in 
common  amongst  all  Ministers  of  the  Choir  who  are  present 
and  recite  the  Psalter.  I  will,  also,  and  bequeath,  that,  on  the 
said  day  of  my  burial,  a  hundred  of  the  poorer  people  be 
provided  with  cloaks  and  hoods,  if  so  many  can  be  procured, 
made  of  thick  cloth,  white  or  grey  ;  and  that  simple  priests 
who  attend  on  the  said  day  of  my  interment,  as  well 
as  all  Religious,   whether  men  or  women,  receive,  each  of

£2"  them,  four  pence.     Also,  if  any   Bishop,   or  Bishops,  shall 

come  to  my  burial,  let  each  of  them  receive  for  his  expenses, 
as  much  as  shall  seem  good  to  my  Executors ;  together 
with  a  Pontifical  ring,  or  a  plain  mitre  embroidered  with 
gold  thread,  or  some  other  fitting  jewel,  unless  he 
has  received  one  from  me  in  my  lifetime.  But  the 
Canons  of  the  Church  of  Exeter  who  attend  on  the  said 
day  are  to  have,  each  of  them,  forty  pence ;  the  Vicars 
who  are  present,  two  shillings  each  ;  the  Secondaries  and 
the  Annivellars,  twelve  pence  each  ;  the  Secondary  Clerks, 
twelve  pence  each  ;  the  boys  of  the  Choir,  six  pence  each  ; 
the  Custors,  for  the  ringing,  provided  that  the  peals  be  short 
and  not  unduly  prolonged,  twelve  pence  each  ;  the  Brothers 
of  the  Hospital  of  St.  John  at  Exeter,  being  priests,  two 
shillings  each  ;  the  infirm  there,  twelve  pence  each  ;  the 
prisoners  at  Exeter,  forty  pence,  to  buy  bread ;  the  infirm 
of  the  House  of  the  Blessed  Mary  Magdalene  at  Exeter,  two 
shillings,  to  be  divided  amongst  them ;  the  Priests  of  St. 
Gabriel  of  Clyst,  two  shillings  each.  Also,  I  bequeath  two 
shillings  to  every  Rector  within  the  City  of  Exeter,  and  to 
every  Holy  Water  bearer  six  pence.  I  will,  also,  that,  from 
the  day  of  my  burial  until  the  thirtieth  day  following, 
the  Exequies  be  said  daily,  and  Mass  celebrated  in  some 
convenient  place.  And  I  wTill  that,  with  the  exception  of 
the  Solemn  Mass  on  the  day  of  my  burial  and  one  Mass 
of  Requiem  on  each  of  the  other  days,  all  the  Masses  that 
shall  be  said  for  me  be  of  the  Blessed  Mary,  together  with  the 
prayer  for  the  dead.  And  throughout  those  thirty  days, 
every  Canon  who,  on  any  day,  shall  have  been  present  at 
the  Mass  and  the  Vigils,  is  to  have  for  each  day  six  pence  ; 
every  Vicar  four  pence ;  every  Secondary  three  pence  ;  and 
every  boy  two  pence.  And  if  any  of  the  Canons  sing  the 
Mass  on  any  day  during  the  Trental,  he  is  to  have,  in 
addition,  six  pence ;  if  a  Vicar,  three  pence.  Also,  I 
desire  that  my  familiars  be  clad,  not  in  black  garments, 
but  in  their  own  robes  of  the  suit  of  the  current  year; 
and  the  priests  and  clerks  of  my  Chapel  in  surplices  and 
white  capes,  as  they  have  been  accustomed.  And  it  is 
not  my  wish  that  there  should  be  a  general  distribution  of 
bread  to  the  poor  on  the  actual  day  of  my  burial,  but  on 
some  other  day,  either  before  or  after  ;  and  that,  as  far  as 
shall  be  possible,  not  in  money  but  in  bread. 
Also,  I  give  and  bequeath  to  the  Church  of  Exeter  my  best 
white  Vestments,  namely,  chasuble,  tunicle,  and  dalmatick, 
with  the  cope,  all  embroidered  with  the  rosary  in  gold 
and  my  arms,  and  with  demi-angels ;  as  well  as  four  of  my 

104.  best  copes,  of  one  suit,  of  white  silk,  diapered  with  beavers

our  Crucified  Lord,  with  the  robbers  hanging  on  either  side. 
Also,  I  bequeath  to  my  Lord,  the  Prince  of  Aquitaine  and

and  to  the  said  Duke's  wife  and  kinswoman  Blanche  :

of  my  Executors,  to  be  kept  in  memory  of  me  ;  also,  to 
the  Lady  Isabella,  eldest  daughter  of  our  Lord  the  King, 
my  best  Psalter.1 

Also,  I  bequeath  to  the  Venerable  Father  in  Christ,  the  Lord 
Archbishop  of  Canterbury  for  the  time  being,  the  great 
dorser  in  my  hall,  representing  the  Coronation  of  the  Blessed 
Mary,  with  the  Apostles  sitting  on  thrones  and  holding 
each  of  them  an  Article  of  the  Creed,  together  with  a 
Pontifical  ring,  to  be  used  when  celebrating,  and  fifty 
marks  sterling  ;  to  the  end  that  he  may  assist  my  Executors 
in  carrying  out  the  provisions  of  my  last  Will,  and  may  not 
harrass  them  ;  and  that  neither  he  himself,  nor  his  official, 
or  others  soever  his  Ministers,  in  his  name,  may  demand  or 
exact  anything  else  from  my  said  Executors  on  any  pretence. 
If  they  do  otherwise,  let  them  forfeit  the  said  legacies  ; 
and  in  such  case  I  bequeath  them  to  the  Treasury  of  our 
Lord  the  Pope,  to  be  taken  charge  of  by  the  Nuncio  of  the 
Apostolick  See  in  England  ;  to  the  intent  that,  on  behalf 
of  our  Lord  the  Pope,  he  may  help  and  protect  my 
Executors.  Also,  I  bequeath  to  the  said  Clerk  or  Nuncio 
of  our  Lord  the  Pope,  in  order  that  he  may  help  and  deal 
favourably  with  my  Executors,  and  be  himself  one  of  them, 
fifty  florins  of  Florence  or  the  equivalent  thereof.

Carmelite  Friars  of  Sutton  forty  shillings,  together  with  a 
simple  Vestment,  unless  they  shall  have  had  one  in  my  life- 
time. 

Also,  I  bequeath  to  the  Parish-Church  of  Chudleigh  the  two 
largest  bells  in  the  belfry  of  my  Chapel  at  Chudleigh. 

Also,  to  each  of  the  Hospitals  for  lepers  and  other  sick  folk 
within  the  Bishoprick  of  Exeter,  according  to  the  number 
of  those  who  dwell  in  them,  to  every  sick  person  twelve 
pence. 

Also,  I  bequeath  to  the  Parish-Church  of  Ashperton,  in  the 
Diocese  of  Hereford,  where  I  was  born,  unless  it  shall  have 
received  the  gift  in  my  life-time,  a  suitable  Vestment  for  a 
priest ;  to  wit,  a  chasuble,  with  albe  apparelled,  stole,  and 
maniple.  Also,  I  bequeath  to  the  Prebendal  Church  of 
Haydor,  near  Grantham,  which  was  my  Prebend  in  the  Church 
of  Lincoln,  a  Vestment,  with  tunicle  and  dalmatic,  unless 
it  shall  have  received  the  gift  in  my  life-time.  But  it  is 
my  will  that,  of  the  Vestments  and  other  Ecclesiastical 
Ornaments  bequeathed  as  above,  those  belonging  to  my 
Chapel  be  so  dealt  with  in  the  first  instance,  as  far  as  they 
suffice  for  the  purpose  ;  and  that,  if  need  be,  the  rest  be 
supplied  from  new  purchases  in  London  ;  so  that,  by  the 
grace  of  God,  not  one  of  the  above-named  Church-legacies 
be  omitted,  but  that  all  be  duly  provided,  if  it  can  be 
conveniently  managed,   out  of  my  goods.

A-D.  As  to  my  ordinary  effects,  my  wearing-apparel  and  bed-furniture, 
except  such  things  as  belong  to  my  chamberlains  by 
custom,  I  will  that  they  be  divided  amongst  poor  priests, 
whether  Rectors  or  Vicars,  being  in  want,  and  the  Vicars- 
Choral  of  the  Collegiate  Church  of  Crediton,  and  honest 
widows  or  recluses,  and  Hospitals,  according  to  the  dis- 
cretion and  judgement  of  my  Executors.  But  all  my  ordinary 
orphreys,  together  with  the  fringes  and  other  things  belong- 
ing to  Ecclesiastical  Vestments  which  have  not  been 
bequeathed,  I  assign  and  bequeath  for  disposal  by  Master 
Nicholas  de  Braybroke  and  Thomas  Tuggell.  But  the 
residue  of  all  my  goods,  if  there  be  any,  of  things  not 
bequeathed,  I  bequeath  for  the  erection  of  a  comely  residence 
for  the  common  use  of  the  Vicars-Choral  of  the  Church  of 
Exeter,  and  for  other  works  of  piety. 
For  the  execution  of  this  my  Testament  or  Last  Will  I  supplicate 
the  Venerable  Fathers  in  Christ,  my  Lords  and  most  dear 
Brother- Bishops,  the  Lords  Lewis  and  William,  by  the  grace 
of  God  Bishops  of  Hereford  and  Worcester1,  to  consent  to 
act  as  the  co-adjutors  and  overseers  and  counsellors  of  my 
Executors.  And  further,  I  ordain,  make,  and  constitute  as 
my  Executors,  Sir  John  de  Montacute,  my  nephew,  also  my 
grandnephew  Master  Philip  de  Bellocampo,  if  he  be  in 
England,  and  also  the  Clerk  of  our  Lord  the  Pope,  Nuncio*2 
for  the  time  being  of  the  Apostolick  See  in  England  ;  also, 
Master  Stephen  de  Pempel,  Dean  of  the  Church  of  Wells,  and, 
in  addition,  Masters  John  de  Shareshulle,  Precentor,  John 
Wyliethe,  Chancellor,  Robert  de  Wykforde,  John  de  Holande, 
and  Nicholas  de  Braybroke,  Canons  of  the  Church  of  Exeter, 
Sir  Andrew  de  Moore,  Warden  of  the  Collegiate  Church  of 
St.  Mary  of  Ottery  ;  also,  William  de  Braybroke,  Sir  John  de 
Mounceaux,  Sir  Thomas  Sage,  and  Sir  Thomas  Tuggel :  so 
that  if  they  are  not  all  of  them  willing  or  able  to  undertake 
the  execution  of  this  my  Testament,  Administration  ma}'  be 
accepted  and  carried  out  by  four,  or  at  least  by  three,  efficient 
and  suitable  men  who  may  put  in  an  appearance.  And  I 
bequeath  to  each  of  my  aforesaid  Executors  undertaking  the 
burden  of  this  Testament,  in  return  for  his  trouble  and  in 
addition  to  his  expenses,  a  silver  cup  with  a  beaker,  or  a  ring 
of  good  value,  or  some  jewel  useful  and  acceptable  to  each 
one  of  them,  together  with  a  hundred  shillings  sterling  ;  the

lm  other  legacies  provided  for  above  for  the  said  Executors,  or 

for  any  of  them,  to'remain,  nevertheless,  in  full  force.  And 
I  adjure  my  aforesaid  Executors,  and  by  the  compassion  of 
the  Mother  of  Mercy  and  the  sprinkling  of  the  Blood  of  Jesus 
Christ,  her  Son,  our  Lord,  beseech  them,  both  to  accept 
Administration  of  this  Testament,  not  excusing  themselves 
voluntarily,  and  also  faithfully,  speedily,  and  diligently  to 
execute  the  same,  taking  care  that  the  expenses  are  moderate 
and  free  from  all  extravagance,  that  they  may  receive  the 
gift  of  everlasting  life  from  the  Re  warder  of  all  good  works. 
And  it  is  my  will,  and  I  hereby  request,  that  a  thin  plate  of 
lead,  to  be  deposited  with  my  body,  be  inscribed  thus, — 
"  Here  lieth  John  de  Grandisson,  the  pitiable  Bishop  of 
Exeter,  most  miserable  servant  of  the  Mother  of  Mercy ; 
whose  compassionate  Son,  through  her  prayers,  has  shewn 
him  mercy,  in  order  that,  ceasing  to  be  miserable,  he  might 
be  made  blessed,  and  that  to  all  others  who  are  in  misery 
might  be  vouchsafed  the  hope  of  bewailing  their  sins." 

In  testimony  of  which  things,  all  and  singular,  this  my  Testa- 
ment is  sealed  with  the  impression  of  my  ring. 

Given  in  my  Manor  of  Chudleigh,  in  the  Diocese  of  Exeter,  on 
the  eighth  day  of  the  month  of  September,  in  the  year  of 
our  Lord  1368,  and  the  forty-first  of  my  Consecration. 

The  Subscription  of  the  Lord  Bishop  of  Exeter,  by  his 
own  hand, — 
I,  John  de  Grandisson  aforesaid,  do  sign  my  aforesaid  Testament 
on  this  most  high  Feast  of  the  ever  Blessed  Virgin  Mary, 
who  brought  a  message  of  joy  to  the  whole  world  ;  of  whom 
was  born  the  Sun  of  Justice,  Christ  our  Lord,  Who  taking 
away  the  curse  bestowed  on  us  a  blessing,  and,  overthrowing 
death,  hath  given  unto  us  everlasting  life.

83  The  dates  from  this  point  are 
taken,  with  few  exceptions,  from  the 
Register  of  Institutions.  It  will  be 
seen  how  continuous  they  are.  The 
"  Black  Death  "  was  desolating  the 
land  ;  and,  as  Parish  after  Parish 
fell  vacant,  newly  appointed  Clerks 
came  to  the  Bishop  at  Chudleigh  for 
Admission,  almost  day  by  day  ;  on 
seme  days  one,  on  others  in  groups; 
and  very  many  of  the  Entries  begin 
with  the  words,  "Item,  eisdem  die 


et  loco."  In  such  cases  I  have  given, 
within  brackets,  the  number  of  Insti- 
tutions on  each  day.  The  Register 
henceforth  provides  but  scanty  ma- 
terials for  an  Itinerary  ;  only  the 
Bishop's  Acts  at  Chudleigh  (for  many 
years  his  head-quarters;,  and  at  some 
few  places,  in  the  immediate  neigh- 
bourhood, are  now  recorded,  all 
separate  quaterni,  as  well  as  his 
Ordination-Lists,  having  long  since 
perished,

siastica  in  eadem  ministranda. 

Item,  intendit  probare  Procurator  antedictus  quod  predecessores  ipsius  Wil- 
lelmi  habuerunt,  optinuerunt,  et  perceperunt  in  dicta  Capella,  per  Vicarium

Capellanum,  ante  fundacionem  Vicarie  de  Stoke  ibidem  celebrantes,  singulis 
septimanis  anni,  Divinorum  celebracionem  ;  videlicet,  feria  secunda,^  feria 
quarta.  feria  sexta,  ac  quolibet  Die  Dominico,  et  quolibet  Festo  feriando, 
secundum  consuetudinem  Exoniensis  Diocesis  usitatam  ;  necnon,  omnibus 
Vigiliis,  ufcpote  Vigilia  Sancti  Joannis  Baptiste,  Vigilia  Apostolorum  Petri 
et  Pauli,  Vigilia  Assumpcionis  Beate  Marie,  Vigilia  Omuium  Sanctorum, 
Natalis  Domini,  Officium  diei  debitum,  et  ante  Pascha  tribus  noctibus 
Servicia  Matutinalia  que  nominantur  Tenebre,  etin  Vigilia  Pasche  cum  Bene- 
diccione  Fontis,  cum  tota  septimana  Pasche,  eteciam  Peutecostes  Servicium 
et  dierum  sequencium  debitum,  sunt  Servicia  Divina  in  Capella  antedicta 
pro  dicta  terra  celebranda. 
Ad  istum  articulum  dicit  sic, — quod  singulis  quartis  et  sextis  feriis  Vicarius 
de  Stoke  qui  pro  tempore  fuerit,  vel  quiscumque  ejus  locum  tenens,  cele- 
brabit  Missam  in  Capella  antedicta  ad  instanciam  Dominorum  de  Wadtone 
(sic)  et  tenendum  de  Wadtone  ;  et  singulis  Diebus  Dominicis  benedicet 
panem  et  aquam  ibidem  et  ministrabit  eisdem  ;  singulis  diebus  omnium 
Festorum  Pasche  et  Natalis  Domini  celebrabitur  una  Missa  in  dicta  Capella 
per  Vicarium  de  Stoke,  vel  per  eorum  (sic)  locum  tenentem  ;  Servicia  Matu- 
tinalia que  nominantur  Tenebre  fient  ibidem  per  eosdem ;  Sacramenta  (sic) 
Baptismatis  conferetur  et  Matrimonia  solempnizabuntur  ibidem  per  eosdem, 
et  omnia  cetera  jura  Ecclesiastica,  excepta  Sepultura.  Et  ista  vidit  et 
audivit  fieri  per  quadraginta  annos  et  amplius  ibidem,  ita  quod  de  ejus 
contrario  nescit  quicquid  depunere.  De  ceteris  in  dicto  articulo  contentis 
ignorat. 

Item,  intendit  probare  Procurator  antedictus  quod  idem  Willelmus,  Dominus 
suus,  toto  tempore  suo,  et  omnes  villani  Parochie  commorautes  in  villa  de 
Wadtone  (sic),  ac  eciam  extranei  declinantes  ad  mausionem  dicti  Willelmi, 
habuerunt,  perceperunt,  et  audiverunt  sic  Divina  celebrari  per  Vicarios  de 
Stoke,  sen  per  Capellanos  eorundem,  sea  per  aliquos  Capellanos  ibidem 
constitutos  in  Divinis  miuistrandis  et  exequeudis  racione  rionacionis  terre 
supradicte. 

Ad  istum  articulum  dicit  quod  dictus  Willelmus,  et  omnes  villanide  Wad- 
tone (sic),  habuerunt  et  perceperunt  et  audiverunt  Divina  celebrari  per 
Vicarium  de  Stokegabryelle  et  Capellanos  eorundem,  prout  in  proximo 
articulo  deposuit. 

Item,  intendit  probare  quod  super  premissis  publica  vox  est  et  fama,  et  fuit 
ante  presens  negocium  institutum,  in  partibus  de  Stoke,  Wadtone,  et 
Peyngtone,  et  aliis  locis  vicinis,  que  nulla  tergiversacione  poterunt  celari. 

Ad  istum  articulum  dicit  quod  eontinet  in  se  veritatem,  prout  super  premissis 
superius  predeposuit. 

Nicholaus  de  Restercombe,  secundus  testis,  quadragenarius  et  amplius,  re- 
quisitus  super  premissis  articulis  omnibus  et  singulis,  sibi  seriosius  lectis  et 
expositis,  in  omnibus  concordat  cum  Johanne  Elias,  conteste  suo  pre- 
examinato  ;  hoc  excepto,  quod  non  est  tante  etatis  prout  dictus  Johannes. 
[Cetera  desunt.]

I. — Concerning  the  murder  of  Bishop)  Stapeldon  and  the  proceed-

The  following  record  is  extracted  from  MS.  No.  1106  in  Lambeth 
Palace  Library.1  It  contains  an  interesting  account  of  Bishop 
Stapeldon's  murder  and  of  the  punishment  meted  out  to  his 
assassins.  The  writer  states,  distinctly,  that  the  mutilated 
body  of  the  victim,  after  being  exposed  to  shameful  indignities, 
was  at  last,  by  the  intervention  of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of 
Exeter,  conveyed  to  the  Cathedral  City  for  interment. 


1  The  greater  part  of  the  Volume  is  a  copy 
of  the  Flores  Historiarum  of  Matthew 
Paris, from  the  Creation. and  continued 
to  A.D.  1341.  On  fol.  93  (1307)  has 
been  written,  by  a  much  later  hand, — 
desinit  Mat'  H'eslutonaster'  in  Lib) is 
impressis ;  and  on  one  of  the  fly- 
leaves, in  a  16th  Century  hand, — 
"This  booke,  though  stiled  Flores 
Historiarum,  is  not  the  same  in  many 
partes  with  Matthew  of  Westminster's 
Flores  Historiarum,  and  seerues  rather 
to  have  bin  done  by  some  of  the  Canons 
of  St.  Paul's  in  London  (vide  au. 
1315  &  1336)."  There  is  no  entry  for 
the  year  1340,  and  only  one  for  the 
following  year, — "  Anno  Domini  M°. 
CCC°xlj°;  Die  Dominica  in  finemensis 
Aprilis,  videlicet  in  Vigilia  Sancti 
Erconwaldi  [the  29th],  Domina  Ma- 
tildis  de  Mounthagu  benedicta  fuit 
in  Abbatissam  de  Berkinge  ab 
Episcopo  Radulpho  Londoniensi,  in 
Ecclesia  Sancti  Pauli,  ad  Summum 
Altare,  cum  magna  sollempnitate ; 
presentibus  Domino  Episcopo  Ely- 
ensi,  fratre  suo,  ac  Priorissa  de  Hali- 
welle,  sorore  dicte  Abbatisse."  The 
latter  portion  of  the  Volume  seems  to 
have  been  written  by  someone  con- 
nected with  St.  Paul's,  and  living  iu 
London  ;  and  there  is  a  note  to  this 
effect  by  Sir  James  Ware,  which 
probably  led  to  its  being  called  "  An- 
nates Paulini"  by  Henry  Wharton, 
who  thought  that  Murimouth  might 
have  been  the  author.  He  was  more 
probably  some  Official  of  the  Ex- 
'  chequer;  for,  under  1319,  he  mentions 
that  on  the  17th  of  September  the 


clerks  of  the  Exchequer  left  London  for 
York,  with  twenty-one  carts  to  carry 
the  Rolls  and  Domesday-Book,  and 
under  1322  that  on  the  5th  of  April 
they  carried  to  York,  in  twenty-four 
carts,  the  Rolls  of  the  Exchequer 
and  other  necessaries  ;  also,  that 
William  de  Ayreminne,  chief  Clerk  of 
the  Exchequer,  having  been  captured 
by  the  Scots,  his  brother  Richard  gave 
2000  marks  for  his  ransom.  And  it  is 
worthy  of  notice,  here,  that  under 
1332  is  mentioned  Bishop  Grandis- 
son's  refusal  to  allow  the  Archbishop 
to  visit  his  Diocese.  There  is  no 
evidence  that  the  Book  ever  belonged 
to  St.  Paul's,  and  there  is  certainly 
nothing  in  it  to  justify  its  being 
described  as  the  "  Annals  "  of  that 
Church ;  the  Bishops,  Deans,  and 
Canons,  and  the  chief  events  con- 
nected with  its  history  are  not  even 
alluded  to  in  its  pages,  with  the 
solitary  exception  of  an  account  of 
the  blessing  of  the  bells  on  fol.  96b, 
with  a  statement  of  the  dimensions 
of  the  Church  and  a  rough  sketch  of 
it  from  the  west  in  the  margin.  But 
it  is  evident  that,  by  this  time,  the 
MS.  had  ceased  to  be  kept  as  a 
regular  Chronicle,  and  these  dis- 
connected additions  may  have  been 
made  by  anybody.  It  will  be  shewn, 
below,  that  the  Volume  was  in  the 
possession  of  Bishop  Grandisson,  and 
was  treated  by  him  as  his  own  pro- 
perty. Richard  Widmore  made  a 
transcript  of  the  MS.,  and  of  some 
other  contemporary  Chronicles,  which 
is    in  the  British  Museum,  and  is,

now,  known  as  MS.  Lansdowne,  No. 
791.  Probably,  it  was  sold  after 
Bishop  Grandisson's  death  ;  or  he 
may  have  given  it  to  the  Church  of 
Ottery-St.  Mary.  It  is  most  interest- 
ing, at  any  rate,  to  know  that  he 
was  its  contemporaneous  (and,  it  can 
scarcely  be  doubted,  its  first )possessor. 
After  his  time  we  lose  sight  of  it  for 
nearly  two  hundred  years  ;  but  its 
subsequent  history,  down  to  our  own 
day,  is  fairly  complete.  At  the  end 
is  written, — "  N.  Brigami  liber  est ; 
perlege,  claude,  vale."  According  to 
Wood's  A  thence  Oxonienses  Brigham 
died  in  1559.  At  the  beginning  we 
find  the  name  of  the  next  possessor, — 
"1566.  M  :  W.  Darelli  liber."  Darell 
was  a  Prebendary  of  Canterbury  at 
the  time,  and  we  learn  from  Cooper 
that  he  was  of  Corpus  Christi  College, 
Cambridge,  and  died  in  1580.  Subse- 
quently, it  came  into  the  hands  of 
Sir  James  Ware,  who  died  in  1666  ; 
and  when,  twenty  years  later,  Ware's 
MSS.  were  sold,  it  was  bought,  in 
Dublin,  by  Henry  Hyde,  second  Earl 
of  Clarendon  and  Lord  Lieutenant  of 
Ireland  1685—1687.  He  sold  them 
to  James  Brydges,  afterwards  (1714) 
created  Duke  of  Chandos ;  at  the 
auction  of  whose  buoks  they  were 
bought  by  Richard  Widmore,  who 
notes  these  particulars  and  describes 
himself  as  "  the  present  owner."  The 


book  was,  at  one  time,  in  the  custody 
of  Dr.  Thomas  Tenison,  Vicar  of  St. 
Martin's-in.the-Fields,  who  deposited 
it  in  St.  Martin's  Library,  where  it 
was  seen  by  Henry  Wharton,  who 
took  notes  from  it,  and  calls  it  MS. 
No.  1  in  Tenison's  Library.  Mr. 
Widmore  gave  19s.  for  it  at  the 
Chandos  sale  (in  ]  746) ;  it  was  No.  2283 
in  the  Catalogue,  and  was  described 
as  "  Flores  Historiarum,  written  on 
vellum."  On  the  17th  of  January, 
1763,  it  was  purchased,  for  five 
guineas,  by  Archbishop  Seeker  of 
the  Rev.  Richard  Widmore,  and  the 
Archbishop  bequeathed  it,  with  his 
other  books,  to  Lambeth  Palace 
Library,  its  present  home.  I  am  in- 
debted to  Mr.  Baigent  for  these 
interesting  particulars,  for  the  careful 
copy  of  the  extracts,  and  for  the  fac- 
similes.

[This  document  is  of  considerable  interest,  giving,  as  it  does,  a  much  earlier 
date  (1284)  than  has  hitherto  been  assigned  for  the  old  Cathedral  clock,  the 
more  recent  representative  of  which  still  occupies  the  original  position 
against  the  north  wall  of  the  north  tower-transept.  It  gives,  also,  the 
names  of  the  members  of  the  Firm  which  was  employed  in  casting  bells  for 
the  Cathedral,  and  was  intrusted  with  the  repairs  and  care  of  the  Organs 
and  the  Clock  in  Bishop  Quivil's  time.  It  belongs,  indeed,  to  Bishop 
Stapeldon's  Episcopate  ;  but  it  may  well  be  included  in  this  Appendix. 
When  Bishop  Grandisson  founded  his  College  at  Ottery,  and  reconstructed 
and  enlarged  the  Parish  Church  there,  he  made  it  what  has  been  truly 
called  a  "  miniature  "  copy  of  his  Cathedral  Church,  converting  the  tran- 
septs into  "twin  towers,"  in  one  of  which  (the  south  tower,  not  the  north 
as  at  Exeter)  he  placed  his  clock,  in  evident  imitation  of  the  old  arrange- 
ment.]

Spiritum  meum  commendo  meo  et  omnium  Creator!  ;  corpus,  vero,  meum, 
quod  corrumpitur  et  aggravavit  animam2,  volo  quod  sepeliatur  extra  ostium 
Occidentale  Ecclesie  Exoniensis,  ita  celeriter  sicut  fieri  poterit  bono  modo, 
non  invitaudo  parentes  nee  magnos  Dominos,  set  solummodo  aliquos  Epi- 
scopum  vel  Episcopos  viciuiores.     Et  volo  iiijor  tantum  cereos  circa  corpus 
meum  poni,  ponderis  uniuscujusque  xx  librarum,  ad  capud  unum,  et  ad 
pedes  et  ad  dexteram  et  sinistram.      Ceteri,  vero,  cerei,  quorum  quilibet  sit 
ponderis  unius  libre,  ponantur  bini  ad  quodlibet  altare  per  Ecclesiam,  et  unus 
remaneat,  et  alii  ecclesiis  parochialibus  in  Civitate  distribuantur.     Inhibeo, 
eciam,  sub  pena  offensionis  divine,  Potaciones  cum  speciebus  fieri  de  nocte 
in  choro  circa   corpus   meum,  set  fiant  si  oportuerit  in  Domo  Capitulari, 
vel  alio  loco  ad  hoc  apto.     Vel,  loco  talium,  Ministris  omnibus  de  choro 
presentibus  et  Psalteria  dicentibus  centum  solidi  communiter  distribuantur. 
Volo,  eciam,  et  lego  quod  eadem  humacionis  die,  centum  pauperiores  In- 
dumenta cum  Capuciis  habeant,  de  panno,  si  inveniri  poterit,  grosso  albo 
seu  griseo.

denarios.     Item,  si  aliquis  Episcopus  vel  Episcopi  venerint  ad  sepulturam

Memoria,  pro  animabus  omnium  Predecessorum  et  Successorum  meorum, 
Episcoporum  Exonie,  faciant  solempuiter  celebrari  ;  et  eciam  pro  animabus 
mea  et  ipsorum,  coram  se  in  Aula,  alioquin  infra  portam  forinsecam,  ubi 
tunc  fuerint  ipso  die,  centum  pauperes  pascant,  absque  fraude  et  favore 
eligendos  ;  quorum  quilibet  percipiet  esculenta  et  poculenta  ad  valorem 
unius  denarii,  vel  ad  minus  uuum  denarium  in  pecunia  numerata  :  et  qui 
hoc  legatum,  vel  hanc  elemosinam,  tarn  michi  quam  Predecessoribus  ac 
Successoribus  meis  comminus  auxerit,  augeat  in  bono  Dominus  dies  suos, 
et  post  banc  vitam  temporalem  tribuat  sibi  perpetuam  et  requiem  sempi- 
ternam.  Hoc  adjecto,  quod  quilibet  Successorum  meorum,  in  recepcione 
dictorum  bourn,  per  Literas  suas  patentes,  que  in  Thesauraria  Ecclesie 
Exonieusis  remaneant,  fateatur  se  dictos  centum  boves  ex  predictis  causis 
recepisse,  et  se  ad  faciendum  dictum  servicium  et  predictam  elemosinam,  et 
ad.  dimittendum  tot  et  tales  boves  in  forma  predicta  Successori  suo  obliga- 
tum  esse  ;  et  forma  predicti  legati  in  hujusmodi  Literis  obligatoriis  de 
verbo  iu  verbum  inseratur.  Et,  si  quis  Successorum  meorum  predicta  facere 
recusaverit  in  recepcione  predicti  legati,  volo  quod  dicti  boves  sibi  non 
liberentur,  set  quod,  iufra  mensem  tunc  sequentem,  per  Executores  tunc 
proximi  Predecessoris,  et  in  ipsorum  defectu  per  Decauum  et  Capitulum 
Exonie,  vendautur,  et  pecunia  hide  provenieus  per  eosdem  Executores,  seu 
per  Decanum  et  Capitulum,  pro  animabus  mea,  Predecessorum  et  Succes- 
sorum meorum,  in  pios  usus  distribuatur.— Quos,  quidem,  boves  fatemur 
de  ipsius  Executoribus,  Magistro  Ricardo  Coletone,  Domino  lticardo  de 
Brayleghe,  et  Domino  Thoma  de  Stapildone  recepisse,  ac  nos  tenore  Pre- 
sencium  obligatos  esse  ad  ipsius  Patris  Obitum,  secundum  ipsius  ultimam 
disposicionem  predictam  tenendum  ;  ac  eciam  centum  boves  Successori 
nostro  dimittendos,  preter  centum  boves  ut  premittitur  debitos  ab  antiquo. 
Et,  quia  in  Ecclesia  Exoniensi  predicta  jam  est  ordinatum  quod  die  Sancti 
Wulfranni  [15  Oct.],  quo  ab  hac  luce  fuerat  idem  Predecessor  noster  sub- 
tractus,  Obitus  ipsius  celebretur,  eodem  die  modo  predicto  tenere  pro- 
mittimus  et  celebrare  faciemus,  ad  ipsius  Ultime  Voluntatis  complecionem. 
Et  ne,  quod  absit,  premissorum  pereat  memoria,  has  Literas  nostras,  pro 
futuris  Successoribus  nostris  simili  modo  obligandis,  penes  Capitulum 
nostrum  Exoniense  dimittimus,  sigillo  nostro  signatas. — Data  apud  Chudde- 
leghe,  die  Martis  in  Vigilia  Festi  Apostolorum  Petri  et  Pauli  [28  June], 
Anno  Domini  Millesimo  CCCmo  vicesimo  octavo. 


VI. — Concerning  Bishop  Grandisso/is  Copy  of  the  Letters  of 
St.  Anselm. 

This  fine  Volume  is  preserved  in  the  British  Museum  among  the 
Cottonian  MSS.  (Claudius,  A,  XI).  It  contains  163  vellum 
folios,  which  measure  10  in.  by  6  in.  The  Letters  are  numbered 
in  the  margin  (apparently  by  the  Bishop  himself)  in  Arabic 
figures.  They  run  from  1  to  416  inclusive.  The  writing  is 
good  and  well  preserved,  and  is  arranged  in  double  columns 
throughout. 

Folios  2 — 7  are  occupied  by  a  Table  of  the  Letters.

THE   CARTULARY   OF   BUCKFAST   ABBEY.  1563 


FRAGMENT     OF     THE 
CARTULARY     OF     BUCKFAST     ABBEY. 

[Amongst  a  mass  of  waste  parchment  and  paper,  bought  by  Mr.  James  Pearse, 
of  Exeter,  from  various  sources,  was  a  fragment  of  a  parchment  book,  which 
once  formed  part  of  the  Cartulary  of  Buckfast  Abbey  ;  but  Mr.  Pearse  is 
unable  to  say  from  whom  it  was  bought. 

It  consists  of  twenty-three  leaves,  paged  from  iij  to  vj,  from  ix  to  xxiiij,  and 
from  cxlij  to  cxliiij,  all  inclusive.  Each  leaf  is  marked  at  the  top  in  red 
ink, — flltrria  }0ars.  The  leaves  are  written  on  both  sides,  and  comprise 
parts  of  two  Charters,  full  copies  of  sixty-three  Charters  (of  which  three 
are  duplicates),  and  copies  of  four  Perambulations.  These  Perambulations 
relate  to  the  Forest  of  Dartmoor,  to  Brent-moor,  Buckfast-moor,  and  South 
Holne-moor.  Along  with  this  MS.  was  found  a  Commission  from  King 
Henry  VIII  to  Sir  Thomas  Denys,  Sir  Philip  Champernoun,  and  others, 
dated  12  July,  1531.  They  were  to  inquire  into  the  bounds  of  the  Forest 
and  the  Moors  ;  and,  as  a  portion  of  the  rinding  of  the  jury,  as  well  as  the 
the  Charters  and  Perambulations,  all  relate  to  lands  in  Buckfastleigh  and 
Holne,  and  the  neighbourhood,  and  throw  light  on  the  bounds  of  the 
Moors  in  question,  it  would  appear  that  the  present  fragment  was  detached 
from  the  Cartulary  with  that  object  in  view.  And  it  is  to  be  feared  that 
the  subsequent  history  of  the  fragment,  and  the  fate  of  the  remaining 
portion,  cannot  now  be  discovered. 

No  mention  is  made  of  the  Cartulary  in  Dugdale's  Monasticon  Anglicanum,  in 
Dr.  Oliver's  Monasticon  of  the  Diocese  of  Exeter,  or  in  Mr.  J.  Brooking-Rowe's 
Cistercian  Houses  of  Devon  ;  and  the  present  fragment  is,  as  far  as  is  known, 
the  only  portion  extant.  It  dates  from  the  reign  of  Henry  III  (and 
possibly  earlier)  down  to  7  Edward  II  ;  and  it  gives  much  information  as 
to  the  early  history  of  the  Abbey  and  the  extent  of  its  possessions.  The 
names  of  some  of  the  Abbats  not  recorded  elsewhere,  and,  also,  of  some  of 
the  Priors  of  Plympton,  may  now  be  added  to  existing  lists;  and  it  records, 
also,  the  names. of  many  early  landowners  and  benefactors  of  the  Abbey. 

The  above  short  Preface  was  written  by  Mr.  Window  Jones,  of  Exmouth,  who 
had  acquired  the  MS.  from  Mr.  Pearse,  and  was  preparing  it  for  publication 
at  the  time  of  his  lamented  death,  which  occurred  on  the  30th  of  July,  1895. 
He  had  made  but  little  progress  with  the  work,  however,  and  had  copied 
only  the  Commission  of  1531.  I  had  promised  to  assist  him  ;  and  I  print 
it,  now,  with  the  kind  permission  of  his  Executors,  in  memonam.  I  make 
no  apology  for  including  it  in  the  present  Volume.  It  is  unique,  and  of 
considerable  interest  and  value  ;  and  it  comprehends,  though  (being,  alas, 
only  a  fragment)  it  does  not  cover,  the  whole  medieval  period. 

I  may  add  that  it  consists  of  four  folios  of  quaternus  iij,  the  whole  of  quaterni 
v  and  vj,  and  three  leaves  of  another  quaternus,  which  has  lost  its  number. 
The  numbering  of  the  folios  given  in  the  margin  belongs  to  the  Tercia  Pars, 
of  which  the  first  two  folios  have  perished .  At  the  foot  of  each  folio, 
throughout,  is  a  second  numbering  in  a  later  hand,  which  was,  evidently, 
made  when  the  Cartulary  was  perfect.  From  this  we  learn  that  folio  iij 
was  then  61,  shewing  that  58  folios  have  been  lost  at  the  beginning,  com- 
prising Prima  Pars  and  Secunda  Pars].

Instructions, — 

Fyrst,  where  {sic)  the  more  called  Sotheholnemore  be  parcelle  of 
the  mauer  of  Sotheholne. 

Item,  whether  the  more  called  Buckfastmore  be  parcelle  of  the 
maner  of  Buckfastleghe. 

Item,  whether  the  therde  more  be  parcelle  of  the  maner  of  Brent. 

Item,  if  the  sayed  abbot  and  his  predecessors,  and  other  free- 
holders adjonynge  to  the  seyde  mores,  oute  of  tyme  of  mynde 
to  the  contrare,  hafe  takyn  the  profittes  of  the  herbage  and 
agestementes  of  the  sayde  mores,  onetylle  now  of  late,  by  the 
space  of  vij  or  viij  yeres. 

Item,  yf  the  sayed  abbot  and  his  predecessors,  and  other  his 
tenans,  hafe  had  pasture  for  ther  catalle  and  bestes  yn  alle  the 
Kyngges  mores,  withowte  any  payenge  therefor,  tylle  now  of 
late,  as  is  aforesayde. 

Item,  to  be  knowyne  what  boundes  and  markes  there  be  by 
twene  the  Kyngges  seyde  fforest  and  the  seyde  mores,  for 
knowlige  of  the  seyde  mores  from  the  Kyngges  seyde  fforest.

Vevedictum  Juratorum,  — 
ffyrst,   we  agree   that  the  three  Mores    called  Sotheholnemore, 
Buckfast  more,   and  brent  more,  be  parcelle  of  the  abbotes 
maners  called  Sotheholne,  Buckfastleghe,  and  Brent. 

The  rest  is  wanting,  except  the  last  six  lines  which  were  written 
on  a  vacant  space  above  the  Commission,  as  follows, — 

.  .  .  and  bestes  yn  the  same  pasturyng  there  to  be  and  goe  yn 
quiete  maner,  withowte  any  furder  vexacion  or  trobelle,  accor- 
dyng  to  the  sayde  abbote  ys  title  and  interest  of  and  yn  the 
same,  or  els  unto  the  tyme  that  furder  direccion  or  determina- 
cion  be  had  thereyn.  And  the  sayde  abbote  and  his  sayde  co- 
vente  dayle  hathe  done,  and  soe  schalle  contynue  there  dayle 
prayers  to  God  for  your  prosperious  continuans  long  to  endure. 

Attached  to  the  Commission  is  a  copy,  written  on  paper,  of  an 
undated  grant  by  Robert  (son  of  William)  Kyllebury  to  Stephen  Ode, 
junior,  his  heirs  and  assigns,  of  three  messuages,  with  the  curtilages 
adjacent,  and  two  closes  of  land  formerly  held  by  William  ffynamore, 
Hugh  Mynchet,  and  Martin  Carru.  The  witnesses  were  Joel  de 
Buckyntone,  William  Boy  vile,  Henry  de  Budetone,  William  de 
Oulecombe,  Robert  de  Betehill,  and  others.  A  Stephen  Ode,  brother 
of  John  Ode,  is  named  in  the  fragment  of  the  first  Charter.  The 
writing  is  of  the  date  of  Henry  VIII ;  it  is  a  very  rough  affair,  and  the 
copyist,  being,  apparently,  unable  to  read  the  original,  left  several 
considerable  blanks.

[I  have  thought  it  well  to  give  this  Fragment,  so  valuable  as  an  unique  record 
and  so  strangely  saved  from  destruction,  exactly  as  it  stands,  with  all  its 
quaint  spelling  and  eccentricities  in  the  use  of  capital  letters.  I  have,  indeed, 
extended  the  contracted  forms  and  supplied  the  punctuation  necessary  to  the 
comfort  of  the  reader,  and,  in  some  instances,  to  the  clear  understanding  of 
the  text.  But  in  all  other  respects  it  is  a  printed  facsimile  of  the  original. 
It  may,  perhaps,  be  as  well  to  mention  that  where  the  letter  "  v  "  is  used  at 
the  beginning  of  a  word,  and  not  the  almost  invariable  "u,"  it  has  not  been 
done  per  incuricim;  the  MS.  has  been  closely  followed  throughout.  The 
Index  to  the  Fragment  will  be  found  at  the  end  of  the  Volume.]

INDEX. 


I  have  arranged  the  Index  in  divisions,  for  greater  convenience  of 
reference : — 

I.  The  Index  to  the  Institutions  ;  that  is,  to  the  contents  of 
Volume  III  of  the  Register.  And  this  Index  is  subdivided 
into 

(1)  An  Index  to  the  Benefices  in  Devonshire  included  in  the 

present  Diocese  of  Exeter  (which  comprises  the  Arch- 
deaconries of  Exeter,  Totnes,  and  Barnstaple). 

(2)  An  Index  to  the  Benefices  in  Cornwall,  the  present  Diocese 

of  Truro.  That  Diocese  is  almost  exactly  conterminous 
with  the  antient  Archdeaconry  of  Cornwall,  which 
always  included,  and  still  includes,  certain  Parishes  in 
Devonshire ;  viz.,  North  Petherwyn,  Werrington,  and 
St.  Giles-in-the-Heath ;  to  which  were  added,  at  the 
time  of  the  separation  of  the  Diocese  of  Truro,  the 
Devonshire  Parishes  of  Broadwoodwidger  and  Virgin- 
stow,  taken  from  the  Archdeaconry  of  Totnes. 

(3)  An  Index  to  the  names  of  the  Beneficed  Clergy  in  Devon- 

shire, with  references  to  the  Benefice,  or  Benefices,  held 
by  each  of  them. 

(4)  A  similar  Index  for  Cornwall. 

(5)  An  Index  to  the  names  of  the  Patrons  of  the  Churches  of 

Devonshire. 

(6)  A  similar  Index  for  Cornwall. 

II.     The  General  Index,  not  including  the  references  contained 
in  Index  I. 

III.     An  Index  to  the  Fragment  of  the  Cartulary  of  Buckfast 
Abbey.

1614         THE    REGISTER    OF    BISHOP    GRANDISSON. 

The  Institutions  were,  for  the  most  part,  entered  with  great  care 
and  regularity ;  and  few,  apparently,  were  omitted.  Some  of  them, 
however,  do  not  appear  in  their  proper  Register,  but  in  the  "  Registrum 
Commune,"  viz.,  in  cases  when,  Inquisition  as  to  vacancy,  the  right  of 
Presentation,  etc.,  having  been  held,  within  the  Rural  Deanery,  by  the 
Bishop's  Commissaries,  they  were  empowered  to  institute,  there  and  then, 
if  they  were  satisfied  on  all  points.  The  references  to  these  Institutions 
are  given  within  brackets.  In  the  cases  of  omitted  Entries  the  dates 
of  the  Institutions  are,  probably,  irrecoverable  ;  but  the  names  of 
the  Incumbents  instituted  occur  incidentally  in,  perhaps,  every  case  ; 
and  to  these,  which  have  been  carefully  collected  from  all  parts 
of  the  Register,  the  references  are  given,  in  their  proper  places, 
also  within  brackets.  It  will  be  observed  that  a  few  such  references 
are  given  between  duly  recorded  Institutions,  in  cases  of  prolonged 
Incumbency,  when,  the  name  of  the  last  Incumbent  being  omitted, 
it  seemed  helpful  to  shew  that  there  had  been  no  unrecorded  change 
in  the  interval.  Some  footnotes  have  been  added, — an  unusual 
feature,  it  may  be,  in  an  Index.  But  they  will  be  found  of  service 
to  the  Student,  for  the  explanation  of  difficulties  and  the  correction 
of  mistakes. 

It  should  be  remembered  that  there  were  many  Institutions,  Sede 
vacante,  after  the  deaths  of  Bishop  Stapeldon  and  Bishop  Berkeley, 
which  were  recorded  in  the  Register  of  Adam  Murimuthe  (the  Arch- 
bishop's Commissary),  preserved  at  Lambeth.  The  Entries  will  be 
found  in  Part  I.  pp.  18 — 23,  where  they  are  arranged  in  alphabetical 
order.

dates  are  so  close  together  ^9  March 
— 24  April)  that  there  is,  really, 
no  room  for  an  intervening  Rector  : 
we  must  read  "  William  Frellarde

1  Not  "  Branwell  "  ;  an  absurd  corrup- 
tion, which  I  am  sorry  to  see  has 
established  itself  in  general  use,  e.g., 
in  the  local  newspapers  and  even  in 
some  official  publications.  This  un- 
warrantable change  of  name  has 
actually  taken  place — I  know  not 
how — within  my  own  memory  ;  and 
I  take  this  opportunity  of  putting  on 
permanent  record  my  protest  against 
it.  The  Manor  of  Brannel  was  given 
by  Richard,  King  of  the  Romans  and 
pari   of    Cornwall,    to    Richard    de 


Cornubia,  his  natural  son  by  Joan  de 
Valletort,  widow  of  Sir  Alexander  de 
Okestone,  Knt.     The  Manor-house  is 
now   represented    by   a   farm-house, 
called  (of  course)  Brannel  ;   no  one, 
apparently,  having  thought  it  worth 
his  while  to  corrupt  that  also. 
Called   "  Elerky  "  at  the  time,— the 
name  of  the  Manor,  now  a  farm. 
Or   "Bossiney,"   as   it    is   frequently 
called  in  the  Registers. 
Erratum  in  the  Text,  here  :  for  Devon 
read  Cornwall.

Suffragan  Bishops. — It  appears  that  I 
am  mistaken  in  giving  this  title  to 
Bishops  who  had  Dioceses  of  their 
own,  merely  because  they  worked, 
from  time  to  time,  in  the  Diocese  of 
Exeter.  I  followed  Bishop  Stubbs, 
who,  in  his  Episcopal  Succession,  Ap- 
pendix V,  gives  a  list  of  sixty- three 
Irish  Bishops  "  who  had  permanent 
duty  as  Suffragans  in  Eogland."  It 
will  be  seen  that  Bishop  Grandisson 
simply  commissioned  such  Bishops  to 
perform  certain  specified  Episcopal 
acts  in  his  stead.     See  page  888.
